div.head: LADIES LETTER.
div.p: LADIES LETTER.

e DRAB NELLIE, What a lot of terrible weather we have had lately. Everything will soon be spoiled under the climatic conditions that have prevailed. Everywhere where there is any shelter is a pleasant refuge from the mirk and mud of the streets. There are always pretty frocks to be seen now. Many rows of etitchery—railway trim- ming, the French call it—adorned the gown that recently I saw with two little shoulder capes a frock of the new elephant grey cloth, worn with a pretty shirt. Just now a khaki-coloured dress, with encrustations of viclet panne and a toque to match is a combination of colouring that is very happy. Sable toques are now to be bought cheaply and these trim lap very %tylishly for the present season. The uprt bow of ribbon and cluster of violets is quite old in style and too general to be pleasing.

Many bodices show a deep chemisette or yoke of cream guipure lace over satin. This yoke is leor- dered with a scanty frill of the cashmere edged with narrow ribbons to match the skirt, and this frill forms small epaulettes at the top of the tight and very long cashmere sleeves. The oollarband of guipure on satin is very high, with a little stand-up frill of lace at the top, and the waistband Is a narrow one of amethyst satin, finished with a small bow. This dress would be useful copied in black cashmere with yoke of steel-beaded or jetted black lace over white or coloured satin. A good house-frock is made of chestnut-brown cashmere, and has one of the new skirts that are set into the band in groups of pleats, which are stitched down closely as far as the level of the knees, but thence are allowed to flPw loosely. The bodice is in itselt a simple full one, but is made stylish by a deep and handsome falling collar—shaped something in sailor style—of pale green tucked velvet, edged with a' 11 frill of cream lac, The sleeves have little cuffs to match the collitr.

It is said that amongst other fashionable tints for materials is that of toast colour, closely approaching khaki. In cloth and velvet it 00rn. poses a very charming costume, with toque in the same materials and colours. The cloth seams of dresses are now often piped with a contrasting shade of colour, and it seems as though piping were about to become as popular as it was some 10 or 12 years since. The shaped flounce round skirts are sometimes piped on—a very good arrangement, and one that an inexperienced dress- maker finds very convenient. Every skirt that have seen recently fits tightly round the hips, but lowa out freely from the knees downwards. Thy underskirts are usually finished with a deep, pleated frill in order to aid this effect.

The widow's cap has been diminishing in size, if nob in significance, for a long time. It is now a graceful little coif, with long ends at the back, and is a decorative addition to a charming head. strongly in contrast is it with the piece of head- gear of some 20 years ago as a widow's cap, which hid nearly all the hair, and could certainly never have been considered ornamental. In fact, its raison didtre seemed to have been the expression, on the part of its wearer, of utter indifference as to her good looks. But fashion has changed since then.

The importance of the health of the little ones is readily recognised and it should be remembered that uniformity of temperature is what they need in our miserable winter alternations of damp cold and dry cold. But what uniformity of warmch can be supplied by a garment that has merely a facade of cloth with a cotton apology at the back? The arms are one of the most sensative portions of the frame to the influence of cold and should be kept warm. True, the arms contain no vital organs. Still, a chill very often begins in the extremities. At the back, where a layer df cloth or flannel might replace the ineptitude of cotton, there are vital organs indeed. The lungs extend almost to the waist. Below it are organs which are only too susceptable to chill. The jackets for winter wear should be lined at the back with flannel, and whoever puts in this lining should refrain from cutting it too carefully away any- where. The motto of fond mothers should be "Let everything be of the warmest." Your loving JINNUL
THE MOST NUTRITIOUS.

div.head: NOBLER THAN REVENGE.
div.p: NOBLER THAN REVENGE.
4 BY ESME STUART,
A.uthor of "In the Dark," "Inscrutable," "A Woman of Forty," "Sara's Mother," &c.
CHAPTER XXIV.

The squire turned away wondering how he should do this work without being seen. He was not answerable for it, and he had no wish to be implicated. He was walking hastily towards the Hall when suddenly he heard footsteps behind him. He did not wish to look back. He was not far from the gate which opened on the path leading direct to the Hall. The steps approached; they were overtaking him. He could hear that they were manly steps. He walked faster, but he was certainly being overtaken. What was he afraid of? He had often met strangers in the road before. He was becoming utterly unnerved. "I beg your pardon," said a voice. Instinctively the squire turned, he could not do otherwise. He looked full at the stranger without saying anything. The stranger looked full at him. "I beg your pardon," he repeated. "Are you Squire Beauworth ? " "Yes. What do you want of me ? " "I am an amateur artist. May I make so bold as to ask leave to sketch your old Hall which I have heard is very interesting? " "I am sorry, but I never give leave to strangers to sketch. There would be no end of it if I once began." "I quite understand. Forgive me for troubling you." "No need," said the squire, turning away sharply. The stranger bowed and walked towards the village inn. Sir Harry looked after him. "What a fool I was not to make him say his name. A gentleman! Humph! A detective sent by Alec most likely! Well, let them come; I know nothing about his affairs." In spite of indifference, Sir Harry went to the village the same day to ask Babbitts if any stranger had been to the inn again. "Yes, sir, it's the same as came the other day. Dr. Murray he called himself. I don't know what 'e come for again, but he said something about sketching." "Has he gone ? "

"Yes, sir; he's gone." "If you ever take him in again, Babbitts, I shall turn you out. Do you understand ? " "It's plain enough," growled the landlord. "I don't want those sketching fellows, so I tell you once for all." The squire went off to his own house, but his brow was clouded; lie no longer saw life under a happy frame of mind. "So he came again, hang the fellow! What does he mean? How could I tell it was the same? Old friends, indeed! I won't have them coming about here. All the luck turned when Ruby went away. I always said she brought the luck, now I know it." He shut himself up again in his room; but this time it was to count over a hoard of sovereigns. He had been accumulating them a long time. "No, I'll hang on to the old place a little longer. Ruby might come back, and then---" When Arthur Murray reached his home he also shut himself up and studied old letters. The next day he went to see Ruby. "Do you bring me any news of papa? You promised to go and see him." He held her hand and looked at her sweet face a long time till Ruby laughed. "0 Dr. Murray, tell me what you are thinking of. That I ought to go back to papa? You tell me that every time you see me." "I won't say so to-day," he answered. "Are you happy, Ruby ? " "Happy? No! If I were with papa I should be happier. But I might find James Felton there and then I should be miserable."

"Is Mrs. Vernon kind to you ? " "Yes, very kind. She says lam not educated, and instead of being useful to her she makes me take lessons. Ido enjoy them, but I feel sure it costs money, and I want to earn my living and not to be taking expensive lessons." "It is no use interfering with Mrs. Vernon. If she takes an idea into her head it is fixed there."
"Have you heard anything of my Cousin Alec? He will be so unhappy." "No, Ruby. I have tried to find him, but up till now it is no use."
"But you did not tell me. Did you go to Yew- dale P"
"You must tell me something first. What is your first recollection in life ? "
"I remember my dear mother. We lived together in a small house in Brisbane."

"And your father? What did your mother tell you about him ? " "She used to say that he would come back some day, and she was always expecting him." , "But he never came when she was alive ? " "Never;• but when she died, then one day he came and took me to England,"..

"Yes, and what did hi; say ? " "That he had gone into the interior and that he had not come back in time to see my mother alive. He was so kind to me when I became good and left off crying. You know I love him, and I would never have left him if it had not been for that man. Oh, I could not, even for father's sake, see him again. Oh, tell me, did you see papa? Did you see my dear home ? " "Yes, Ruby, I saw your father at Yewdale." "But you did not tell him where I was? You promised." "I kept my promise. He would not see me or talk to me."

"And you say you are an old friend?" "Yes, I was an old friend." "He could not have known that. He always hated strangers." "Ruby, if your father was in trouble and wanted you, would you go to him ? " "Yes, I would go if-" "If your father's cousin was not there? _

"Ye; ; I will never marry him. Oh, there is Mrs. Vernon's bell. It is Pompey's lunch time." Dr. Murray laughed. "So you must not stay. But one word more, Ruby. If you had to give up—to choose between your father and—riches, what would you do ? " "I would go with him if he was in trouble and wanted me. Of course I would."

div.head: CHAPTER XXV.
div.p: CHAPTER XXV.

The squire went out late that evening ---c-vh-e—n he thought that no one could possibly be about, and he called up Bob to accompany him. "Bob, go and saddle Hero and bring the dog- cart round. You need not disturb anyone." . . .

"Yes, sir," said Bob, starting up, glad to be in movement. He was very anxious to hear about Alec, and not a word had transpired since he had taken him to the station, but it had leaked out that Mr. James nag hunting after him in London. Bob knew that this was most likely true. If Mr. James found him there was little chance for his friend. This time he would not be defeated. Bob had a plan of his own, and he had turned it over all day without coming to a decision. This evening he felt that the squire's manner meant something. It was very unusual to order out the dog-cart so late in the evening. Bob wished now that he had accepted Alec's gold. His plan was to go and find his friend in town and warn him that his enemies were on his track again. But how was he to get to London? He had the address, certainly, but no money to get there. His mother would not help him to go alone, for she would never be able to understand why Bob Bhould wish to go to a stranger. As Bob drove along he thought that, by hook or by crook, he must find Mr. Alec and warn him that Mr. James had not gone back to Australia. The squire was very silent. Bob could see that something was wrong with him. He got down at the post-office and went in. "You have a telegram for me not to be sent on ? " said Sir Harry. "Yes, sir; here it is."
Sir Harry tore it open. It was from James.

"Don't 'understand your letter. Come up to Victoria Hotel. If safe, bring Bob. I want a stupid lad. No news of It., but the other will be located in two days.—Felton." Sir Harry wrote down: "Will come first train to-morrow and bring Bob with me." Then giving orders to the .post-misNss that this was to be stmt the first thing in the morning, the squire returned to Bob. "I am going to see your father, Bob, and ask if he will let you go to London." Bob stared at the squire, as it seemed to him impossible news, being just the very thing he most wished for.
"Don't you understand ? " "No, sir; what am I to do in London?" "Do exactly what you a,r3 told, and do nothing more and nothin2 less."

"Father will let me go. tie don't care where I go, it's mother, she don't like my being away. she'll make a fuss." Bob was mucn afraid of appearing too willing to go, his conscience hinting that the squire was only laying a trap for him. "Your mother is of no consequence, and I am sure that your father will want you to do as I tell you; but remember that if you once disobey me or Mr. James, you'll live to be sorry for it." "Yes, sir I" said Bob, with a stupid smile, then he thought: "The devil ain't so cunning as I took him to be I Why, he might have guessed that I helped Mr. Alec out of that darned hole!" The Dog and Duck was quiet this evening. The squire called Babbitts out of the bar to talk in his private room. Mrs. Babbitts came out to chat to her son.
"I wish you'd come back, Bob, that I do! You never come here now."

"Squire wants me to go to London, mother. If you let me go, I'll do the best I can." "They'll take you into bad company, Bob, and what shall Ido then? You always was a good boy, if a bit obstinate; but London is a dreadful place." "No worse than this one, mother, and I shall see Mr. Alec. I say, mother, have you got a sov: I could take with me ? "

"I'll see, Bob, if you wait a bit. Have you heard anything of that poor young lady ? " "Hush mother, don't you say nothing; but I'll find her, never fear. Mr. Alec, he'll know. There's something up. The squire seems so strange, and was so angry about a stranger as come along here."

"It's all bad about here, and that's the truth. What shall I do if you don't come back yourself, Bob ? " Bob smiled. "I am only going because I'm too stupid to see anything, mother. I'll come back, don't you be afeared. Ods Daggs! I wouldn't live in any place but where you was." After this Bob's mother was comforted, and went off to see if she could find a sovereign for her boy. There were ways and means of squeezing money from the landlord, but it was not easy. When Sir Harry returned he seemed in better spirits, and informed Bob that his father had agreed to his going to London for a little while. Bob was cautious and said nothing, especially as his mother just managed at that moment to slip a sovereign into his hand, unseen by the squire and her husband. Bob took care to shew no signs of his delight. He didn't mean to be taken in again. The next morning he got up early, full of hopes that now at last he should be even with Mr. Alec's enemies, though how this was to be done he had no idea.

"If I'm wanted," thought Bob, "it's for some dirty work, and I'm not going to be turned into a sweep, no, not for all the Mr. Jameses in Australia. I daresay that he's a gaol-bird him- self, if it was only known. Ain't got to be proud of his doings, anyway. He's like father, much of a pair I should say." As the squire dashed up to the station with Bob and the coachman, the squire looked at his watch. There were five minutes to spare. "Don't let anyone into the house," said the squire, in a low voice to his coachman. "I don't know how long I shall be away. I have told Nancy to send Jane away, and you three must look after everything, just as if I was at home. Beep all the doors locked."

"And if Miss Ruby was to come back ? " said the old man, for all the household expected to see Ruby come back to her own home. "If she comes back, telegraph to me. Now, Bob, wait on the platform." Bob obeyed. As he did so he saw a little dog- cart dash up to the station. A slim man in a great coat got out, and also went into the ticket- office. The train came up and the squire gave Bob his ticket, and told him to get into a third-class carriage. Then Sir Harry followed the porter, who opened a first-class carriage door. "I wish to be alone," said the squire, giving the porter a shilling. The man with a great coat approached, but the porter opened another door for him and the train moved on. There were only two stopping-places. At first the slim man with the great coat got down, but just as the train was moving off, Bob, who was looking out, heard him exclaim:

, "I have left a parcel in the carriage." "Too late, sir, said the guard. "Then I'll jump in here," and the man with the great coat suited his action to his words, and almost tumbled into Bob's carriage. "I almost lost that parcel," he said, panting. "Are you going to London, young man ? " he said, looking at Bob. "I'm going where the train goes," said Bob, looking stupid. His companion examined him, and thought that this W,AS indeed a raw country yokel. "I suppose you are not going alone if you know no more about London than that? " he said, smiling. "I'm going with my master," answered Bob. "Your master is that gentleman I saw get in at the same time as you did? " "I don't know if he got in at the same time." The man smiled under his moustache. ' "Have you been long in service ? " Bob was on his guard. This was an uncommonly curious gentleman. "I don't know how long I've been cutting round; even since I was a tiny chap." "Not always in the same place?" "Yes, mostly. Father's so queer I had to manage somehow." The man hid another smile. "Where are you going to-day ? " "Dunno," said Bob, looking blank. "With your master? " , "Dunno ; I never asked and he never tells." "You are a trusting young man." "1 dunno," said Bob, blankly. ' "I suppose you know your master's name ? " Bob considered if he should answer this, but he could hardly get out of it. "He's called the squire." _

"Squire of Yewdale. I have been there." "Yes. Then you know," said Bob. "Ain't no use asking." There was nothing to be got out of this boy, and the man with the great coat hid his face behind his newspaper. When they reached London, Sir Harry hurried out, called a four-wheeler, and telling Bob to get up with the driver, they drove off to the hotel. When they reached it the squire told Bob to wait in the hall for him whilst he went to talk to James Felton. Bob was not going to shew any ignorance before all the sharp pigmies in buttons, who gave condescending squints as they hurried about with telegrams or messages. He neither expressed nor looked surprised at anything. He kept a sharp look-out, and drew his own con- clusions. He had hardly been five minutes in the hall when, to his surprise, he saw the slim man with the great coat pass into the hall. "He don't see me," thought Bob. "It's odd he has come here too. Wonder now if he is some friend of Mr. James, as wishes to spy on us, but he shan't." Bob was within hearing of the office, and he opened his ears. "No. That room has just been taken." "The next one to it will do." "But that is a double-bedded room. It's dearer." "Never mind, that will do. I may be having a friend to join me." As the gentleman hurried out he dame face to face with Bob. Their eyes met, but there was no recognition in the man's face. "Ods Daggs 1" said Bob to himself. "If he don't remember me half-an-hour after he's seen me, his memory ain't good, that's all, but he can't take me in. He's pretending. I'm not fine enough to be known here, that's what it is. Mr. Alec wouldn't have done that, I know." Bob was tired of waiting before James Felton hurried down and gave him a nod. Bob could not bear the sight of the man. He knew him only too well, but he must be on his guard. It was with the same stupid, uninterested look that he met Mr. Alec's enemy. "So you're come," he said. "Whatever has the squire brought you here for? " "I don't know, sir," was the answer. "It's the biggest show you've ever been to, I reckon." _ _
---'-A lot of streets ain't very different to one," said Bob. _ ___

"Oh, well, you'll see. You must try to use your wits, if you have any, and find your way about. I'm not going to pay for a private guide for you." "No, sir." "You've got to look sharp, that's your business." "Yes, sir." "Now listen, take this note to this address, and wait for the answer." "Yes, sir." "And don't talk to anyone. Just mind your business." "Yes, sir."
"When you have given this note they'll tell you what to do. Then come back here and you can have your dinner." " -- - .

div.head: "WOMEN'S CHAT."
div.p: "WOMEN'S CHAT."

The Queen who has always been distinguished for her kindly thoughtfulnees for others, has manifested in a very marked way her interest in her gallant soldiers fighting in South Africa. On several occasions she has caused application to be made to relatives of deceased officers for portraits of those who had been killed, and we now learn from a letter which her Equerry wrote to a brother of General Hector Macdonald, that the Queen is anxious to have portraits of the principal officers now serving in South Africa. Her Majesty has shown by several acts that ale bears her soldiers of all reeks con- stantly in mind, and this application for photographs is only one more example of the way in which she takes every opportunity of displaying ber gratitude towards those who are fighting for their Queen and country, or have fallen upon the field of battle. Apropos of photographs, it Las been estimated that at least sixteen theusand copies of the Princess of Wales are sold annually. Her Royal Highness usually poses her- self, a proceeding, needless to say, invariably attended with the greatest success. Every movement, every at- titude of the Princess's is gracefulness itself. One copy of each "sitting" given during the past quarter of a cen- tury, the Princess has caused to be preserved, and this collection has been formed into a fashion album. The dates are given on each photograph, and frequently patterns of the fabric of which tbe gown worn, was built, is fixed alongside. Her Royal Highness can by re- ferring to this album, see exactly how she dressed at any period during the past five and twenty years, and it is said she frequently has copied some or other little detail, contained in a one time favourite toilette. The young Duke of Westminster intends to follow the Duke of Marlborough in going on active service at the front. He has just returned from the Cape, but pro- poses to shortly leave again, to take some part in the war. The Grosvenor family is already well represented in this respect. Among the officers of the Imperial Yeomanry are Lord R. H, Grosvenor, and the Hon. R. Grosvenor, of the Cheshire Yeomanry. There are indeed few of the leading families who have not some of their members engaged in the war. There are come instances ie which the war and its politics are differently viewed in the same family. Mr. Courtney, who almost stands alone in his severe cordernnation of everything connec- ted with it, has feur repte;ws who have all recently volunteered for active service in South Africa. In Par- liament too we have the spectacle of Lard Edmond Fitz- maerice leading the attack on the Department for which his brother Lord Lansclowue is responsible. The County of Middlesex has just passed a new bye- law which will be much appreciated by cycliste when the weather improves, and it is possible to get about on the wheel again. This makes it a criminal offence to leave in the roadway " any piece of broken article of glass, or other sharp subetance, not being road ma- terial." In Germany, where the people rejoice in the blessings of a " paternal Government" it is an offence to throw waste paper or other litter in the streets,ntuch less broken glass, or dangerous material. In this country we are net so accustomed to have what we do or say regulated by law, but there is much to be said for the good intentions of the County Council of Middlesex, which are designed as much for the protection of the public, as well as for cyclists in particular. Among the various movements in the feminine world, which have been born of mcdern enlightenment, none is more important than the increased attentinn now de- voted to the subject of physical training for women. There was an exeellent display of what can be done in this direction, given at the Imperial Institute last week, by one of the Londc,n Gyrnnae.ic Training Colleges for women. This particular Institution has only been in existence for one year, but it appears to be well sup- ported, the students showing great efficiency in step- marching, club and wand displays, and other physical exercises. Systematic training of this description is now being taken up in all the leading girls' schools, and there is a great demand for proficient teachers. There are, in fact, few employments, to which women are now turn- ing their attention, which are so well paid as this office in the colleges, and principal educational establish, meets. The little may bolero,makes a delightful addition to a toilette, particularly just now. It affords an opportunity for a bright dash of colour, andwarmth just where this is needed. Many ot the very newest specimens are built with chort, round, plain sleeves, lightly fringed at the odee. A gown that hoe seen better days can be rendered quite smart and up-to-date, by a dainty lit tie addition Euch as this. Piping is again included in our list of trimmings, an item likely to be eepecially appreciated by the amateur dressmaker. Seams are en evidence piped with a con- trasting colour, and flounces are frequently laid on in a similar manner. A black gown piped with white id an extremely effective creation. Black and white are sure to be extensively worn at the forthcoming Drawing Rooms, as mourning is, alas, the general rule. Pauve promises again to take the place of velvet and brocade for trsins, indeed many leading mo- distes are using nothing else for this particular purpose, and chiffon is likely to no in greater request than ever. The sequin has at length taken its departure into the limits of dead and gone fashicns, and jet is once again restored to favour. - _
On a recent occasion a number of bands from the Northern and Midland etllnativ, gave a performance at the Albert Hall. Tiao promoters of the concert adver-

Used that it would prove a "revelation to the musical publie of London," who are accustomed to think they hear very good music from the military bands. Those who were present at the Albert Ball ,freely acknowledged that there was justification for the promise contained in the advertisement, and the occa,ion once more proved that there are some things in which the provinces are ahead of the metropolis. Mr. James Lowther recently denounced the practice of having floral decorations at funerals. We had, be said, got rid of the hearse drawn by six horses, plumed and draped, together with the long string of mourning coaches, with the crowds of mutes and persons in atten- dance. Much had been done to reform the Euperfluous pomp and aesoeiations on these sad occasions, but there had grown up the custom, which was almost a mania to indulge in an excess of floral decorations, and this Mr. Lowther thought was quite as much in reed of reform, as some of the old hideous formalities which had now disappeared. There is a good deal to be said for this point of view. There was something beautiful and touching in the simple offering of flowers gathered by a friend of the deceased, tut this sentiment has no place in the florist's shop,or in the plentatious display of costly blooms.
" DittADGE."

div.p: SOLVING THE LAND PROBLEM.

Twenty-five years ago an attempt was made in the village of Histon. near Cambridge, to solve the problem. how to make land pay in the face:of foreign competition? The country was then at one of, its educational epochs. We were being taught the vast food and health value of fruit. lecidentally, else, we were slowly gaining the knowledge that pure sugar, properly treated, was one of the greatest nutrients, in a small compass with which man has been blessed. Further that sugar and fruit in combination—when the latter is fresh, ripe and imcinus —makes a most valuable addition to our daily dietary, especially to that of children. So that at the time above referred to, the importance of growing fruit for jam and fruit flavouring was then attracting atten- tion. The firm gradually expanded until they are now the largest fruit cultivating jam and jelly makers in Great Britain. The watchwords have been ,pure and fresh material, with the most positive cleanliness in the inanu fscturing processes. And as Chivers' Gold Medal Jellies are prepared from the best obtainable materials, and as their delicious flavours are real fruit juices expressed by the firm themselves from fruit grown under their own care, we cannot wonder that Chivers' Gold Medal Jellies have the largest sale and greatest popularity. "Here is some money. You must tell me how you have spent it. After a few more remarks an directions Bob was sent off. He looked about NA wondering if he should see Mr. Alec in the streetad but he was soon bewildered, and realised that London was a huge desert of houses. He got mixed about the directions given to him, and paused often to think. At last he addressed someone just behind him.

"Will you tell me if this is the way to Carey- street ? " The next moment he was aware that he was speaking to the slim man in the great coat. "Ode Daggs!" muttered Bob. "I am going there; if you will follow me I will shew you the shortest way," Bob looked at the man's face. There was not a spark of recognition in it. Well, Bob wasn't going to say anything if he didn't, so he followed in silence. At last they reached a house where there Iva,-; a board put up in the hall. "Here you will find the place you are looking for."
Bob looked at his paper of instructions, and read the name on the board, "Heel and Chapman, Architects."
The man waited as Bob read the board. "You want the architects. Third floor, left- hand side."
"Thank you." "I am going there, shall I take your letter ? " "I am going to do my own business," said Bob. The man made no answer, but walked on before him.
When Bob reached the door it was already open. He handed in his letter, and was told to walk in and wait.
"I wish to talk to Mr. Heel. I will wait," said the slim man.

So it happened that Bob found himself again sitting in the company of the man who would not recognise him. When the office man returned, he said to Bob: "Tell the gentleman who sent you that the gentle- man he wishes to see has not yet returned, and we do not know how soon he will. You can come to-morrow."
"Is that ail? " said Bob. "Yes, that's all. We will tell you the address when we know it."

Bob said: "Thank you," and prepared to go. "Mr. Heel is engaged and cannot Jsee you, sir,' said the servant, turning to the gentleman in the great coat. "Thank you, it does not matter." Then Bob heard the man following him down— stairs.
"Don't know why he keeps a-dodging me, and it's time I did know."
When he got to the bottom of the stairs he turned sharp round upon the stranger. Bob looked formidable.

"Are you following me or are you not ? " "Following you ? " asked the man, looking:much surprised. "Yes, you came up with me in the train." "Are you the same? Bless me, I hardly looked at you! "Yes, you did," said Bob, "and you're doing it on purpose." He smiled at the boy. "London isn't like the country. One may meet some people we want or one may not." "I don't want you, anyways. Wish you good- morning." Bob ran downstairs and found his way horn. alone this time. He was so afraid that if he talked to another man it might again prove to be the man in the great coat. When he reached home, Mr. James met him.
"Well," he said. Bob gave his message. "Oh, you must go.everyrday. Is that all that was said to you? " "Yes, sir.

"Well, go and have your dinner, and for to-day I don't want you any more. You had better learn to find your way about town." "So I will," said Bob to himself. "I'll find Mr. Alec now, and warn him that that old gentleman is in town too."
(To be continued.)

div.head: RIGHT AFTER DINNER.
div.p: RIGHT AFTER DINNER.

If there is a time in the day's round whoa one ought to feel content and comfortable it is just after a good meal. If a man will lend you Looney at all he will do a when his stomach is full and his pipe going nicely. He inclined to be what we call "good," and tends to think his worst enemy more a fool than a deliberate fraud and liar.

The centre of the civilising forces is undoubtedly it tomach full up with first-dais fooa, tlia gastric juices distilling freely upon it, and the peristaltic movement mix;rig the whole into chvrne. Were it possible to maintain this gracious condition vamong rulers and Politicians,the Peac: Society might well go out of businesi. The lion would lie down with the lamb without being tempted to make a meat off the latter.

But, alas 4. so delightful a state of things implies not only plenty of excellent grub to be had cheap, but a perfect digestion. And that desideratum, sad to say, is exactly what we haven't got—except to a very limited extent.

There is such a tremendous lot of us who are com- pelled to talk as this woman does. "After meals," she says, "I had pain at the chest and back, sometimes to the very bottom of the spine. My fo3d lay in my stomach like an iron weight. It failed to warm me or stimulate me. In a little while a nasty gas would cnne up into my throat that would set my nerves all on end with J:liigust. Often I would belch up a fluid sour as vinegar and bitter as wormwood. "In hope of relieving this trouble I left off eating solid food and tried to get along on slops. This kind of diet, however, did not nourish me. I got so weak Ino longer walked, I merely crawled about. Even with the liquid food I bad awful pains and cre.mps in the stomach and occasional diicharg,s of blood from the bowels.

" For eight years I lived this vrt of life, a life hardly crnrthy the name. N)t one week of all that time was a lanppy week, for my infirmity was always with me. The j4y of eating at table in social converse with °there wag denied me, for to me eating was not a pleasure but rather an affliction. I need not go icto details. Every dyspeptic knows the horrors of such an existence. "In summer, what with the warmth and outdoor air, I might feel a trifle better, but when the dreary autumn and winter weather set in I was bad as ever. I saw one doctor after another and attended at the Chichester In- firmary, but no medicine did me any good. One doctor said my disease was ulceration of the bowels.

"In April of last year (1898) I real about Mother Seieel's Syrup, and was led to believe it might help me. I tried it. The first bottll did roe great good ; it made me feel much better. My food no locnger hurt me, I could eat with some relish, and digest without the old pain and distress. I kept on with the syrup and the complaint was gradually overcome. _ .M 7 atrength came hack and I was once more able to do my hnuaework. "1 am glad to say, truthfully, that I have not felt the slightest sign of my farmer ailineat since. The horrible thing is gone, and the credit of curing it in honestly due to Mother Soigel's Syrup. I 11.)ps if any women shall see these words in print, that they will believe them,and put foil faith in this medicine for any of the trouble our sex is so liable to, especially indigestion, constipation, and the pains and aches cauad 117 a dhordered stomach and liver."—(igned) (Mrs.) Loui3a Foord Ficketty Cottages, Thakeham, near nalborough, Sussex, May 4, 1899.

" F3r many years," says a7r;!..ler, " I was a marty to liver complaint and indigestion. I had .a bad taste in the mouth and little ryt3,3tfte. After meals I was all Ways unc anfortable. A sharp pain took me under the hcart and I was troubled with Palpitation.

"I usually felt dreadfully tired and heavy. At night my sleep was disturbed and insufll3iont ; I felt little better for going to bed. No treatment helped me until I began using Mother Soil' s Syiup. In a few weeks that cured me, and I am novean altogether different man."—(Signed) George Ferry, 24, Rogerson's Terrace, Croxdale, Durham, August 16, 1399. The man and women who cln alt a full and hearty meal and then sit iu comfo:t and peace while digestion it.utly dcoes its splendid work are not as numerous aer. they ought to be,but with every bottle of Mother Seigel' Syrup sent to the right place ong man will be added t he number.

div.head: PROPOSED PRESENTATION TO WARRINGTON VOLUNTEERS.
div.p: PROPOSED PRESENTA- TION TO WARRINGTON VOLUNTEERS.

Meeting in the Town Hall. There was an encouraging response to the Mayor's invitation to the townspeople of Warring- ton to assemble in the Town Hall last Thursday evening to consider what steps should be taken to accord the local volunteers a hearty send-off on their departure for South Africa. In the circular convening the meeting, the Mayor stated that the detachment,consisting of 58 men of the local volun- teers who had been accepted for active service would leave the Warrington Barracks in about three weeks from now. Ile believed that his fellow- townspeople were anxious to show their apprecia- tion of the men's devotion to their country by according to them a loyal and hearty send-off. It had been suggested that there should be presented to each man a pair of field glasses, which would not enly be extremely useful in alltual warfare, but b 3 a personal memeato of his native town. It had also been sugge4ed that a policy on the life of each volunteer should be eff.-xted in the sum of £lOO. It is estimated that to carry out both the proposals named, a sum of £2OO will be required. The chair eves occupied by the Mayor (Alderman 'Rob r ) and amongst these present were Mr. Pierpoint M.P., Alderman Wright, Aldermao Hutchinson, Coun- cillors Bennett, Roves, Shillcock. John Beane, Rees. Fathers Whittle and Wilson, Rev. J Yonge, Messrs. J Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Wll J Jenkins, R Draper, G F F White, F G Freser. G Venn, Dr Guest Gernall, E England, E 3 flall, W Crompton, Charles Plineton,R T Fairclough, J Clough, R Garnett, J E Seeker. fi 'dough. ton w s Howard and J Twiss. Letters were read fr en the following ladies and gentlemen in response to the circular ,e3nt out, all of whom:promised to subscribe : —Mr Leuis Voisee, Mrs Broldb2nt. Mr F Monks, Mrs W Fleteher, Mr Thomas Tenets'', Rev J hn Yonee, Major Bu kton, Mr Gilbert, Al 7. E M Crosfield, Mr Seger Oxen, Mr William Owen, Id: Travers Pickmere, Mr Robert Daviee, Mrs Litton, Mr J.itin Feirclpug,h, Mr Thomas May. Mr J Chariton Parr. Mr Z Armitage, Mr H M Ashton' Mr vere B Devise, Mr Atn:ur B Cresfield, Miss Bessie Dutton, the Rector (Cenen Willi!), and Mr John White. The Meerea said thole c3cs'ltuted the lettere he had received up o det,e. Becore anneuecine the subscrip- tions received perhaps he oueht to say a few words in explanation of the circular sent out. They tbiAlt not all ba aware that the actual allowance by the War 0 ffic e for the equipment of velunteers was slot conlidered sufficient for the purpose. No doubt from the War Office point of view for the regular army it might be considered sufficient. Some weeks ago it was intimated to him that it woeld be desirable to add some additional amount for the perpose of making the equipment:of their own eolunt?ers as complete as p.eoible. In view of the appeal before the public for the purpose of reliev- ing the wives and *the: dependents of the reservists be did not think it was desirable to make this question of additional equipment the subject of a special appeal and rememberine that the Corpora- tion had given to them a considerable sum of money by Sir Peter Walker, he (the Mayor) communicated with Mr. Henry Greene!' and asked him if he would ascsr- tain whether Sir Peter Walker approved of the appro- priation of such a portion of his gift as Might be necessary for the purpose of equipp- ing the Volunteers. He at once received a re- ply to the effect that Sir Peter Walker apvroved most cordially of the sugestion and hoped the fund would be at their disposal to whatever extent mieht be necessary. Re had very muck pleasure in making that announce- ment because it relieved them of some little anx!ety. -Therefore so far as the equipment of the Volunteers was concerned it was complete and from the source he had named. (Applause.) In addition to that it was con- sidered desirable that the gifts of woollen clothing which were sent out to such a liberal extent for the South Lancashire Regiment should also be made to the local volunteers and th se Would be provided by the ladies who took an interest in the battalion and t'-esir friends, (Applause) They now came to the question of what other means of a desirable and useful character could be employed to show the appreciation which they all felt of the action of their townsmen ache were going out to South -Africa. He did not need to say anything to them to commend their action. It had been the sub- •ject of admiration from the first day of their offer up to the present, and it had confi-med the old impression which had been characteristic of Warrington for so many,many years that as a loyal town Warrington had an superior in the United Cnzdom. (Hear, hear.) What- ever they might have done to help their reservists, their militia, or others, certainly they ought not •to come behind in the treatment of their own townsmen who were . doing this noble work at the present time. (Hear, hear.) He theught the best policy to adopt before deciding upon any course, Was to ennsult the military members of the Re!ief Committee who had been acting with him for so many weeks_east._ Th ret suggestion on the circular,

that of providing field glasses, Was made by the military men alluded to and was not the suggestion of a civilian. Remight :te that in the war between China and Japan every member of the Japanese army was supplied with a pair of field glasses and the utility of that equipment was recoenised immediately after the war com:nanced, and it proved to be of very great service. Then every fourth man in the Boer arm! was supplied with a field glass, and one could net read the papers and as a civilian try to appreciate the difficulties without coming to the conclusion that the British soldiers ought to be equipped in every respect with the equipment of their enemies. (Hear, hear.) Having the recommendation of the mili- tary memoers cif the relief committee and knowing that field glasses were found to be of considerable serviee and the further fact that there was no difficulty on the part of the War Oace authorities in regard to the carry- ' ing of this part of the 3oldi:,rs kit, which was borne out by the fact that the City of London volunteers were Provided with them, he hoped the suggestion would Meet with their apprehation. With regard to the life insurance scheme perhaps it. might have a gruesome ap- pearance, but- they had t face this crieetion in all its details and were bound to recognise the fact that some of those noble- men of whem they were so proud might not live through this campaign, and in that event surely it was not an improper thing to prepare for eventualities Which might occur. It was their duty as well as Privilege to make suitable provision for every wife and child who might suffer the loss of one near and dear to them. It was on these grounds which were senti- mental, but which, he thought were practical, that the insurance proposal was included in tho scheme. To accomplish these two objects about £2OO were needed, and towarde that amount promises had come in to the amount of £B2 15s. Eli. (Applause.) The largest amount sent in one sum was a stitncrirrion of £3O which had been handed to him by Councillor John Evans on behalf of himself and his business friends. It was a Very handsome gift, and pracfically made the proposal safe. (Heal, hear.) The suggestions made were not intended in any way to prejudice the better judgment of the meetine, and he would be glad to hear of any other suggestions. (Applause.) Mr. PIRRPOINT, M.P., sail he had very great pleasure Indeed in acceding to the request of the Mayor that he should open the discussion, though his worship had done it so admirably that it was almost a work of supereroea- tion for him to attempt to do eo. He need scarcely say that the present was an exceedingly anxious and momentous time in the history of the country and he bad simply to say Amen to the words of praise which the Mayor had used concerning their fellow townsmen who were giving their services for the Queen and their co•lntry. (Hear, tr:ar.l He was-sure that the feeling of the inhabitants of Warring- ton woeld be that net enly should these !nen he funs- equipped but if poeeible that they should be more than fullv eqeipped or At least equipped equal to any body of men which was helag sent out. He was very glad to hear the Mayor say that the War Office had not nisappreved of the suggestion which bad been made to previde field glasses and that if they were given the men they would be allowed to wear them and use them. In this matter he was prepared to accept the opinien of the military men who had suggested them for they who were civilians were not in the same position to say whether they were Rood or not. From histexperience of the use of a field Bins he would say that they would be of the greatest value. As to the insurance scheme there he bowed entirely to the opinieh of the Mayor. Re did Provide not think there was anything more advisable than to this insurance. He eincerely hoped that the pre- miums tenni( be paid but that there would be no benefit to anybode out of them. But whether there was a benefit or whether there was net they would have the satisfaction of knowing that they had done their duty towards the good friends who were going out to help them so many thousands of mile.; away. He would like to express his extreme pleasure to find that in these , anxious times party feeling, sectarian feeling and every other feeling had gone to the wall and Englishmen un- like any other people on the earth were standing shoulder to shoulder joining hand in hand, determined o_r see the matter through. (Applause.) Mr. t e W. H. J. JENKINS in referring to the proposal to provide field glasses, said his experience on the coast of Africa and in the Cape was that the reflection Of the sun's rays from the sandy ground greatly affected the eyesight of Englishmen, and ho should think the pro- vision of field glasses a very wise one. He thought the money would be raised with ont the slightest difficulty. Councillor BENT,TErr moved A resolution that the sug- gestions made in the circular convening the meeting be adopted. Both the sugeestions were good ones, and With regard to the one reeving to life insurance he did not think is was possible Le have any serious criticism of that part of the scheme. They were bound to face the contingencies and although they hoped every one of the Volunteers would come back unharmed, it was possible some might not. and in that case they would have done the best they could for their families if the worst happened. With regard to field glasses, that proposal corahleaded itself to him even more then the ether. (Applause.)

Alderman Wniour seconded the resolution re a mem- ber of the reliet comini,(es. He did not think it was possible to come to a wiser conclusion. Be had not the slightest thubt but that they would raise all the money required. (Bear, hear.) Mr. R. T. FAIRCLOUGIi said as an old volunteer he did not 13oliove the field glasses would be as useful as some people s2emed to think. When rivn were on a, long' march they did not want to carry anything more than they could help. They might be useful on short journeys but on long marches they would be very much in the way. Alderman HUTCHINSON was of opinion that in such an extraordinary country as that in which the war was raging field-glasses would be very useful. Mr. CIIA.RLES PLINSTON said he was of the opireon that the tisld glasses would be an incumbrancs but he was prepared to sink his own opinions in def-ence to the opinion of military officers. Hu , was greatly in favonr of the insuranea scheme, but he did not think a £lO9 premium was sutileieat. He would propoze an amenrnent that it be increised to £200..... . .

Mr. E. J. 13/3.7,1, pointed out that Major Rimington was itsuing an appeal for field glasses for the boly of men he was commanding in South Africa. With reference to the insurance it might be necessary to keep them in force for a longer period than was at preseat thought requisite, and we did not know at present whethrr more volunteers would not he required. Ho should like to c engretulate the Mayor on navine so favourable' inter-, prated the wishes of the town in expressing the desire to honour the Volurceers who were leaviug for Sea'ch Africa. (Applause.) The Ray. Father WHITTLE thought the Ceminittem might be able themselves to iacrease the premiu.n to £2OO in the event of any of tne volunteers being killed. Mr, DRAPER thought it was possible tO Olstain p olie:es which would cover won sling as well as fatal aecidente. In the event of a man being incepacitated from follesving his emplayment aterwards it „;would to necessary to make some provision for him. Tne MAYOR said the sugeeetion made by Mr. Draper was one which would be considered by tbe csinnaitt.!e. He did not know of any sunh policies but it was (Dice possible there might be some issued in the present Case. ,If so, it was desirable that they should b. 3 taken into consideration. . In regard to the suggestion to double the amount. that would depend on the response to the appeal. There were one or two little incidentals which he had overloeked. It was deslrable that they should at least provide as they did for the Militia bettalicre some- thing like £2O worth of tobacco and cigars when on board ship on their way to South Africb,. There might be other matters too. fie rejoiced equ illy witlfMr Pier- peint:in the united froet which the British nation presenred to the worli at tha present time. Their 'duty for the moment was to get rid of this war as quickly as possible and make such a job of it as would prevent a repetition of it for many years to exile. He thought as ho believed everyone in that room thoueht, that the British soldier was worthy of all they could do for him.' They had had in the repors which they bad read from day to day examples of courage and devotion and everytlaine that wee noble in the character of men such as the history of their own country did not include in its page'. There were some who Wiwi about the possible decay of Englishmen, bat we had not seen it yet and as long as the same spirit which animated the British army from one end to the other, was maintained we need have no fear of the future of the ceuetry of whited' we were all so proud. (Applause.) The reeelution was unanimously carried. The Mayor exhibited a handsome field glass which has been purchased specially for Captain Appleton, and the meeting signified its approval of the step talc '.II. 1 The MAYOR'S services in the chair were ackanwledgad on the proposition of Mr. Pierpoint, seconded by the Rev. J. Yong,e, and the meeting then terminated. The total amount already promised for this fu id is £1209i. . _

div.head: CAUGHT BY THE LEG.
div.p: CAUGHT BY THE LEG.
Strange Accident to a Carman.

South Africa has no monopoly of hairbreadth escapes, as is shown by a curious accident reported in the " Dunsley Gazette," which gives a portrait of the hero. A carter, named Re bins, living at Hillesley, near Woot- ton-under-Edge, went jute a wood for fuel, using a long stick aith an iron crook to pull down dry branches. Whilst standing in the stump of a tree and pulling at a branch.the crook straightened and he fell to the ground. with hie foot fixed in the stump, causing a fracture of the small bone of the leg and wrenching the ankle-bone. This happened two years ago. "For over six months I did net do a stroke of work," said Mr. Robins." as, although my leg seemed to be set all right, there woe always a large quantity of con- gealed blood round it, and on more than one occasion the doctor told me I must have my leg off. I did not , knew what to do, but declined to follow his advice, and trusted to Providence." "And so Providence did not betray your trust ?" re- marked the reporter. "No," was the reply. " When I was almost entirely broken down in health and hope from the fact that treatment in two hospitzle had not cured my leg, a book came through the posttelling me of the many wonderful cures Dr. William: pink pills for pale people had brought about Though I had tried other medicines without any effect, I thought I woul-I give them a trial, so I purchased a couple of leeses. Of course the broken bone had long since uni'e ; I should not have expected medicine to effect that. It was the subsequent pain I could not get rid of, but before I had takea one box ful of the pills named I was stronger Ira myself. my leg was better, and the palpitation of the heart which I had been suffering from quite disappeared." Mrs. Robins her joined in the cenveaation, remark- ing: "Mrs. Cox, of Box well Lodge, recommended me to indece him to try them, as she had found them so valuable herself." The good wife also related with evident excitement that, after having taken three boxes of Dr. Williams' pink pills, her husband one day came in and danced round the house, shouting," Good old Dr Williams ; he has cured my leg and put me right." "He quite frightened the children," continued Mrs. Robins, ace after that he continued to take the pills, saying he would have his pills if be didn't have bread. He took six boxes of Dr. Williams' pink pills ,altogether, and I now give them to my children when they are not well." It is net, of course, suggested that this remedy is an alternative treatment for the surgeon's art ; the lesson taught by the above incident is the same as that learned , by thousands of people in broken health, who have had- their whole after-lives changed by this simple medicine. Ire Mr. Robins' case Dr. Williams' pink pills restored tone to the nervous system, and enriched the enfeebled blood. Acting the same way, these pills have cured thousands of cases of anretnia, general weakness, loss of appetite, palpitation, shortness of breath, early decay, all forms of female weakness, hysteria, paralysis, locemotor ataxy, rheumatism, sciatica, serefula. rickets, chronic erysipelas, consump- tion of the bowels and lungs. 'these pills are tonic in action, and are not purgative ; but they are genuine only with full name, Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people (seven words), an are sold by most retailers, and Dr. Williams' Medicine Company, Holborn Viaduct, London, at two shillings and ninepence a box, or six boxes for thirteen and nine, post free. They invigorate ,he system after overwork, warry, and indiscretion of

Warrington Y.M.O A.—Annual Meeting. The annual meeting of the Y. A.C.A , was held in the Lecture Hall, on Friday evening lett week. The chair was taken by Mr J C Parr (president), who was supported by Mr R Pierpoint, M.P., and Mr J Fairclough (vice-presidents). After the meeting had been opened with prayer, Mr A E Windle read tbe report for the past year, which showed that the association had been doing a good work and has in- creased its membership —The Chairman in moving the adoption of the report, said the past had been the first fall year of working under the auspices, if he might so express it, of their energeic Secretary, Mr. Windle, and he was sure they would agree with him when he said he had given the most complete satisfaction. (Hear, hear.) Not that the statement of their financial position was altogether satisfac- tory. They were no: pleased to see the deficit so large asit was (1156 17s Bd),but it showed:improve- ment. They would observe that the main item, members' subscriptions for 1898 was .£23 103 3d,and for 1899, £4l 25., a net increase of £22 8s 3d. (Ap- plause.) Remembering the old saying that" when the night ie darkest, the dawn is nearest," he be- lieved the darkest hour for the WarrinetenY.M.C.A. was past, and that dawn was near. (Hear, hear.) He should be sorry to let the opportunity slip with- out paying a tribute to the ladies who bad so assiduously helped them in their eff efts and who had made up their minds that the place shall be clear of debt. He would like to impress members with the necessity of self-help. They must also work hand in hand and do what they could to pro- mate the interest. of the association. The member- ship had increased, was still increasing; bat re- doubled efforts were still necessary. Ultimate suc- cess rested with them individually, net only with the trustees, or Managing Committee, but with each individual member. (Applause.)— Mr John Fairclough in a few well chosen remarks seconded the adoption of the reports,and the motion was carried unanimously.—The following officers ware elected :—President, Mr J C Parr: hon. treasurer, Dr J Guest Gornall ; bon. auditors, Coun- cillor Arthur Bennett and Mr J Proctor Jones; com- mittee, Messrs 11 M Aehton, W H Bayley, J Bile- brough, W Clegz. S Pay, F Garside, A Griffiths, W Hickman, .T 'Rotten, P Johnson, A Jolley, H T Kane, A Pitt, S B Stringer,ll Taylor,and It Wyllie; general secretary, Mr Albert E Windle. The trustees are Messrs J C Parr, John Fairclougb, A H Crosfield,and E Garnett. LINSEED COIIPOUND ' for Cough 3 ar I CJId s allays irritation. Gives immediate relief.—Advt.

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 2, 1900. NOTES ON GAMES AND RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT ATHLETICS. COUNCIL.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 2, 1900. NOTES ON GAMES AND RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT ATHLETICS. COUNCIL.

The usual fortnightly meeting of the abave Council, was held at the Workhouse, Dutton, on Tuesday, when there were present:—Mlsrs Joseph Eno wles (chairman), J M,seley Williams, C E Li raker,W Fletcher, T Wright, J B Chadwick, Admiral Jones Parry, .0 Roylance, James TuJor, J Stokes, T Darlington, E Clarke, Joseph Whit- low, J G Kydd, T Lewis, W Bradford, S Horton, J W Baugley, J Spruce, Joseph Mounfielel, Joseph Nickson. with Mr George F Ashton (clerk), Mr W G Hough (as- sistant clerk), Mr Jarms Farrington (inspector), Messrs W Diggle and J Swinton (surveyors), and Dr J Adams (medical officer).

, SOME OBSERVATIONS FROM THELWALL PARISH COUNCIL. Mr. W. B. Cook, clerk to the Thelwall Parish Council, wrote st ting that the Parish Council considered the at- tempt to improve the drain at the corner of Waste lane to be unsati: factory and they r quested that the sur- veyor be instructed to put it in a satisfactory etete of repair. They also desired to draw the attention of the District Council to the fact that nothing had been done to improve the footpath in the village, the pebbles o! wide!' were requested to be taken up. Neither bad any- thing been done to the road at Maeeey Brook Hill. They wisbed to point out that tee . Lymm Urban District Council was repairing the road on the Lyrnm side of the brook, and they thought that the Tnelwall sicie should also be repaired. The attentiou of the District Council was also requested to the state of the "sign posts" in the parish which in their opinion required painting and re-lettering. The Parish Council t.u-sted these matters would receive favourable consideration In a subsequent letter Mr. Cook wrote: "In consequence of the oat- break of diphtheria:in tha villige the Parish Council I would like to know if the Medical Officer of Heelth and the Sanitary Inspector et 3r visited the village, and if se when ?" The Clerk was instructed to reply and point out that the Medical Officer and Inspector had visited the parish as recorded in their reeves Irene time to time. THE PROPOSED WIDNES AN() RUNCORN BRIDE. Messrs. Alsop, Stevens, Harvey, and Crooks, of 14, Castle-street, Liverpool, weote, as follows under date 26th January :—" We enclo io a eient of the above bill i which is being promoted by a committee of which Sir John Brunner is chairman, for the coustructien of a Transporter Bridge acresa the river Mersey at Runcorn in order to afford improved communication between the adjacent poreions of Cheshire and Lancashire. The pro- posed brier would supply a want which has long been felt, and they believed that the scheme was one wh:ch would be heartily weleemed by the inhabitants in your district. The scheme. however, "is likely to receive oppesition from vested int >rests. and the promoters wish to be in a poertion to satiefy Perliement that it is supported by the local authorities chiefly interested. We shall be obliged if you will bring the metter before yoar Council, and we trust they will see their way to pass a resolution approving of the scheme. We shall be happy to afford any information reepecting the proposed bridge iwhich your Cennci* may desire.' The matter was delegated to the Parliamentary Committee.

TAR WESTON WATER SUPPLY. Mr. James Collier, clerk to the Weiton Parish Council forwarded the following copy of a reso' tit:ion passed at a meeting of That body .n Fri iav nieht :—" That the Clerk of the Parish Council write to the Clerk of Use Runcorn District Council, (-tiling attontion to the fact, that a considPrable number of houses in Weston are short of a sufficient supply of water, and to ask the Council to take action in the matter. Mr. J. Farrington yid as a result of his eramination of the village he found there were 51 hou,es with an insufficieet water supply. The reasons given for the defective supply were that the mains were almost cor- roded up. the n, xt was the Water Company did not pump sufficient water, and the third was a very bad season, that they had not the pump. (Laughter). Mr. Tudor and Mr. J. 11. Chadwick sum:ested that the Council should approach the Runcorn Urban District Couocil with a vies of getting a composite committee of that body and the Weston Parish Council to cons:der the matter.

This course was agreed to. THE SURVEYORS' RAI" 'MIES. The Clerk ropor,ed that the lighway Cont:nittee had met. The question of the price of a steam roller was deferred. The applications of the surveyors for increased salaries had been canaidered and dele,gated to a sub- committee ; and the question of engaginz Mr. Swinton as clerk of works was deferred pending further in- quii THE LIVERPOOL CORPORATION MILE BILL. The Clerk in reply to Mr Linaker intimated that a copy of the proposed Bill of the Liverpool Corporation had come to hand the previous day. It was decided that the Parliamentary Cammittf,e should take the mater into consideration.

Efe wanted to be ante to hold the Medical Officer with someone else responsible for those cases. Whilst at pr sent they could bold no one responsible. STOCKTON HEATH AV, THE NEW RAILWAY. 17, Cliffe View, Stockton Beath, 25th January, 1900.

George F. Ashton Esq., Clerk to the Runcorn Rural Distsict Council. Dear Sir,—At a parish meeting held on the 11th inst., the following resolution was unani- mously adopted, " That this meeting of Ratepayers of Stockton Heath Pariah consider the scheme for the pro- posed Warrington and North v:ich Light Railway to be objectienable on many grounua, particularly on account of ths narrowness of the roads which ought net to he used as a railway track, and alsl that the draft Order is dsfective in many respects, and the meeting hereby calls upon the Parish Council to repre4tine such objections and defects to the Runcorn Rural District Council, the County Council, and to the Light Railway Commis- sioners." Enclosed I send you a list sf principal objections and suggestions of this Council, which in con- sequence of the attitude taken by your Council will have to be reported at the inquiry. The Commissioners have expressed their willingness to hoar the case for the Parish Council. Yours truly, EDWIN BRADSHLW. OBJECTIONS AND SUGGESTIONS OF THE-Pififcff

div.head: Rugby Football.
div.p: Rugby Football.
[By "Oval ist."]

Runcorn got one step nearer the caveted cup on Satur- day at the evpente bf Warrington—that team from which so nsueh was hoped earlier in the seasoa. The boys in green soon proved themselves mast,rs of the situation and from start to finish they easily held Warrington in check. There was a goodly crowd present—in fact it is quite remarkable how the people turn up regularly to watch Warrington perform in a fashion fit to make the Gods weep. Some of the" pates "have ben a bit less than last year, but Saturday's total of 00 was consi- dered a satisfactory harvest. Oae or two hundred people came from Runcorn, gni they made thekr presence evi- dentteluring the course of the game.

There ot breezl and Runcorn had tl-e good fortune to win the toss. That they selected the best attacking position goes withriut saying, and by goed bunting aad following up soon had Warrington defend- ing strenuously. Sundry failures weie chronicled and then Faulkner wade emends by scoring smartly near the corner. The try was a good one, though unexpected, and demonstrated the vertu's ability to make the most of stray chances. Very soon afterwards Harris made a sad bungle in the Waarington quarter and prosented the green-jerseyeal forwards witu a chance which they quickly turned to accoue: After a retali.tory effort or two est Warrington's part the Cheshire men had another slice of luck. Jones, who was none too reliable at full neck stumbled and missed his catch, Faulkner the watchful getting a walk-over behind the posts. Jolley enhanced the point by a goal. At half-time Warrington were in the enviable position of having to give a better team 11 poiats start in the second moiety.

Notwithstanding several curtain lectures from in- dividuals in antbority and souls who were not, the War- rington men chapel no better when they had the big advantage afforded by the wind. Their kicking was poor, their tactics were bad, and their whole display wretched in the extreme. Had the men only shown seene'ot the dash displayed against Swinton the deficit of points would have been lessened, but they showed no disposition to exert themselves more thais enough to keep off a shivering fit. They ought to be ashamed of them- selves. That they could have done better was proved at Runcorn, when they only lost by a try with a much weaker team. It was all right for Runcorn however. They defended coolly and easily, occasionally making raids into the Warrington half, where Fish generally barred the way. Their win was well-deserved, and the score jest about demonstrates their superiority on the day's play.

Runcorn struck me as being an excledingly strong and well-balanced team, but with a better defence than attack. Indeed for defeusive tactics, the " Linnets " would require a lot of beating, hut their attacking powers are ant at all out of the ordinary. Yet the backs can all be relied on, and with the exception of Wilkin- son there is no weakness apparent. Forward the advaa- tage over most teams will be apparent at once. The front rank are both speedy and strong, though they tf,ek vary lictle out of the Warrington lot. A really speedy, clover wing man would he an acquisition to Runcorn. How would Fish suit the Linnets ? Some of them say he is too-good for Warrington.

Iliought3n played as well as ever on Saturday, but he still shows a tendency to play for the gallery, and this met with its own punishment. There was no need for the ex-Internationa,l to indulge in a sprint on one occa- sion, and by doing so he rot upset in a fsshion which m.de him pull sev.tral ugly grimacEs. There vr,a no- thing commendable either in t,le way he kicked tr. :ouch with a smile of &limn whenever Warrington bare down on him. .1. Buttervorth was the best of the three- quarters, and Faulkner the smartest at half-back. Butte played the game, and the same may ha laid of the rest'

On the Warrington side there were seweral non-triers, and a 3 many more ont of cnutition. Training rulAs and even temperate tivime; are sad!y neglected if what I hear is true. Fish WU the hest back by far, Burgess and Isherwomd comine next. Tb. 3 Committee made a mistake in taking Jones off the wing. He and Smith were very strong together, though the latter is playing badly at present. Forward and half back there is room fora lot of in3prevement, and the chances in the cup ties appear far from rosy, the deterioraion [139 bzeo so great here.

Warrington have not VVOI2 evea a home match in the Llncashire League for three months! Think of that. Whim NVPre things in such a state ? The last two points Warrington ~ot at Wilvierspo,l were at the expetEe of Tylde3ley on October 20.-h, 1899. Five home matches have been lost in succession, and only three won away in all 0113 time. It is evfm worse than I thought.
The Lancialairs League table up-to-date is as fol-

There was a peculiarity abut the three-quarter line last S,turday. which may not have hem noticed by my readers. If they look at the names of the players telow they will " see the pit." F ish. I sherwood. S mith. H arris.

--- To-day Warrington go away from home, and nerhaps they may do better in consequence. Certainly the team has played worse at home than away this season, and if all are triers they may astonish the Rangers at Bronghton. Drastic changes have again been made in the teirn and this week I am inclined to think they are an improvement Die most important event is the reappearance of the skipper, " Smack " Bate at half back in place of Allen. Bate's experience and generalilf p has been sadly missed of late and he should strengthen the back di7ision con- siderably if he is anything like fit. Hallam takes the full back positien, Jones returning t 3 the right wing, while Morrison and Antro'ius replace Hatton and Fair- hurst in the forwards. Antrobus is a Runcorn youth, and comes from a place where good forwards seem to grow like grass.

Broughton Rangers won at Warrington by a try to nil, and I should very much like to see the score reversed to-day. Without the formidable Jackson the Raneers are not one whit better than Warrington, f the local lads only play as they know hew, and not carelessly as of late, they ought to turn the tables on Om burly foes. Perhaps it is to much to hope for, but I fel sure the team is capable of doing it if they try hard enough.

Harriers. rho Sankey club had Farnworth Harriers (VVidnes) as visitors on Saturday, to decide their second inter-club race of the season, the one previously being won by Sankey by 12 points. The pack of 36 runners, compris- ing la of Sankey and a like number of Farnworth,turned out from the Sloop Hotel, Liverpool-road, and wont at a good pace. J Hosker (Farnworth), last year's Northern champion, took the lead after traversing about three miles, and maintained it to the finish, and ultimately woo an exciting race by thirty yards from Jack Riley : George Eastwood (both of Saukoy) finishinz third. The teams finished in the ibllowing order :—Sankey, Jack Riley 2, George Eastwoo3 3, T Devlin 5, Len. Green 7, R Throssell 9, J Wilding 13-39 points. Farnw-rth : J Flosker 1, Li7htfoot 4, Jones 6, Fallon 8, Ratcliffe 10, Cadman 11-40 points. Sankey just won by one solitary point.

Heathside Continuation School. On Monday evening a lecture upon" nalces!' was given to the students of the above schools and a number of elder day school scholars by Councillor Linnxus Greening, Amongst those present were Councillor A J Jolley, (representing the managers), Mr. J %V Faker (headmaster), Messrs. T Edden, F J Emson, A Malcolm,F Longshaw, and Miss Foster members of the teaching staff. The lecture was illustrated by a splendid set of 80 slides. The heads under which the lecturer spoke were as follows : Snakes, their place in nature" ; " Tiow snakes came to be snakes"; " Anatomy of Snakes"; and " Life and habits of snakes: Councillor Jolley, who presided, in proposing a vote of thanks to the lecturer, referred to the splendid collection of snakes, supposed to be the finest out of London, recently presented to the Museum by Ml,Greening. —Mr. Parker seconded the vote,which was heartily carried.--Mr. Greening, in replying, announced that he would give a book to the boy who wrote the best ei•say upon the subject of the lecture.—A , -tote of thanks was passed to the chairman.

div.p: COUNCIL.

(1) The Parish Council will challenge the description of the railway, and are not satisfie that the same will not be dangerous to vehicles, bicycles. etc. (2) The ra:ish Council object o steam being us las a motive power. (3) That the words " Local Autherity " and '• Road Authority " should include Parish Councils se far as Stockton Heath is concerned on the ground that the population of Stockton Heath is so large that Urban powers ought to be delegated to it. (4) That in eiseb and every eve where seven or fourteen days notice is mentioned the words "two calendar mouths " shall be substituted. (5) That the words " sewers end drains " be inserted to follow the words '' wires and apparatus "in sectiou 38. Sub section 2 (B). (6) That in section 43 the words " end Sir Ile- ton Heath Parish Council be ioserted after the words" Urban District Council of Northwich, that the words" truck or waggon" b inse.ted after the wo:d " carriage" in the second part of the section and that the letter "6 " be added to Council in the sub-section to section 43. (7) That a light shall be placed on each side of efech vehicle and that restriction shall ta? placed on the number of trucks to be used and that the words "or truck ;* shall be inserted after carriage in the second line of section 48. (8) That all section 63 after the end of the litia line be eliminated. (9) That the rates for carriage are excessive and should be considerably reduced. (10) That the roads in the 'Parish tube traversed by the railwaY should not be less than 40 feet from kerb to kerb. That 60 feet footpaths should be provided and"that the pas- senger line should rine down the centre of the road. (11) That gc ads traffic should be diverted at London B idee and not be allowed to run through the s'reets. (12) That the Ceenel shall be consulted as to the position of loops, sidings, and depots. WIDENING OF THE RAILWAY BRIDGE AT WALTON. _

Messrs. Heenan and Frnude eng.c: •3 and railway Contractors, Preston, submitted a tracing showing the proposal to widen the viaduct over the river Mersey at Welton for the L. and N. W. Railway Company. It was nscesiary for them to lay a temporary lino across the road on the South West side of the exiting bridge. This will not interfere with the small amount of traffic on this road, as it would be a level crossing. They trusted the Council saw no objection to this. Tbo Clerk intimated he had wriran for some further plans necessary for tbe consideration of the above, but they had not come to hand. It was decided that the mat•r be left in the hands of the Clerk to bring before the necessary Comtnittce when the infernaation was to hand.

div.head: HALTON WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: HALTON WATER SUPPLY.

Mr. Farrington reported the result of the analysis of the Halton Water supply as received from Professor Smethem, of the Lancashire Royal Agricultural Salley, and supposed that the matter would be forwarded to the Parechial Committee for their consideration. Mr. T. Wright obseived that the analysis was a very satisfactory one. Two samples had been taken one from the mains and one from the reservoir, and although Pre- lessor Smethem did not know the soure,m of those samples, be had testified they were idemical Showing that he knew something about his work. The analysis was most satisfactory and the people could drink the water without fear. Dr. Adams called attenticn to the high percentage of mineral matter which was given. filet would no doubt account for the peculiar taste generally complained of, though it was satisfactory to observe that Prof. Striethem's b.icterialogical examination had resulted in showing there was an entire ale-ience of disease producing baetella. Mr. Fariington added that he had compared tho analysis with several of those previowily oblained from Dr. BM, and they seer*ici to coincide very much:

A meeting. of this Board Wa 9 held in the Board Room at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Mr. A. J. Jolley presided and there were also orasent : Mrs. Clay, Rev. W El Drummond, Messrs. _ ABSEN r MEMBERS.—NO r GONE TO THE WAR. The CHAIRMAN, at the commencemeit of the business, said he was sorry there was such a small attendance uf the members, but it was not due to them beicg at the seat of war but to sickness. The Clerk was one of those who was:unable to attend owing to illness. air. HOUGHTON said he had heard that it was safer to be at the seat of war now than in England. (Liughter.) It was far pleasanter beiag in South Africa than in Eng- land. The CHAIRMAN: I did think of volunteering myself. It is so nice and warm out there. (Renewt,d lav7lltn.) A later was read from Mr. Monks (treasurer of the Warrington and District Nunilog Association) asking for an increased subscription to the Association owing to its increased work, two additional nurses having been engaged. The Rev. %V. 11. DREMIOND supported the application on the ground that the work had much increased, especi- ally amongst the poor, who were the peop'e who would bs claiming relief from the Guardians. Toe association was doing a work which was saving the Board money ; six nurses instead of four wore now at work, and there was a prima facie case for an inlreased subscripLion. He thought as a matter of economy that it paid them to support the Association. seeing' that it took up cases and proventc I them from coming Upon the Guar- di. ns. Tri,l CLEak ruled that notice of the proposed increase would have to be given. ; Mr. EIOUGIITON What is the amount proposed ? . _

_ Mr. FILLING: No amount is stated. The CLERK replied thac two years ago the amount was fixed at £lO, and now Mr. Moak. asked for that amount to be iooreassd, and gava his reasons The Rev. Mr. FICMCIFITON thought that what was g:ven to the association ought to be given by the Town Cluncil. ' Although the country parishes of the Uniori subscribed to the association, they had no chance of receiving any benelit from it as its op3rations were confined to the borough of Warrington. The CHAIRMAN suggested that it would be better to discuss the matter when .the proposal we: brougut for- ward. It was deeded to inform Mr. Monks th it a proposal to increase the amount would elle considered at a sub- equent meeting. 'ME FLOODING OF HE WORKHOUSE CELLIR3 . At a meeting of the House Cenamittee the Maser WAO directed to consult with Mr. Owen as to the desirability of altering the drainage syeetri. 'defects of wnieo re- cently caused flooding of the cellars. The CHAIRMAN in moving the confirmation of minute, asked the Beard to empower the committee to at on Mr. Owen's report ',nen releived. It was decided to empower the cotnnaittee to take what action was necessary.

The CHAIRMAN proposed that the communication lie on the table. Mr. PILLING said he believed that the fees fixed were only done so experimentally for twelve rnenths. It was understood that they should go into the matter again at the end of the twelvemonths. He pro osad that they support th e resolution. The CHAIRMAN said he did not agree with the resolu- tion. It must not be forgotten that although the vaccina- tion officers received a larger remuneration at the same time they were doing a great deal more work. He did not think they ought to csenmit themselves to a policy of opposing a scheme which had only had twelve months' trial. Mr. PILLIp : It is perfectly plain thet it will go worse.
