Billiard Match, A most enjoyable evening was spent in the rooms o the above Association, Winwick-Areet, Warrington on Saturday. The rooms were crowded with a meat enthus- isastio audieace the chief attraction being the billiard match, between the members of the club and St Mary's Liverpool who by the way are at the bead of the Liver- pool Y.M.S. Billiard League and who have for severs years bees recognised as the best exponents of the game In the Liverpool Y.M.S. Championship League having Wein several championships. The game created a deal of excitement and there were some splendid games played. In the end the Warringtonians won the match by 144. For the wieners Messrs G Darton, T Walker, E Gereghty and J Cunningham played finely. For the visitors Messrs J Belger, E Deaney, and T Green were in gcand form. Result : WAVIIIGTON. Special sermons were preeched at Wycliffe Congrega- tional Church on Sund.y, on behaif of aie Lancashire Congrezational Union, an organization which has for I main object the assisting of village churches and missions in places where they are unable to suppoit themselves, The preacher for the eceasion.was the Rev. G. Lard of Liverpool. At the morning service he Lased his remark; on the text" Jesus went snout all the citics and villages teaching in their synagogues and preaching the gospel of the kineelom." St. Matthew, 9.1. 35v. He said these words made it perfectly clear that Jebr prtached in the villages as well as in the cities. He pr - ceeded to point out the necessity of preaching the evan- gelical faith in every vi!lage et this country especially In 'view of the Recnanizng influences at work in the ' Church of-England, The pas'cre of the Congregatiocat churches in villages cor,plalned that they were not supported 135. the town and city churches as they ought to be. They were fiting against many difficulties. llUst of their men:theca lett for the centres of popnhtion a3d the support re- ceived from the Union w4s inadequate. Let them not forget that men and women were p-rishing in their sin tied it was only as they heard the Gospe! of the Kingdom that they could be saved from their sins. It was not insence, vestments or elaherzte ritual that could save the people, but an honest conception of the gospel of the kingdom which Je3119 preached in the cities and villages nearly nineteen nendred years ego.—A collec- tion was taken at both services on behalf of the Union.

LORD SALISBURY has MOTO Lord Salisbury and than Once indicated his the British Constitution. dissatisfaction with our Parliconentary Constitu- tion. He would like to see the House of Lords resemble the American Senate, though he has not been favourable to any schemes for its amendment. He has now attacked the British Constitution "as an instrument of war," and he also declares that the way in which the Treasury dominates "every department of the Government is not for the public benefit." What he means has to be inferred from his general remarks and from the criticisms to which he in this ironical manner replies. Parlia- ment has wisely prevented the calling out of the Reserves without its authority and certain other precautions, Hence Lord SALISBURY means to imply that earlier last year, when danger threatened in South Africa, the Government would have acted if it could. The excuse is a lame one. Parliament was sitting in July and into August, and if Ministers thought that the calling out of the Reserves and the embodiment of the Militia would be required it could have acted at once, and it had .the majority to enforce its wishes. Similarly with regard to the needed Secret Service Fund. If the ignorance of the War-Office weighed upon Ministers, they could have asked for and have obtained as much money as they wanted. The history of the abolition of the Secret Service Fund reflects no credit on the patriotism of the Conservative party. That fund was reduced and destroyed to meet Conservative demands. But when the Committee of National Defence was formed there was a chance of retrac- ing our steps. If the Committee felt itself ham- pered and had insufficient knowledge, how was it that in 1896 Parliament was not invited to place sufficient means at the disposal of this Com- mittee and the Intelligence Department to ascertain what was going on abroad as to military preparations and invent7ons The answer must he, we fear, that there was a lack of capacity. Agents would have ascertained for us where the Creuset guns were being F.3nt and the large purchases of ammunition on the Continent by the Transvaal. We could not have stopped these importations into the Transvaal had we known about them, is Lord SALISBURY'S reply. Here, again, we have a confession of impotence. Was it impossible to have imposed new duties on the Cape Government? Was it impossible to have made a new treaty with Portugal, to prevent military materials being sent into Delagoa Bay? It cannot be urged that the British Parliament would have checked the Government, when it had so dominating a majority in either House of Parliament. In complaining of Parliamentary checks Lord SALISBURY is taking up the peevish role Mr. ISALFoun has cast him fcr on former 'occasions. It is most humiliating to reflect that Conservative statesmen are not loyal and resner!tful to the Con- stitution,and do not believe in its virtue, capacity, and flexibility. To complain of it at a critical period is to confess a weakness that is almost con- temptible. Well might Lord ROSEBERY desire to see a loftier patriotism in our Ministers when they flout the Constitution to excuse their ignor- ance and incapacity. Parliamentary checks are wise things, but they never stood in the way of determined and vigorous statesmen, who can always get what they want, and get it right speedily. It is a novel spectacle for our respon- sible Ministers to seek a cover for their own blundering and incapacity in sneers at the Con- stitution which they laud to the skies whenever any reformer seeks to decisively amend it.

WHAT foreigners are Foreign Critics on saying about us at the Our Army. present time must not be brusquely brushed aside. Let us make every allowance for jealousy and racial feeling, and con- cede that some of the remarks that gall us so much are the result bf petulance and There will still be left a sufficient amount of solid material to provide us with many useful lessons. We have to remember that or Army has not really met a white foe since the Crimean War, and that our military reputation rests upon conflicts with unskilled warriors, trusting to shock and cunning rather than to scientific methods, and unar,ned with the latest weapons of precision. We did better in our ',campaign against the Khalifa than we did in our war against the Zulus, and we more , easily beat the Afridis than we did the Afghans. But we are doing as badly against the Boers as we over did in our most disastrous campaigns. We are told that our strategy is defective, and that this is due to the imperfect theoretical training of our officers, who too frequently take up arms as a temporary profession and then return to civil life. They are unversed in Cie real art of war, because they rarely studylit effectively. They trust too much to dash and personal bravery. They go heath i )ng int) " booby-traps," and think that they can dispense with tke "slimness" which

should enable them to avoid the wiles of an enemy 1 because they are brave as lions. Is it over incumb- ent upon our officers to make military topography a part of their general studies? Every officer in the British army, as soon as difficulties aroso in South Africa,ought to have made a sectional study of the ground it was likely to occupy or defend in case war broke out. Oar sectional military maps ought to have been as complete as time and money could make them. Instead of this we are caught in a war crisis, and few of our generals even who knew the country, knew what the Boers were likely to do, or were ready to pit science and knowledge against wile and guerilla methods. Our artillery was defecttve, and our scouting has been poor. The enemy has always known what we were about to do. In a word, our army System had been found wanting. We are always 131undering, and we act on beliefs which turn out to be erroneous. The BLitish army, in short, is an imposing sham. Our officers atte:apt to do great things with too few men. The officers do not act Promptly enough. Politicians at home are per- mitted to interfere with the plans in the field. These summarised criticis:ns come to us from America, France, Austria, and Germany. Friends are disappointed at the poor ability shown by our officers, whilst full of admiration for the magnifi- cent qualities of our private soldiers. In South Africa we have never given a single powerful display ofimilitary ability. Tao selection of the GI encoe- Ladysmith linit was a mistake. Tao sitting down of General WHITE at L sdysmith was inexcusable, gplenclid as .is the defence he has made. Lord AlurnuEN's advance to the IVlodder has bean marked by some victories, but it has failed of its Object, if that were the relief of Kimberley or a march up )n 131o3mfoutein. It is painful to con- dense into inoffensive laugnage tie savage attacks of Continental enemies. But we are bound to ad- mit that Touch of them is true, and that is the sad- dest part of the whole business.

The influence of war calamities appears to have manifested itself in the apparel worn by those attending the Houses of Parliament. In the House of Lords, en the opening day of the session, ladies are allowed to occupy the benches of the Peers, and, as this is t 1 unique privilege, surpassed only by that given to women in leap year, it is seized by ladies of high degree in large numbers. It is an ccasion for an elaborate display of millinery, and it is hardly necessary to add that this week black Was the predominant colour. So many families have been placed in mourning that others felt it to be a matter of good taste to consort with them in dark raiment. There were others, how- ever, less considerate, and the splashes of garish colour struck the correspondents as being harsh and out of place. These correspondents are all men, and they were not aware, apparently, that considerations of Complexion ruled this matter. It is a popular fallacy that black suits every face. It does not disagree with any, but some figures want a stronger distinction than can be obtained by Silhouetting. In the Commons, among the men, there was small chance of variety, as black coats are usually worn, but it was noticed that button- holes were fewer, and Mr. Chamberlain forsook the red orchid, which he wore when minfatory last autumn, for a white one. The ladies there. are hidden behind a grille, and it was no great sacrifice on their part to avoid the sharper tints,of relief. In the lobbies they are seen occasionally, but not until the time for tea on the terrace will they be tempted to assume gay costumes.

-- At any other time the National Sporting Club might receive some very frank reminders that the patience of English people in reference to fatal glove fights is not inexhaustible. We have no de- sire to emulate the United States in this matter, however much we may envy her records in other spheres. The death that occurred the other day after a glove fight in London is, we believe, the third in a comparatively short period. Accidents Will happen, of course. A man may be weakened in a vital patt by overtraining. He may insist Upon a contest, for which he knows he is not fit, from motives of pride, or be buoyed up by delusive hopes. This does not make butchery in the ring any the more acceptable or excusable. If boxing is to continue as a whole • some exercise, it must be under conditions that Preclude all possibility of accident. Glove fights for money are neither necessary to keep the scieeco alive nor wholesome and stimulative as a Spectacle. They put mones, into the pockets of men who rarely use it wisely, and provide a momentary excitement for speculative or sensa- tion loving people who might be far better and ?uore profitably employed. Nothing that the world is better for woulct be lost if such contests were forbidden. Some day, perhaps, when Parliament has time to think about it, a little useful legisla- tion on the subject may be attempted.

-- Warrington possesses a man whose foot is alleged to be responsible for another man's aeath, the loot of course being actuated by the mind of its owner. Newton possesses a man with an irresponsible foot Which has likewise got him into trouble. This foot has a tendency, according to evidence, to " swing round." Now there can no harm in a foot indulging in these pleasing gyrations, say, on the South African veldt, where space is fairly plentiful. Perhaps even in the privacy of its own residence the foot might be permitted " swing round " to its heart's content, if we may use the' phrase in this connec- tion. But when it takes to swinging in the bar of a.olace where men (and women) do congregate, and happens to collide with the ob- structive shin of a lady, then the consequences become serious. This is precisely what happened at Newton. Our friend's irresponsible foot in- dulged in an ill timed "swing" with the result indicated. The aggrieved lady prosecuted the owner of the foot, and an unfeeling bench fined him sundry shillings. We should advise Edward Jones to argue it out with a foot which has contracted so suspicious and dangerous a habit. Let him stipulate that its " swinging round shall be done when none are near. 'T would be cheaper.

The townspeople of Warrington have very pro- perly decided to show in a thoroughly practical manner their appreciation of the patriotic action of our local volunteers who are at an early date to nosed to South Africa. At the public meetings held under the presidency of the Mayor it wa unanimously decided to presont each man with a pair of field glasses and to effect an insur- ance policy on the life of every man in the sum of elOO. The first named suggestion called forth a, little criticism but seeing that it has been brouglt forward on the initiation of military officers ho completely understand the needs of the soldiers at the front, it was wisely adopted. A civilian is certainly not accustomed to see our soldiers with field glasses dangling at their sides as though on a military picnic, but this extraordinary war has taught us to adapt ourselves to the cir- cumstances of the case, and if field glasses have been found of great utility to the enemy there is every reason why our local soldiers should be equipped in a similar manner. The difficulty of raising the necessary funds, amounting to about £2009 has oeen partly overcome already. Over half of the amount required has been promised and the remainder w;11 certainly be forthcoming Tnefore many days are over.

ACCIDENT TO THE "FOUR BROTHERS" OF RUNCORN. Whilst the " tour brothors '' of Runcorn as lying at the Duke'a Dock. Liverpool, on Thurqlay, she was run into by the steamer" Optic "of Belfast. The steamer fouled her in some unaccountable way and carried away the bowsprit and dacriaged the nose of the " Four Brothers.' Subsequently the injured vessel was towed into Runcorn Dock for repairs. The "Four Brothers " is owned by Messq. Anaerson and Thomas Raynor, of Northwich. POPULAR CONCERTS AT WIDNES _ .. .

At the popular concert held in the Baths Assembly Rooms, Widnes, on Saturday, Mr. W. Carey occupied the ctair. The chief artistes were Messrs. Hat ry Gill and Montagu Fo_ter, two Liverpool humorists, who created a great impression with their votsitility. Mr. W. Jackson gave selecti 'us from "rho Bohemian Girl" on the violin, and Mr. R. Jackson gave a mouth organ selection, Mr. Beeson contributed a couple of sketches, "Mimicry" and the "Magistrate." MERSEY MISSION CONCERT.

The weekly concert at the above Institute was as well patronised as ever. Mr Rod presided, and an excellent programme was provided by the following ladies and gentlemen :—Misses Grxrrie, Gibson, N Douglas - and Messrs J J Lunt, Corrin, and J Rutter. " Blundering, Barney," a humorous sketch, was admirably submitted by Miss N Douglas, Mr T Wakefield and Mrs L Marsh. The accompanist was Miss Glrrie. The umil votes of thanks having been accorded, the proceedings closed with the singing of the National Anthem. FUNERAL OF MR. J. WOODCOCK, RUNCORN. . _ . _

On S-a-tu—rdTia-fternoon the remains of Mr. John Wood. dock, aged 58 years, who resid,.d in Stanley-street, Run- corn, and whose death occurred on the 23rd inst., were interred in the Runcorn Cemetery. For many years the deceased held the position of foreman over the Capper Department at Wigg's Works, and was well known. [toe p-ocession which stsrted frcm decea,ed's late residence, included relatives and about 50 men from the works named, the latter walking in front of the hearse. There were a number of choice fl ,ral tributes. The coffin was of oak with brass furniture, and bore a plate on which was inscribed deceased's name, age, &c. Mr. W. Bankes performed the duties of undertaker. AMUSING EPISODE IN THE COUNTY COURT• . _

His Honour Judge Gwnne James the newly appointed judge is evidently something of a sartorial artist. At the Runcorn Court on Tuesday James Outram, a tailor, of The Brow, Kingsley, sued a pig dealer named George Felons of the same village for the sum of being the pric, of a pair of trousers—Mr J Burton appeared fer the plaintiff. The defendant alleged that the trousers were a misfit and he had tnerefore returned them.—Tly plaintiff produced the trousers in Court and his Honour ordered the defendant to adj )urn into a retiring room and don the disputed garments.—The defendant did so and on returning into curt was led to the Bench and displayed his figure before the Judge who made a careful examination of the disputed trousers. His Honour declared them to be a p -rfectly reasonable fit and gave judgment for the Vaintiff. The incident caused much amusement.

div.head: INTERESrING TO PROPERTY OWNERS
div.p: INTERESrING TO PROPERTY OWNERS

At Runcorn County Court, on Tuesday, before His Honour Judge Gwnne James,Thomas Ainsworth,farmer, Marsh-lane, Frodsham, sued John Wilson Lightburn accsuntant, secretary of the Lancashire and Cheshire Building Society for £5 2 , for services rendered in emptying the aslapits of 32 houses at Frcdsham.—The plaintiff alleged that the defendant had agreed to pay 33. per hong-, but in cross-examination acknowledged that in 1897-8 he had only charged two guineas for the same work. The plaintiff's son confirmed the agreement. For the defence Mr. F A Lake stated that the defendant had paid £3 Bs. into court at the rate of 24 per ashpit, which he contended was a reasonable price. Percy Jones, agent and collector for the property, said the price arranged was 23. pez ashpic. Three shillings was never mentioned.—The Judge said the plaintiff had failed to satisfy him as t'o the price and ho gave judg- ment for the amount paid into court, the plaintiff to pay costs.
_ SONS OF TEMPERANCIL -CHESHIRE GRAND DIVISION, _ _

_ The annual meeting of this association was held on Saturday. in the Greenway-road school, Runcorn. A good number of representatives attended from Crewe, Winsford, Weston, Northwich and Runcorn. Mr. Tla.:mas Cooke, G.W.P., occupied the chair. He reviewed the past year, and pointed out that progress had been made, and as an order they stood better to-day than they had ever done before in their history, financially and numerically. The past year had been the Jubilee I year and special eff •,rts had been made to extend the Order. Tqey had been encouraged in the Past and bo urged them to" Provoke each other to good works."— Mr. John Brown, G. Patron of cadets, gave a very satis- factory report, and he spoke very hopefully of the future. Mr. Thomas J. Holt, G.S., gave a very encouraging report both as to numbers and finances. The membership was much better than it had been for many years. The various reports gave satis- faction to the Grand Division, and were accepted on the motion of Mr. Daniel Bisbrown. The election of officers then took place, with the following results :—Mr William Dunbabin, Weston, G.W.P. ; Mr Thomas J Holt, grand saribo ; Mr Thomas Heesom, Runc,rn, troasurer ; Mr James Moores, chaplain ; Mr W Kennelly, Winsford, conductor ; Mr John Weston, G. W. I Patron ;Mr J Bell, Crewe, sentinel ; Messrs J Jones, I Joseph &meting, and Themas Whyte, trustees ; Messrs Samuel Dodd and A Noden, auditors. Mr Thomas Heesom, of Runcorn, presented each officer and repre- sentativa with a bound volume of the" Sons of Temper- ance " in commemoration of the Jubilee year of the Order. For this gtnerous gift he was heartily thanked, on the motion of Messrs A Noden and Thomas J 'Holt. Northwich was eolecttd for the next place of meeting. A substantial tea was provided by Mrs. Shingler.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT.]

One does not like to complain of everything, yet one cannot help indulging in a little grumble at the way in which "our Volunteers" were invited to a dinner and entertainment, at which they got dinner good enough; but for entertainment were corn- pelled to listen to a lot of dry speeches relieved with precious little fun.

The town hears with concern of Mr. Taylor's ill- ness, and on all sides prayers for his rapid recovery ascend. Our sympathies are with him, and the heart of the town throbs when assailed with the thought that his illness is to deprive it of his ser- vices for some considerable time. During the week he has been missed by the Volunteers, the aged people, and the Council, and in a hundred other corners where his form is ever a welcome one. We feel the disappointment keenly; he more so. It must be some comfort, however, for him to know that he has so worked his way into our hearts, and affections, that when he is depressed, we are; and when he is wounded and dispirited, his fellow townsmen experience a more than passing concern in his welfare, and wish him a speedy recovery.

The Runcorn Urban District Council have been successful in their application for an extension of time in which to repay the £4,000 to be borrowed for the laying out of Runcorn Heath and Common. The work is being taken in hand gradually, and Mr. Bisbrown has evidently expressed his intention of holding a " watching brief." He reserves to himself the right of opposing any further steps than those proposed atThursday's meeting,and will no doubt be useful in keeping the Council's" nose to the grindstone" so far as their promise of economy extends.

The Council have decided to support the Trans- porter Bridge subject to certain conditions. Some we‘ks ago I advocated the Council thoroughly sift- ing the question as to the utility and workability of such a bridge, and if satisfied on such points ad- vised having a share in the capital, and making use of the clause so thoughtfully provided by Sir J. T. Brunner. lam still of that opinion. For if the bridge is to be a success, that success depends to a large degree upon Runcorn,and who has more right to benefit than the townspeople of Runcorn. On the other hand,if the Council is—after due investigation of course—of opinion that the Transporter Bridge is not a scheme they can conscientiously invest in,l should advocate opposing it. This is a point that refers equally to Widnes Town Council, and the County Councils of Lancashire and Cheshire. What is really required between the two towns is a bridge for the public, owned by the public, or at least controlled by them.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Runcorn beat Warrington thoroughly this time, as was fully expected. Bnt perhaps the best indi- cation of Runcorn's superiority over the" wire- pullers " was the display of the A" team ; four- teen of whom beat Warrington "A" on their merits.

The match against Stockport was a deeidedly keen and rough one. But it was marked for one particular feature : its one-sidednesc. From start to finish there was but one team in it. That team was Runcorn, and from the outset the only question at issue was " how many points."

To look at the game I would not have travelled far—having many times seen both teams play bet- ter games. But then it was fully recognised at the outset, that things were to be lively. Mr J Smith, (Widnes), is, however, to be congratulated for the manner he kept the "hot spirit,* "down ; but the Stockport man,whom he turned off,was not the only one who surreptuously " played the man "instead of the ball,

div.head: EXAMINER. FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 2, 1900.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 2, 1900.
RUNCORN R.F.O.

History of the Club. The chief feature of late years in Cheshire football has been the rise of the Runcorn Club, composed from the start almost entirely of working men, who, by combina- tion and keen interest in the game' have brought the club to the very front rank of Rugby and Northern Union football. For more than half the present season Runcorn have been at the top of the Lancashire Senior Competition, and at the time of writing they continue to lead the way. At present the team is playing as well as ever it did, and how well that is may be judged by the fact that no Northern Union team in the Lancashire section has a record to compaie with it. The fact, how- ever, which reflects the most credit on the club and the town is that all the players are local men, there being not one imported player in the team. Por an organi- sation that has had such a comparatively short career— it has only been in existence some twenty years—its record cannot be beaten by any Rugby team in the country, and its position to-day speaks well both for the skill of Runcorn born players aud for the enthusiasm of its officials and supporters. BIRTH OF THE CLUB. The club was formeJ in 1878-79, and arose out of an athletic society held in connection with the Y. M.C.A. , which existed for two years before the club was pro- perly constituted and the name Runcorn F.C. taken over. Mr. Charles Pownall was the first secretary, and among those associaed with him were Messrs. Forrester Bate (captain), J E Longshaw, Hugh Hughes, ichard and Robert Hughes., F Joule, W Wright, Frank Tate, W H Broady, T E Booth, the Rileys. and others. The first ground was behind the waterworks, and the teams met included Warrington, Fairfield, Z ingari, Penketh, Pad- gate, Chester, and Crewe Alexandra. An amalgamation was made with the cricket club in the second season,but as the arrangement did not prove satisfactory either from a financial or athletic point of view, it only lasted one season. A large number of members joined the cub, and by the time the third season was reached a second team had been organised, a very strong fifteen being got together. In 1831-2 out of fourteen matches played against such teams as Glod wick, Crewe, Dingle, Crewe Britannia, Werneth, Newton Heath,:Higher Broughton, Sze., eleven were won, two lost, and one drawn. Mr J E Langshaw become assistant secretary to Mr Pownall a year later, and Hughie Hughes entered on his honour- able years of captaincy. This position he retained for ten years, and few players have done more for the fifteen. In his first season as skipper not a single match was lost,while in the next campaign only one defeat was recorded in nineteen engagements. Among the fixtures were such club; cs. 7 Werneth, Walkden, S. Helens Recreation, Warrington, St. Helens, S outhport, Olympic, and Liverpool Victoria, and the team consisted of the following :—W Hughes. full back ; II C Speakman, T Johnson, and W H Broady, three-quarter back; ; FI Hughes (captain) and H G Andrews half-backs ; W Wright, J Dean, J Burns, J Clarke, J Gatley, J Lewis, W Cox, R Roberts, A Lightburn, and F Joule, forwards. 01 these H Hughes, Wright, and Broady gained county honours, and from that time Runcorn was the backbone of the Cheshire team. IN THE FRONT RANK. -

Each season the fixtures became more attractive, and about 1886 Runcorn had leaped right into the front rink. The club colours had been changed from amber and black to the now famous myrtle green in 1883-84, and it was at this time tl at Mr J E Langshaw became secretary, Mr Po wnall caking over the duties of treasurer. In 1885-86 Cardiff and Llanelly were met on a tour taken in South Wales, while the club ran up to the semi-final in the West Lancashire Cup. In 1386-87 matches were played with Salford, Rochdale Hornets, Leeds Parish Church, Widnes, Castleford, Bradforcl,Hali- f as, Liverpool Old Boys, &3, In fact, all the chief clubs in the North were me'-, with the exception of Swinton and Oldham ; and in 1887 the two latter were also in- cluded in the fixtures. No fewer than ten of the team playing at that time were appe ari ng for Cheshire,nanaely, H Hughes, W Hughes, T Woods, T H Davies, H C Speak- man, W Riley, W Wright, W Faulkner, W U Broady,and W H Crawley. The club had a magnificent seasoa in 1889-90, and they may he said to have reached the zenith of their fame in that season. All the chief clubs in the Kingdom were met, and up to Christmas every match had been won. Then Swansea were mot away, and like Runcorn they were also undefeated up to that time. The Cheshire team were beaten, but on only two other occasions did they suffer defeat that season, Bradford and Broughton Rangers being the fortunate clubs. However, Bradford were badly beaten at Runcorn, and among the well-known combinations that had to bow the knee to the Cestrians were Leeds St John's, Huddersfield, Salford, Oldham, Swinton, Rochdale Hornets, Mauningham, D^wsbury,and others. Altogether, only three go,mes were lost out of over thirty matches.

div.head: FAMOUS TEAM.
div.p: A FAMOUS TEAM.

The team was one of the bust that has ever appeered on a football: field. Every man had earned county honours, the list being as follows :—J Braz sedale, lull back ; H C Speakman, J H Crompton, and T El Davies, three-quarter backs; U Hughes (captain), and Evans, half-backs; W Faulkner, W Hughes, W H Broady, J G is/tor, F Hancock, J Riley, S Abrams, A Hanson P Dalan, and W Rigby, forwards. Brazendale was one of the finest kicks in England, and would have probably earned International honours, but for an injury which summarily checked his career. Speakman went out to Australia with Shaw and Shrewsbury's team, while of the others Crempton de- serves special mention. In his opening match with the first team he dropped no fewer than Fir goals, and in the season under notice scored no fewer than sixth-three tries, a record in first class football ; while Tommy Davies obtained forty eight tries. Crompton also played and scored in every county match with Cheshire, and for the Rest of England against Yorkshire obtained both the drapped goal and try which was his side's only score. Unfortunately his brilliant season was net improved upon by the Runcorn youth, for repeated injuries spoilt his career. Altogether in that season Runcorn obtainel something like 100 goals and a similar number of tries— a wonderful record which has probably never been equalled. In 1890-91 the team was scarcely less successful. A splendid substitute was found for Brazendale in S Houghton, while H Hughes, after assisting the Rest of England against Lancashire retired. It is impossible to speak too highly of this player. He was connected with the club from its formation, and he was the captain for ten years, and it was his great ability as a leader that brought the team to such an honourable position. He was one of the best half-backs in the North.and he captained the Ch.shire team for five years. A non-drinker and non-smoker, he was a splendid example to the players under him. Despite tempting offers from many clubs, he always stuck to his amateur principles. He refused an invitation to go out with Shaw and Shrewebury's team, arid on his retirement was ere- seated with a gold watch and chain and an illuminated address subscribed for by nearly everybody in the town.

div.head: CONTINUED SUCCESS.
div.p: CONTINUED SUCCESS.

The club continued its brilliant career each succeeding season, and it is really wonderful how many capable players the comparatively small town has turned out Will Faulkner succeeded Hughes as captain, and under him were such young players as J Faulkner, Warder, Butterworth, Taylor, 0 Hughes and others. In 1892 both Faulkner and Boughton played for the North, and the last-named played for England against Ireland. On the formation of the Northern Union Houghton went to Birkenhead Wanderers, and played for Eagland against Wales. Despite his defection Runcorn did splendidly, tieing with Oldham for third place in the combination and first place in the Lancashire section. The two clubs were ordered to play off for possession ef the challenge cup. and met on the Broughton Rangers' ground before a large gate on April 29th. Runcorn played so well that they won the championship by one penalty goal,one try (fix peints) to one gee( (five points). The next season Runcorn finished fourth in the Lancashire Senior Com- petition, while the season before last was the most disastrous ever experienced. The Cestrians occupied the tenth place in the Northern Union table, winning only nine out of twenty-six engagements, and losing fifteen and drawing two. Messrs. Langshaw and Jones fought against the professional clause, as even on amateur lines the club cnly just paid its way. Two of the best players, J. Faulkner and Butterworth, refused to turn out owing to the smallness of the pay, but the officials were firm, and the men named dropped out of foothill for some time. Last season the club occupied the seventh place in the Lancashire section, and had a I much superior record to that of the previous season. In I 1898 the club suffered a great loss by the death of Mr. La.ngshaw, who had been a splendid secretary for so many years. Mr. J. Ellison, an old member of the club, succeeded him, and with him are associated Mr Pownall, who has been in office since the club was formed, Mr Walter Jones, the e'elegate to the N.U., Mr W Carroll, and many others who have done so much to make Run. corn the fine organisation it is to-lay, The most famous player in the team now is Sam Houghton, the captain, who after eleven years' hard work in first-class football, has still no superior at full back. He is playing a great game this season, and to him the Runcorn Club owe much for their present position at the head of the N.U. table.

div.p: WONDERFUL SUCCESS.

div.p: RUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT
COUNCIL.

The usual monthly meeting ot the above Council was held at the Town Hall, Runcorn, on Thursday morning, when there were present :—Messrs James Pritchard, vv Handley, E Imisoo, T Jones, E Gatley, I Wilson, J Bisbrown, G Hewitt, T Dean, S Walton G H Kirkham, HJ. Grice, R Posnett, with Mr T Mari:hall (secretary), Mr F A Lake (law clerk), Mr James Wildi -1g (surveyor), aud Dr F McDougall (medical officer).
ABSENCE OF THE CHAIRBIAN.
The Secretary stated that Mr Wissvall having been subpceaed for the Manchester 11,43iZ99, ha l to go that morning. Ile had telegraphed his inability to be pre- sent. _ _ _ .

The Law Clerk intimated that owing to illness, the vice-chairman (Mr S Taylor) was absent too, so that the Council would have to elect one for the day. The choice fell upon Mr James Pritchard, who was unanimously asked to preside.

A FLOURISHING WATERING PLACE. Dr McDougall submitted his report, which Showed the health of the district to be good. Twenty-six deaths. and 50 births were registered. The death rate Was 164 per cent per thousand estimated population. During the corresponding period last year 22 deaths and 43 births were registered. Mr Handley observed the report was very satisfactory. Dr McDougall added for the whole month of January not a single notifiable disease had been registered, and they were on the high road to becoming really and truly a flourishing watering place. (Laughter.)

THE ACCEPTANCE OF TENDERS. Mr. J Wilson proposed the adoption of the Highway Committee's minutes, which included the acceptance of MPssrs. Brundrett and Co's. tender for the supply of 1250 tons of 1 Penmaenrnaur stone, and the 1,250 tons of 2 ditto, detivered at Stone Croft,Tap Locks,Runcora; the acceptance of Mr. William Moorestencler for sewering Moughland-lane, and sewering and road making (at3ross the Common) at Rock Savage. and Heath oads, as well as:for excavating on Runcern Heath. Mr. Kirkham seconded.

Mr: Bisbrown raised an objection to the latter portion of the minutes. They were bound in honour, in accord- ance with their agreement with the Marquis of Cholmondley,to go on with the road making so he would not oppose that. But with regard to the work on th 9 Common they were under no obligation to carry that on: Indeed ho understood there was a disposition amongst some of the members of the Committee to hold back a litile and nut incar so much expense. .

Mr. Handley explained that the agreemmt with the Marquis of Cholmondley did not mean the expenditure of £1,250. It was infinitely less. That figure included the macadam road, and the road across to Weston as well as the excavation of part of the c nn:non for the purpose of providing a " catch pit" for the drainage and also some sewerage work. He was glad to hear from Mr Bisbrown thac he was prepared to vote for the resolution that morning, but teat he reserved the right to oppose any further movement at any future tim,!. The minutes were then agre,,d to.
THE LEAKAGE OF BRANDY.

Mr. T. Dean propesed the adoption of the following report of the sub-committee appointed to report as to the alleged leakage of brandy at the hospital, and em- bodied in the Health Committee's minates :—" Your sub-committee beg to report that they have visited the hospital for the purpose of enquiring as to the large quantity of brandy used. The matron and nurse were interviewed and the committee find that the brandy had been administered by them on the instructions of the Medical Practitioner in attendance and they were in no way responsible for the quantity used. The committee satisfied themselves that the instruction of the Health Committee to the effect that the following words be added to tho diet table, namely, wines and spirits will be considered as medicine and must be paid for by the patient,' had been duly carried out. It will thus be im- possible for an account for spirits to be again charged to the committee. Your committee noted that it wa, stated in a. newspaper by a correspondent that one of the ob- jectA of the visit to 'the hospital was to discharge the patients. Such an ilea was not entertained by any member of the sub-committee and they had no intention whatever of instructing the matron to discharge the patients ,without the concurrence of the M 3dical Practi- tioner in attendance." Mr 8 Walton seconded.

_ Mr E Gatley repudiated tent the matter was noted from any newspaper. It was a matter brought out by a letter which had been left there—(at the Town Hall) complaining, and did not ecainate from any newspaper. Mr Bisbrown said he took a great interest in the matter, and was present when the sub-committee gave their report. He was satisfied that the matter had been proved ro the bottom, and there would in the future be no more cases of the kind. (sear. bear.) _ _ _ _ .
The report was approved and adopted unanimously. THE BRIDGE ACROSS THE MERSEY. DESERVING OF SUPPORT.

The Parliamentary aaeL.General Purposes Committee reported that they had had under consideration the Bill which was being promoted to authorize the construction of a bridge across the River Mersey between Widnes and Runcorn, and for other purposes. Mr Aisop, solicitor, and Mr Wood, eegineer, had attended a meeting of the committee. The questions of the tolls and charges, contracts, roadway, sewers, and other matters were discussed. The commit-ee were informed by the solicitor that neither he nor the engineer could pledge the promoters with regard to the sug- gested reduction of tolls and chutes, and as to contract tickets being issued altogether they personally were of opinion that much lower figures would be charged than the maximum charges and tolls mentioned in the Schedule of the Bill, and, also, that probably con- tract tickets would be issued. The committee recom- mend the adoption of the following minute :—" That in the opinion of this Coancil the construction of the pro- posed Transporter Bridge beween Runcorn and Wichr , would be of great public advantage and that this Council cordially supports the Bill now before Parliament subject to such clauses being inserted as the Council may con- sider necessary for the protection of the district, and that the Chairman and other members of the Council be authorised if required to give evidence in favour of the Bill before the Parliamentary Committee." Mr. Handley said, in proposing the adoption of the above report, it would be very satisfactory for them all te hear that the conditions mentioned were likely to be I granted.

Mr. G. Hewitt seconded. Mr. Bisbrown poiro.ei out that the qaestion of con tracts for workmen had been specially considered, and they understood that such would be granted. though for the present nothing definite had been settled. Mr. Handley stated it would not be fair to make known the whole of the negotiations. Everything was going on satisfactorily. They had virtually agreed that contact tickets should he issued for the Transporter B ridge. Tim Chairman thought it was an undertaking that the community might give their full support to. The minutes were agreed to. EXTENSION OF TIME. The Local Government Board wrote sanctioning the extension of the time for the repayment of the loan upon the proposed park and pleasurt grouad from 23 to 30 years. RUNCORN VOLUNTEERS —a, LIiT OF HONOUR. On the motion of Mr. Imison, seconded by Mr Wilson, it was unanimously decided to record on the minutes of the Council the names of the volunteers of Runcorn who had offered themselves for the front, and also to record in red ink the names of those who were accepted as well as the fact that they had been entertained by th,.3 vice-chairman. A sub-committee was alQo appcinted to consider the best way in which to put the list on permanent record in the Council Chamber. and something in the form of a "list of honour placed on the wall was suggested." The committee consisted of: The Chairman, vice Chairman, and Mr E Imison.

Warrington Training College. At the annual meeting of the Chesser Diocesan Board of Education held at Chester Cathedral on Wednesday,—Canon A P Holme read the report of the Executive Committee, which stated that the total receipts in 1893 were £931 lie 21 and in 1899, £912 13s 4d. The Training College at Warrington maintained its well-earned position among the training colleges for mistresses. There was a great desire on the part of the authorities, of the college to enlarge its accommodation by taking in the buildings of the Clergy Daughters' School, the Clergy Daughters' School being removed to some other station.—On the motion of the Bishop the report was adopted.—Canon Maitland Woad thought at that time Training Colleges should be brought to the front. School manag,ers did not seem to see that lose their Training Colleges was to lose the teaching of the teachers and also in that way to lose the teaching of the children. Just then the position of the Training Colleges was of the first importance. They wanted help, for there could be no doubt that the Warrington Training College should be enlarged and the Chester Training College wanted looking up. He moved that the Bishop be requuted to appoint a committee to consider and report on the actual working of the Code in the agricultural parts of the diocese.—This was seconded and carried. div.head: RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB. .••• ••.•1 A Progressive Year.
div.p: RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB. .••• ••.•1 A Progressive Year.

Oa Tuesday evening the annual meeting of the mem- bers of the ab3ve organisation *as held in the temporary buildings, Foresters' Hall, Runcorn. There was a good attendance, over which Mr. W. B. Brimelow presided.

THE SECRETARY'S REPJRT. The Secretary, in his annual report, said it was satis- fac!ory to report progress, and to note that the ordinary income had been more than sufficient to meet the expenditure, leaving a credit balance of 220 lie 7d, an increase over last* year of £l2 9; Id, and which hal further, reduced the amount owing on the club premises from £260 12; 10d to £240 is 3d. During the summer the Committee arranged a picnic and although a considerable number availed themselves of the opportunity of visiting the L Ike district, a slight logs resulted through. the weather being unfavourable. During the year the hand of death had removed one of the vice-presidents, Mr P Speakman, J.P., C.A. From the &et inception of the club he had ever taken the warmest interest in its welfare, and his sudden and un- expected decease left a blank which it would be difficult to fill. The club was represented at the funeral by the officers and numerous members, and the committee afterwards passed a resolution of sympathy with the family. In the last report, attention was drawn to the inadequacy of the club premises. Toe cominittee then stated they had for some time felt that the present structural arrangement; of the club premises did not allow for their making suitable pre- vision for the literary and educational side of its work. It was important that the comparatively near approach of a general election should fled the club not only con- veniently situated but also other wise saitable as the local centre for the district whsnever that event happened. and with a view to that the committee had anxiously considered how those two objeoto could be adequately provided for in the present Ibuilding. Through the usual generous consideration and assistance of their member Sir John Brunner, to whom the plan of the proposed alterations was submitted as the president of the club, it was unanimously decided to proceed with the work of reconstruction at once and which when com- pleted the committee felt sure would greatly add to the comfort and convenience of the members from the social and recreative standpoint; and also afford facilities for the discussion of political questions by the large number of Liberals in their district who for want of such a local educational centre had not hitherto taken such an active interest in the club as was desirable. The reconstruction would provide on the ground floor, a news room, secretary's office, large lecture room, store rooms, kc. ; and on the upper floor, a large billiard room with refreshment alcove. The lighting and ven- tilation had been much improved by the addition of large side windows, sky lights, and patent roof ve itila- tors. The committee felt that those alteration; would justify themselves in the club 1113r0 fully realising the purpose of its establishment not only in, as hitherto, providing for the social recreation of its atembers,but in becoming a convenient and much needed rallying place for the Liberal party of Runcorn and the surroun Hog district. _ _ _
Tee report wis alopt3l on, tin motioi of Mr. C. Kaiveton, seconded by Mr. Carter.

THE PROPOSED ALTERATIONS.

The committee gave additional ptrticulars with reg. ir I to the proposed alterations at the club, which showed that it would be a nee3t c)mcnodious building, in every way adaptel to the requirements of such a community. In concluding, he thanked Mr. Handley for his great assistance in bringin.; the alterations to such a success- ful termination. _ _ _ _

Mr. Handley replying thanked the Chairm tn fot his kind sentitnents and remarked that whatevr he hat done had la ,ea d)ae for the advancement of Liberalism in Runcorn. THE EDUC&TION OF THE MEMBERS IN LIBER&L PRINCIPLES.

Mr. Moore thought that a strong recommendation should g) from that annual meeting to the Committ3e to do all in th-ir power to make greater 1198 of the rule applying to the education of the members in political principles so that they would be better fitted to meet their opponents face to face, not in fisticuffs, but in argument.
La supported saving that if the ranmniendation was carried out by th 3 new clinmittee it would prove of greater benefit to thems_lveq and the town as well.

div.head: DEATH OF THE WESTON POINT CENTENARIAN.
div.p: DEATH OF THE WESTON POINT CENTENARIAN.
A Wonderful Old Woman.

Mrs. Mary Hudson, a widow,who has resided for some years with her daughter and her son-in-law, Mr and Mrs Burrows, in the Salt Union Works, Weston Point, d'ed on Saturday evening at the age of 103 years. The evidence as to her age is testified by a certificate of baptism at Overton Parish Church, Frodsham. She was born at Kingsley, and resided with her parents until verging on womanhood, when she entered into service at Manchester. After enjourning there a short time she feil in love with Patrick Martin, who belonged to he 60th Rifles, and in due course she became united in vrcd- lock at the eld Parish Ceurch. For 14 years they travelled from barracks to barracks visiting various parts of England and Ireland and going to ) Jersey. They had issue five children. When in Liver- pool her husband died, and the soldiers gave him ' a decent burial. 'Three days later his pension would have become due to him, but the widow did not receive a penny. She was left with five children, none of whom were sufficiently old te earn anything. Being a woman of very strong constitution, she succeeded in maietaining herself and teem by, to quote her own words, "working like a horse." Several years later she was married t 3 John McKenn, gauger in the employ of Messrs. Brassey and McCormack, contractors, who were engaged in carrying out large works in Liverpool. About 40 years ago she removed to Widnee where she resided a score of years. Having again been left a widow she re-entered the bonds of matrimony, her third hus- band being Robert Hudson. After his death she took up her residence 25 years ago with her son-in-law, Mr Bur- rows, who then lived at Winsford, but who has dwelt at Weston Point during the last nine years. The deceased was a most remarkable woman. Up to her last she was in full possession of her faculties, and for one of her years was surprisingly active. Until quite recently she was to be seen daily taking her walks abroad. Some 23 years ago she met with an accident which necessitated her having to use a stick. She was gathering herbs when she fell down a marl pit, and nar- rowly escaped being drowned. She fractured her wrist and injured her hip. As a proof of the strength of her frame it may be scene that before going home she went to the house of the doctor who attended her. Through her advanced age the injury to her wrist was never re- paired. The old lady had been fond of exercise during her youth, when she walked from Liverpool to Manches- ter. During her stay in Winsford she frequently went to North wich and back on foot. When she had almost reach her hundredth birthday she astonished her friends , by walking from Weston Point to Sham's Cross and back in one thy. Rer eyesight was almost unimpaired,while her hearing was quite good until the last. She had always enjoyed good health, as can be judged from the fact that during her long existence she could boast that see had not taken snore than five bottles of medicine. She was fond of relating her experienees when a soldier's wife, speaking of the memories of days of long, long ago, and refer,ing to the chengee that had taken place since her girlhood. She distinctly remembered Welnes when it was nothing snore than a rural district, and the , houses were few and far between, and when there were

no works With blackened Bmok3 to plllute the atmcS• phere. She is survived by two children, namely. Mrs. Burrows and Mrs. Ecoleston, of Sandy-lane, Weston Point. Up to a few years ago she bMieved that two GI her sons were still alive, although she had not beard anything respectun then for a quarter of a century. One was a soldier and the other a sailor, and she enter- tained the opinion that she would see them befbre she died.

div.head: OLD FOLK'S TREAT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE OLD FOLK'S TREAT AT RUNCORN.
Tea and Entertainment.

Eighteen years ago the Old Folk's Treat Fund was launched, and year after year as time rolled on, the aged of Runcorn. have assembled at the Public Hall, and been afforded a" treat " worthy of the name. Tea has been provided, as well as diver- sity in the shape of an enjoyable entertainment ; and the "old folk" having been well pleased by o'er- whelming attentions to their gastronomic require- ments—paid to them by a corps of enthusiastic youthful assistants—their eyes and ears have been provided with that which so amused them as to make them shake with laughter.

The treat this year was no exception. The committee worked with its usual assiduity, and ferreted out the aged from all quarters, and Borne 460 invitations were issued. Only 365 responded however, and the inability of the absentees to get to the treat is regrettable. Tnough in no way could the committee be responsible for it, for every eff )rt was made ; and even the local cabs ware available for those who could'aot walk. The hall was decorated plainly, but effec-Avely, and exhibited a most inviting appearance with its well laid snowy tables replete with toothsome edibles. Everything was abundant, wholesome, and well-served. The natural sequence bbing that everyone enjoyed themselves, just as the committee desired.. After tea, the old women were provided with two ounce packets of tea, and the old risen with tins of tobacco. The latter was the gift of Messrs Ogden Limited,through Mr R Moore, tobacconist, Runcorn. The following ladies presided at the tabs :—Mre Imison and Mrs Dykes; Mrs Whittaker and Mrs Jones ; Mrs W Leathwood and Mrs TeWhinystes; Mrs fr Bowyer and Mrs Percival; Mrs and Miss Wit wall; Mrs Tsroperley and Mrs Morris; Mrs W Yarwood and Mrs W Cooke ; Miss Taylor and Mrs Dudley; Mrs Turner and Mrs F J Norman; Miss Millington aud Mrs Hallwoad ; Mrs R Moore and Mrs T Cooke ; Mrs P Leathwood and Miss Woodland; Mrs G Frith Mrs Crosby ; Mrs Coventry and ICH Firragher ; Mrs J Bate and Mrs J R Frith; Mrs Monks and Mss J U Ws- ton; Mrs Hewitt and MiSTS Broadhurst ; Miss Linaker and Miss Riley; Mrs Lake and Mrs Walton; Mr G Bellamy and Mrs 3 D Jones ; Mrs Allen and Mrs Howard; Mrs Rowlands and Mrs T 11,-iynolds ; Mrs G W Temperley and Mr T Wood ; Mrs Meredith and Mrs Williams ; Mrs Beck and Mrs Posnett ; Miss Pearson and Mrs Kirkham ; Mrs A R Norman and Mrs D Littlenoore ; Mrs W Jones and Mrs Harding ; Mrs Lightburn and Mrs J M Firth; and were ably assisted by the memb of the Committee, and a carps of assistants who gave their services gratis. THE ENTERTAINMENT.

Mr. F. Wilma took the chair at this function, and in doing so heartily welcomed all the aged people on behalf of the committee. The one desire of that body was that all slaoeld enjoy themselves, and he hoped they would. He was delighted to tell them of the pleasure it gave him to preside at that function, but he was sorry that his old friend Mr. Samuel Taylor—(applause)—was ill with influenza and unable to attend. S:ill though absent in the body he was present in spirit as they would see from the letter he would rea I. "Rydal Mount.Runcorn January 31st, 1900. Dear Mr Wiswall. Please tell the old people lam sorry I cannot be with you to-night.—lt is the first entertainment I failed to attend since we com- menced giving them,—and hops they will have a very pleasant and enjoyable evening,—Yours truly, Samuel Taylor." (Loud apolause).—Mr Win- wall then referred to tue (segue shown more generally all over the country, of doing something for our old folk. It was illustrated by V. s talked of schnme for old age pensions. He spoke of the pity it was that so many of their old folk foetid their way into the work- house through no fault of their own. (Hear, hear.) Re wished them well for miey years to come, and hoped they would be able to attend other gatherings of that nature, for there would be other gatherings, and he for one would do his level best to roll the chariot along. (Applause.) The programme was then proceeded with. Mr. Booth's gramaplaoneiwas the first item, but it is difficult to tall the feelings of the aged ones at that wonderful " talking trumpet," probably they were more akin to awe than anything else. Miss Simkin and party. Misses Kitty Carter (queen), Millington, Uns worth, Stone, A Cooke, Bisbrown, Ball, Williams, McDenald, Leadstone, and E Taylor formed a troupe of attractive zinger', and for the cantata "Wandering Gipsies" received well merited applause. Miss Clara Taylor followed with "Rule Britannia." It was a treat in itself, and so captivated the audience that without invitation they joined in the chorous. A recall was undeniable.- Mr. W. Shaw took the opportunity bsfore Miss Taylor left the platform, of expressine the pleasure the old people felt at the great interest Mr. Taylor had taken in them for so many years past. He felt that they oueht to ask Miss Taylor to take to her father on their behalf the appreciation they all felt at his kindness, and also their deep sympathy with him in his illness. Mr. W. Millington had very great pleasare in seconding the proposition. He could tell them, though doubtless they knew before, that if there was one man more than another in Runcorn who had worked ungrudgingly for the success ot that cans s that man was Mr Taylor. Be knew the vote would meet with their hearty response. Personally he very mach regretted Mr. Taylor's absence, but he hoped that he would be there another year, and for fleetly ye srs to 001119. (Applause.) The vote was carried with acclamation. _

The Chairmen intimated that Miss Taylor wished to thank them very much for the expression of good feel- ing, and would deliver the message to her father. (Ap- plause.) Continuing the programme Miss Temperley and party executed a mandoline selection of "popular airs." Miss A. Caoke (in character) depicted how" I persuaded him:" The exhibition of the poker seemed to be the key to the song. She was encored and responded with a serio-comic. Muter Jack Rutter increased his popu- larity with "Scarlet and Blue." Mr. W. Fraser Jones was good in two humorous sketches "Visit to Caernar- von" and "Going to the Pantomime" and provided the aged with plenty to laugh it. "Soldiers of the Queen" by Master Fred Outhwaite (soloist) and Masters W Shaw and Leonard Tanks secured a recall. The refrain was repeated by the assembly. Mrs. Temperley delighted with " Home sweet horns" and the" Last Mile Stone."" A Soldier and a Man" was ably rendered by Miss Kittle Carter. and Mr. Walter Shaw was deservedly applauded for" Tommy Atkins." The Success of the evening, however, was the humorous duet. " &8.C." by Miss Effie Taylor and Miss Stringer. Miss Taylor was inimitable, and made a _ _ _ _ _

_ perfect" dunce " to Miss Stringer's " schoolmistress," I Both were superb juvenile impersonators. "You shan't , play in our yard" from the lips of Miss Nellie Temperley was accompanied with quaint but pleasing action. " Maids young and old," was another item well staged by Misses Cameron. and Handing. "The Ole Umbrella.' was rendered by Miss Simliiniand Miss Wood(though Bur fering from a' bad cold) contributed a humorous noon- song" True Blue "another sweetly rendered mandoline selection by Miss Ternperley and Party was the conclud- ing piece. The efficient accompanist was Mr. W Cooke A.R.0.0., and Miss Forrester also rendered valuable assistance as accompanist to the "A.8.C." duet. On the proposal of Mr. W. Shaw, seconded by Mr. J. Wilding a vote of thanks was passed to the.donors, tea- makers, assistants and arzistes, on behalf of the old people. The Chairman was accorded a like honour on the mo- tion of Mr. Coventry, seconded by Mr. W. Cooke. The proceedings concluded with the National Anthem. The cemmittee desire to thank all who assisted in the success of the evening, and especially the local cab proprietors who so kindly net their vehicles at tke dis- posal of the aged both to come and return.

NEWTON COUNCIL AND THE SOUTH LANCASHIRE ; TRAMWAY BILL.
A special meeting of the Council of the Urban District of Newton-in-Makertielti, was held on

Wednesday evening, in the Town Ilan, Earlestown. Mr. CB F Borron, J P, CC, presided, and there were also present :—Messrs. It Stone, W Gilmour, Dr Patterson, J Simpson, F J Wood, W Thomps sn I Ormand, with W W 3hirley, (clerk),and T A Bowes (surveyor).
THE LATE LIEUTENANT MCCORQUODALE

The Chairman said before commtnicing the business which had called them together, be wished to expresi his deep re4ret—and he was sure hewas voicing their 6nti- me.nts—at the loss they had sustained by the death of Lieutenant 11:igh Stewart 11.1CorTiodale, wh) was the son of the late Colonel McCerquodale whose memory was revered in that district; with feelings of universal respect: For many years Colonel AV:Coign&laie ozcu- pied tbe chair of the Board al Cemmicsioners, and the Lose which had now been sustained by his widow must be a very severe one. He was sure that their sympathies went out to her in the lo 3s of her son. He was a young man with ample means at his disposal to command a life of luxury in this country, but ho visa one of those of whom they had had many instances of late who volunteered to go and serve for the honour and credit of the Queen and to do his duty before the enemies of his country. Ha bad fallen in the fight and had found a soldier's grave. He was proud to say that there were many left in this country who were prepared to go to the front. Only yeeterdsy they saw a number from that district leave Liverpool with the Yeomanry They hoped they would return having performed their duty. Hear, hear.)
THE C3IINCIL AND THE SOUTH LANCASHIRE TRAMWAYS COMPANY. • A SATISFACTORY ARRANGEMENT,

- The Chairman said the business of that afternoon was to hear a statement of the result of the negotiations ' which had taken place between Me Stone and hinvelf (on behalf of the Council), and the South Lancashire Tramwaye Company, with reference to the proposed tramways in that d strict. They spent many hours in going into the matter, and the negotiations were pro- longed and perhaps severe. They were obliged to Show considerable resistance in considering the interests of the 'district. Some of the suggestions they made bad not been thought of by the other authorities through whose districts the tramways would run. They had not obtained all the security that they wished. They felt that they ought to have a sufficient sum guaranteed to replace the road should the tramway be given up or otherwise a certain amount to compensate them for the increased cost of repair of roads. Certain sums were named but it was found difficult to carry out the suggestion. They had a clause which they thought would cover to a certain extent any expenditure which might be incurred by the tramway system coming into their district. They hid epncially looked after the interests. of High-street and Church-street in Newton and they tad obtained an undertaking from the Tramway Company that they would pave the whole length of these two s'.reetsp with setts at their own costs. They had also agreed that the whole of Market-s!ret, Reitway-streenand Quecreetreet, sheuld also be paved at the Tramway Company's ex- pense. Mr. 13L433 had z-nade a Celculatfon of the cost of these improvements and he estimated it at about £1,603 By a clause which hal been inserted the Tramway Com- pany were bound to h tve a nad of 27 feet alien the en- tire length except at such places by agreement with the Council where it Could not otherwise be avoided: With reference to the capital of the Company nothing could be done at their roads until two thirds of the capital reqeired had been provided for. That was a security that the work would be per- formed before touching their roads. They had also arranged that the Tremway Company should take away the snow if any fell, and not leave it on the road- side to the inconvenience of the passengers, as they pre- viously intended ten do. They hid also agreed that a new bridge forty feet wide should be censtructed over the canal at Newton Common in place of the present drawbridge. That would improve the thoroughfare in that part of the district. There might he a difference of opinion as to the advantages and disadvantaners %Caine might follow the introduction of tramwa.ys, -but it was not in their hands to prevent their construction if they wished to do so, because the other districts which were in favour of the tramways constituted a majority and the Tramway Company could ride over their heads it they wished to do so. flo was not of the opinion that the tramway would not be of very great benefit to the district although it might beef general advantage. He hoped the Council would endorse the arrangemeats which they had 'made with the Company and he would now ask Mr. Shirley to read the clauses which formed part of the agreement wth the Tramway Company and the Council. The following are the clauses specially relating to he Newton Council :—(1) Where two lines o, railway are laid by the company, the cnnoany to pave between two such lines of tramway with granite setts and in all cases where the nearest railway is of leas distance than seven feet from the outer edge of the footpath or boundary of the road on either side the intervening space between the rail and the footpath to be also paved by the company.. (2) The company shall where possible construet their tramways in snob pod- \Mons as to allow a space of not less than 9 feet 6 inches be- tween the footpath and the nearest rail of the tramway on one side and not less than 12 feet 6 incises between the out- en or side of the footpath and the nearest rail of the tramway on the other side. (3) The company to pave the entire lengths and widths of High-st. and Church-at.. N Willows, and Market-ste, Queea-street and Railway-st. to the junction of King-street, Harlestown, with good granitewto-1 other approved setts and to compensate the Council for lass to trees (it any) in High-street. Newt ea. Material taken from these streets to belong to the company. (4) So much of the road in Crow-lane upon which tramway No. I may be con- structed as is Not now macadamised for the full width thereof between the curbs shall be taken up by the company and re-censtracted into the uniform macadam pavermnt. (5) The company shall not permit any carriage used on the tramways to be so laden that any part of the load shall extend beyond the width • of such carriage. (6) Toe height of any trolly wire or wires constructed by the company within the district of the Council shall not be less than 21ft from the g :mind of the road. (7) The company,to erect a new permanent fixeS bridge 40 feet wide across the canal at Newton Common aceording boa plan to be approved by the Council in lieu of the present draw-bridge. (8) The company shall refund to the Council such reasonable cost as may be incurred by them in adjust- ing the level and approach of the intended division by the Council of Wharf-road at Newton Common to the level of the approach to the prop easd bridee over the canal at Newton Common. (9) Any question which may arise between the Connell and the company with reference to this aec ion or anything to be done or not to be done therein shell be clete- mieed by arbitration. The Clerk also read out the sections which had been agreed te by the company whh the Abram, Golbornen Haydock, Ince anti Newtoz-in-alikerfieni Councils. One clause stated ehat two-thirds of the catntal of the com- pany (£733,000) shall be subscribed unner contract be- fore the company cin uninence the construction of the tramways. The company also indemnify the Council against any expense is connection with the repair or maintecance of any street or road where tramways will he constructed. Another clause stipulates that the company shall not sell or le3s3 tramways in the district, and the power of purchase shall be exercisable only after the expiration of 30 years from the passing of tee Act. Dlr. Simpson : At what hour will the trams tun. The Clerk : Not later than six o'clock in the morning nor earlier than five o'clock in the evening. Mr. Galnaour : I suppose there will be special fares for workpeople ? The Clerk : They will be able to travel for a fare of ooe half penny a mile. The Chairman propoeed the following resolution : "That the Urban District Council of Newton-in- Makerfield in the County of Lancaster, do herebe con- sent to the South Lancashire Tramway Bill, which has been denositel for prometioa in the Session of Perna- ment,l9oo, and that the common sost of the Council be affixed eo such consent." Mr. Thompson seconded and the resolution was unanimously carried.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
STEALING POSTAL ORDER 3 FROM MESSRS. CROSFIELDS.

On Friday at the Warricgton Police Court. before Mr. Hepherd (in the chair), Cour.cillor Smethurst and Dr. Goma% Alfred Stanley Wilcox, 71, Manchester-road and Thomas Wakefield, 59, Ellesinere-street, youths, were chimed with stealine twe postal orders value £1 3.3 31 the property of MM33r3. Joseph Crosfield and Song, Limited on November 20th, 1899.—Wilcox who was represented by Mr. Hislop, solicitor. of Manchester, pleaded not guilty.—Mr. A. Browne prosecuted on be- half of the firm. He said that between the 18th of November and the 16th of December a number of postal-orders were missed and suspicion be- gan to be aroused. The only four people who could touch the postal orders were the two defendants and two other boys under the superintendence of Mr. Houghton. The precees was, the letters were opened by the boys, the contents taken out, and the postal orders and cheques were compared with the advice letters and taken by Wilcox only, to the cashier in another room. They were going to call the boy Wakefield to give evi- dence against Wilcoe. What happened was this. The. firm could not discover whose hand writing the stolen postal orders were in until Mr. Wa rdle bethought him self that it was like the writing in the telephone book. The boy Wakefield had charge of the telephone and on compering the wzitiag in the telephone book, with the writing on the orders by permission of tne Post Master, it was found that the word Liverpool on the two orders in the charge was exactly the same writing as the word Liverpool in the telephone hook. Wakefield was confronted by the heads of the firm, and at first denied knowing anything about it. When it was pointed out that the writing was exactly the same as that in the telephone book, he admitted it, and merle a confession without any promise being made to him beforehand, and implicated the boy Wile3X. He said that he never thought of taking any postal orders until one day about the 16th of November, when two postal orders for £1 3s 3d were received. Wilcox came to him after he was supposed to have taken them to the cashier and he said " Look here; If you will fills in the forms and keep these postal orders we will go and cash them and divide the money." There- upon the boy Wakefield at the suggestion of Wilcox put the postal orders in the telephone box,so that if they were searched 'the orders would not be found upon them. Wakefield filled in the orders the name A. Pearce, Liver- pooliThey went to Liverpool on the 20th November and cashed one order for 203. Tha boy Wilcox did not go inside the post office but waited outside. The cunning- ness of Wilcox bad been shown in every detail. He had done nothing himself but induced the other boy to do 83. Wilcox had stayed outside the Post Office in every instance whilst Wakefield cashed the orders. When it was found out that Wakefield had signed the orders and made the confession Mr. Wardle at once began to suspect Wilcox, and told him that he and Wakefield had been together a lot lately. Mr. Wardle asked them if they did not go to Liverpool together. Wilcox said "No I have never been to Liverpool since May." The following morning Wilcox came to Mr. Wardle and told him he was very serry, but ho was at Liverpool on Saturday with Wakefield. Mr. Wardle said" Very well that will be all right." An independent witness saw the boys on a Monday in the 9.30 train from Liverpool Wilcox was most impudent and impertinent when he was charged with the offence. When the Chief Con- stable 'evicted out a certain thing to him he turned round and said "That's as much for me as against me." Wakefield had told how they spent the money. They bought an air gun and a revolver and some ties and collars with the actual *owe, drawn from Liverpool. The boys were, of course, instantly dismissed, and no promise of anything was made to Wakefield before be made the confession. Wilcox had been in the employ of the firm for four years.—Evidence was then called in support of this statement ; and the witnesses included the defendant Thomas Wakefield, against whom the ebarge was withdrawn.—Mr. Browne intimated that other orders had been stolen but were not in the charge as if the amount was over 40e they would have to go to the Quarter Sessions.—The Mayor Mr. Henry Roberts, the managing director for the firm, said that Wilcox had some time ago admitted tampering with private drawers and desks in the office, but bad not been discharged in sympathy with his father.—The defence was a strong denial of the theft, and Mr Hislop thought that it was on account of the impudence of Wilcox that the case had been persevered in.—Defendant gave evidence and said he had never given Wakefield one postal order.—The Bench came to the decisi u to fine Wilcox 20s and costs and at the same time thought that it was a pity Messrs Crosfield did not discharge him when he was found tampering with the desks. They also thought that Wakefield should havo been in the box as well:--The Mayor again explained that the matter of tampering with the desire was overlooked out of sym- pathy with the boy's father.
A PERgISTENT THIEF WELL PUNISHED.

Elizabeth lenegskaw is one of the most versistent thieves in Warrington. She has been many times cost- victed of felony, and altogether her appearances at the Polies Court number elevee. She has a little girl aged ten years and she has now begun to instruct her in th " art" of thieving. Her husband at the present time i in gaol, and she has up till recently bees living at a com- mon lodging-house in Scotland-road. he again figured at the Police Court on Wednesday when she was charged with stealing from the dwelling-heuse' No. 1, Lower sank-street, between six and seven o'clock on Tuesday evening, a shawl valued at 6s 63, the property of Mar- garet Flannaghan. She pleaded guilty.—lt nppears that shortly after six o'clock Mrs. Flannaghan went to the house of a neighbour leaving her shawl in the house. On her return a few minutes later she found it had ,disappeared. She reported the matter to the police and inquiries wore made. It was ascertained that Mrs. Longshaw and hor little girl had keen seen loitering about the house. Later on in the evening, the woman was tound by Superintendent Mnnaghan end Sergeant Chcenoy in Walker'a Vaults drinking with a lot, of men. When accesed of the theft she made use of filthy and threatening language. The shawl bad been pledged by her for 2;. 63. in the name of Ward, Cartwright-street. The magistrates sent her to Strangeways for three months with hard labour.

CRUELTY TO A MARE —Fred :%fassey, 18, Ship-yard, was summoned for illtreating a mare on the 21st inst. by kicking it.—P.C. Turner proved the cai!3ant a firte of 103. was im- posed.
