clongh. SCHooL ATTENDANCE 0i8F.3 —The following Were dealt with for neglecting to send their children to school regu- larly, the oases being proved by Mr. W. Joneg, chief school attendance officer :—John Baguley, 135, Dallam-lane, 53; Charles Bampton, 16, Antrobus-street. order for child to at- tend school; George R Burdett, 19, Beswick-street, Sc; John Chadwick, 18, Back Dallam-lane. 2s; James Coleman, 23, Howard-street, 2s 63 ; James Davidson, 23, Cartwrlght-et., 53 ; Arthur Deeley, 7. Admiral-street, 53 ; John Dumbell, 35, Po' hergill-street. order; John Fiddler, 14, Ellen-street, 58 ; Thomas Ryder, 10, Silver-square, order and fined 21 63; Wm. Ryder. 25, Portland-street, Os; William Wright, 6, Bakehouse Yard. is, THREE Alorags von A MILIFIA MAN.—Samuel Williams. a militiaman,was charged with being a convict on license and failing to report himself at Warrington on his arrival on the 18th January. He pleaded enlity,—Superintendent M o naghan said that in March, 1896, the prisoner was sen- teaced to five ye us penal servitude at the Liverpo )1 assizes, He was liberated on license on the 10th of that (the present) month at Bristol, and proceeded to London. From there he proceeded to Liverpool, wnere he said he was going to re- side. He seemed to have entered the militia in the name of Weston, giving an address in London where he said he had worked 12 months. to obtain a character from. He then came to Warrington and was in town a week, but did not report himself. Lie had no license and said be had lost it. He (witness) arrested him on Friday night in company with Detectiv-, Forster, He was in uniform. The prisoner : They told me I was to report myself on the first Saturday in each month. The Clerk said the prisoner should have reported himself within the first 48 hours of his arrival,— Prisoner was sent to gaol for tbree months. MONDAY.—Before Mr. F. Monks (in the chair), Alderman Blackhurst, Councillor Smethurst, and Messrs. Birchall

and S. Wright. Bataan:so Wrsonws.—Sarah Leonard, Ship Yard, was charged with being drunk and disorderly la Ship Yard at 4.45 on Saturd,y afternoon, and with breaking three panes of glass in the window of the dwelling-house of Mary O'Toole, doing damage to the amount of le 6d.—P.O. Dalatray said that at 4-40 on Saturday afternoon he was on duty in Bridge-street, and in conseqaence of information ha received he proceeded to Ship Yard. if e there saw the prisoner who was drunk, and making use of obscene language. Her hand was bleeding, the result of breaking the glass mentioned in the charge. He took her into custody " and she became very violent, making use of filthy language. With the assistance of P.C. Baxendale he took her to the Police Station.—Prisouer. who is a stranger to tha town, was fined 53 and ordered to pay le 6d the amount of the damage.--'Mary Locker, last trona Manchester, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridue-street at 11.10 on Saturday night, and with wilfully breaking a plate glass door panel at the shop of Lewis Flem- ing, doing damage to the amount of lbs.—P.o- Turner said that at the time named he was on duty in Bridge-street in company with P.O. Taylor when his attention was called to Mr. Fleming's shop: On proceeding there he saw the prisoner, who was drunk. She was making use of the most filthy language to Mrs. Fleming. Mrs. Fleming told him that the prisoner came into the shop, pulled her shoe off, and broke the glass panel in the door.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for two months. DaunirENNEps.—A fine of 5s and costs was imposed on Michael Melia, 7, Carlisle-street, and Peter Ward. 2, Old- road, for being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarker-street at 11-30 on Saturday night • Joseph Jackson, 26, Percy-st.. was fined be for a similar ofionce.

15,RKFRE.HISENT ROUSE ICiMmit FINED.—TAras; Bayne, re- freshment housekeeper, 37, llersey-street, was etimmoned for keeping his house open for the sale of refreshments when it should have been closed,—on the 23th January at 11-55 p.m.—P.C. Cooper said that at 11-55 on the date in question he was on duty in Slersey-street. He found three young men in defendant's refreshment house, eating chipped potatoes. He celled the defendant's attention to the time and told him that he would be reported.—A fine of 5s was imposed. OBSCENE LANGUAGE.—Thomas Topping, 44, Longford-st. was fined Sc for making use of obscene language in Long- ford-street on the 23th January. ILLTREATING A Hoes-E.—Peter Lockett, •' Ring o' Bells" Inn, Daresburv, a youth, was summoned for illtreating a horse by working it whilst in an unfit condition on the 17th January.—?&r W H J Jenkins appeared far the defendant and admitted the offence, but said the case was not one of any seriousneas. The defcndant was, on the 17th inst. told by his master, fir Phillip 3, to go to the Slate Company's premises at Warrington tor 110 brick; and 2cwts. of lime—a very light load indeed. He did not tell the youth what horse he sheuld take, there being a number in the stable,and Peter foolishly took the worst horse in the stable. In Warringtoa Inspector Brown,ef the B.S.P C.A., saw the horse which had fallen lame en being brought on the setts. 14e asked the youth if be knew what the condition of the le,rse was, and he innocently said it had been lame "on and off." The horse as taken out of the shafts and another horse was sent for to take the load home. The Inspector was satisfied that Mr. Phillips was not to blame as he did not know thF t Lockett was using the horse—lnspector Brown having given evidence, the case as dismissed on payment of costs (16s).

div.p: Runcorn Petty Sessions. MONDAY.—Before idessrs._A. Thomas (presiding) and A R
Norman

A. FAMILY Jut—Charles Creswell, and John Cresswell, Miter and son, residing in ffelsun-strtet, Runcorn. had a row witn alother member of the family on Saturday night' which resulted in the mother going for Constable Wil quit, to restore orde*. The result of the Constable's intervention was that Charles Cresswell was proceeded against for ob- scene language, and John Cresswell for drunkenness. The former was discharged, and the latter lined 6s.

COIL DEALERS- FINED FOB SHORT WEIGHT.—Thomas Evans, coal dealer, in the employ of Hr. Samuel Crosby, was summoned by William Dunlope Laird, chief inspector of weights and measures for the County of Cheshire, for that he on the Bth January unlawfully offered for sale coal in bags of less weight than that shown on the label attached to the bags. —Defendant pleaded not gulity.—From the evidence of Mr. A. Timmins (weights and measures inspector). It appeared Evans was a coal carter in the employ of Mr. Samuel Crosby. On the Bth of the preseht month Inspecor Timmins met him In Alcock-street, and asked him if he was selling coal. He replied he was for Mr. Crosby and the price was 10d per cwt. There were tour bags in his cart and he asked him to weigh thorn. He did so and the *eighing was checked ey witness and his assistants. All four bags were 3, 12, 7or 6 pounds light of the "cwt" which was displayed noon the label of the bags. Defendant suggested to witness that the coal had been weighed In the scoop scale at the yard. Subse- quently the bags were weighed at the yard upon the original scale, and although there was a slight difference, the amount was still shown to be short Defendant a ,mitted the evidence of Mr. Timmins, but stated that ths coal had been weighed on the idaturday, and possibly had been tampered with after- wards.—ne magistrates did not think that was any excuse. He would be fined ICs and 9s 6d costs.—Willia n Henry Charlesworth, charged with a similar offence pleaded guilty. —ln this instance the Inspector said there were 14 bags upon the lurry only three of which were of eerrect weight. The discrepancies varied from about 14 to one pound. Defendant was a partner of the firm of Chariesworth and Enamel, coal dealers. Runcorn.—Fined lOs and 93 6d costs.

NEIGHBOULS AT VARIANCE.—NIary Clarke was summoned by Mary Blizabeth Bil Hinton, for using abusive language towards her on the 23rd of Januiry.— he reopie were neighbours in frivarn's Place, and had been broght to log- gerheads through a row originating with the children, whicu culminated In Clarke using the abuse complained of. Blizu- beth Basnett swore else heard the abase.—Defendant who denied the offence was fined ss.

Frodsham Petty Sessions WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs Charles Reynolds (presiding), A. Thomas, J. C, Taylor, and J. Crosfleid. DEFRAUDING Tag RAILWAY COMPANIES -blugine Hunt- ington, was charged with giving false inf ,rmation as to the quantity of milk despitched by her, on behalf of Mr. Jeffs, farmer, of Dunham o' th' Hill. by the London and North- Western and Great Western Railways, on the 11th. 15th, 16th and 17tb of November last, and Martha Huntington (her mother) was charged with aiding and abetting her on the same dates.—Mr. Penne, armoire," for the Railway Com- panies, and Mr. H. N. Linaker, defended.— it aupeared (hat the Huntingtons were in the habit of despatching milk on behalf of Mr. Jeffs to a Mr. Baohley.o° Weaste,the milk being consigned to him at Seedley Station. They forwarded him on an average 16 gallons a day in each of two tins, and filled up the " way-bill " to the effect that 14 gallons was the arnount.—Bvidence was given by Detective Sergeant 13 Croft, of the Railway Company, as to weighing the cans and finding there was more in than was shown on the way- bill, and also by a number of witnesses to the effiet that the defendants had admitted knowledge of that fact.— Mr. Buckley, 473. Bury hew-raid. Wens -e, the I consignee also produced bills w ich showed he had been charged for the full quantity and not fia accordance with the way-bill accounts.—For the defence Mr. Linaker submitted that his clients had no intention of defrauding the Railway Co., and the daughter had only carried out her moth-rs' orelers in filling uu the way-bills.—The mother, who was the sister-in-law of Mr. Jeffs, swore she was under the im- pression thst she could send 12 gallons and under for 9d ; and over that amount for Is, and that as she sometimes sent less than 14 gallons and sometimes o7er. she was striking a fair average by so doing.—The Bench considered there could ha no doubt abotr, a conviction, and fined the daughter 10s and lOs costs in each case; and the mother 103 and Vs costs in each subsequent case, or 14 days in default. The money £8 63 was paid. MINOR CASES.—Frederick Parker, of Frodahans, Was fined 5s and lOs 64 costs for trespassing in pursuit of game.-An order was granted to the Runcorn Rural District Council to supply water to houses in Helsby belonging to Messrs. Jirdsph Baton and William Jones.—Jos,ph Norcross for assaulting his wife and giving her a black eye, was fined 5s and 8s 6d costs. or H days. From the evidence of his wife it appeared that during the last year the man bad, not earned sufficient to keep himself, to say nothing of herself and the children. He was always in drink.—Defendant said it was owing to his bad temper that he emu ted his wife:—The Chairman : If I drunk like that, I too should be short tern- pered.—Edward Davies, for being found drunk was ordered to pay 5s fine—George Mains, who admitted using obscene language. whilst sober, was fined ss.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION. LANCASHIRE. SENIOR COMPETITION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION. LANCASHIRE. SENIOR COMPETITION.
Runcorn Win Easily at Warrington.

There was slain excitement in War.rington on Satur- day on account of the yisi,.; of Runcorn, the leaders of tha competition. Nimt people in tills part of the county would like to sec the Rtincorais.na win the trophy, bat

still there were more than a few who were siniihus co see Warrington inflict that long-egpected defeat on the " Linnets." Toe fact that Warrington only lost by a try at Runcorn encouraged these latter folk. Runcorn were determined to make no mistakes, and brought their strongest possible team for the occasion, Warrince•on snaking only one change, Swift for W. Ashton. During the greater porion of th match, the weather was fine, but towaris the 608 C a et srna of hail deseonded on the players. The ground was oo th.a soft side. Mr. Mc- Cutcheon (Oldham), was the referee, and the teams lined out before 5,000 spectators as follows : Runcorn: 8 Houghton, full back ; C Butterworth, J Butterworth,T Warder.and Wilkinson, three-quarters; Jolley and Faulkner,half backs ; Farmer, Gaytsr,Walker Lightfoot, k1ug1367, Darlington, Reece and Tomlinson, ferwards.

Warrington : Jones, full back ; Harris, Smith, Isher- , woad, and Fish, three-quarters ; Borgess and Allen, half ' backs ; Taylor, Baaralinan. Fairhurst, Swift, Elea, Ntoreweather, Scholz, and Hatton, forwards. Houghton won the toss and Runcorn took advantage of a strong breeze blowing almost from goal to god. Jones set the ball in motion, and a scrimmage followed at centre. -Runcorn got the ball out, and passing by Jo:ley, Faulkner and Butterworth, carried play into the Warringtoa half, Butterworth kmking the ball 'deed. Burgess dribbled away from the scrimmage and reached Houghton, the full back p'clainer up and clearing finely. Runcorn continnei to nave the best of matters, flouoh- ton trying unsuccessfnly to drop a goal. A mull by Isherwood oava the visitors a position on the home line. Burze3s kicke4 from the pack but sent the ball into Faulkner'a hands, and the latolir ran over smartly amid cheers from the Runcoru portion of the crowd. Jolley failed at goal. Warrington now went off with more dash and forced Runcorn back. Burgess kicked trickily across to Fish, and the wing man doaged splendidly to the line, only to be floored from behind by C Butterworth. Jolley and Butterworth sent Warrinoten back, Harris running across to save near the 25 flag. He secured and then lost passession,the Run- earn forwards sweeping past him to the line, where Gayter got a particularly soft try. No goal followed. Warder was soon to the fore with a dashing run, and Warrington had to act continually on the defensive, the strong wing making their efhrts at attack useless. A knock on by Houghton gave re'ief, Isherwoad following up the advantage with a fine run and punt. The ball went in touch however and was soon back in the home ' half. Jolley punted loftily from a pack, and Jones stumbling when going for the ball, Faulkner was able to Profit by good following up and scored lochiad the posts. Jallev bad no difficulty this time in landing a goal. Faulkner and C Butterworth ran And passed well, but were checked nsar tie line. Then Fish made another splendid individual effort, failing by a trifle to cross the lino. Half-time came with Ruac on leading by eleven points to nil. Farmer restarted, and Burgess returned. Warrington were slow to take advantage sof the wind, and J Butter- worth led the way into the home half, where Jones ' rarissed him promptly. Smith and Harris started the attack for Warrington and Runcorn had to fall back, Jolley marking with great coalness near the goal. Even yet Roncorn had the best of matters, Warrington play- ing in a spiritless fashion both forward and back. Fish ' and Burgess were the only two who seemed to have any dash waar,over. Tae two Butter °alas male several dashing runs along the right, but found Fish too watch- ful for them,and their efforts at scoring came to nought. Houghton took things easy, and for a :pit of gallery play was tackled heavily by 51ereweatlier and bait. Be was soon able to resume and amused himself by kicking into touch on every opportunity. Warrington made one or two spasmodic rushes. bat the Ruucorn defence was impouetrabla, and the final came withqhe score readiog: Etuncora 1 goal, 3 tries ; Warrington nil.

div.head: Runcorn Turn the Tables on Stockport.
div.p: Runcorn Turn the Tables on Stockport.

Before a crowd of about 3,000, a Ir well-lane on Wed nesday, the return match between Runcorn and Stock port was duly played off. As will be vcollen:ed Stock- port so far have proved the only succsssful team against Runcorn in the Lancislaira Senior Competition, when they secured " two "points fro.n Runcorn, by defeating them at Stockport by eight points t 3 nil. Naturally the game excited considerable interest, not only as affecting the League, bat also as having at stake the champion- ship of Cheshire.

The game opened rough aryl continued so. Within three minutes of the start Jo?ley secured an advantage to the Linnets by dropping a fine goal. Play continued fast, but developed wares as regards roughness. Foster was turned off for striking one of the Runcorn men. Fluirsorn attacked and from a beautiful passing bout by Faulkner, Warder, J But!.erworth, and C Butterworth, the latter got in at the corner. Jaßey converted. Stock- were hard pressed, but defended magnificently, and for a time kept their charge intact. Breaking away Stock- port had to retire at the biddiog of Eieughton whose dodging wag magnificent. Nothing further routed up to half-time when the score wai :—Runcorn 2 goals, 1 try (7 points) ; Stockport nil. When the gams re-opened Wilkinson and Houghton made a lot of geoued for the home team, and a pro- longed stay was made in the visitors' half. Saville clearid and gained a respite, but good footwork on the part of Walker, Farmer, Darlinotoa and Wilkinson, agein took the oval close to the visitors' posts"! Jolley was conspicu- ous for clever work. A suoces4ion of marks prevented anything tangible. Later Jolley started a nice move and C Butterworth was responsible for a good run, Saville, however, brought bins up. A bewildering melee occurred shortly afterwards under the Stockport posts, but no try resulted. Stockport would not allow the gams to open at all and Run- corn could not find a sinzle openin. Butterworcn was within an ace of scoring.; and so too was Faulkner. At last Wilkinson got in at the bottom corner, and left Jolley with an ;awkward one to improve. His attempt just want under iustoad oE over the bar. Stockport towards the latter portion opened out and pressed for a few mioutns. BottArworth marking caused a change. Hodgson took a-beautifel pass, but 'ma too keenly tackled to improve it. Stockport now played like a beaten team, and before the end a further goal was drepoed by Jolley.—Fiaal result : Rencorn 3 goals, 2 tries, 12 points ; to nil.

div.head: Runcorn A. v. Warrington A.
div.p: Runcorn A. v. Warrington A.

The unfavourable weather on Saturday, resulted in but a small crowd assembling to witness the match bs- tween the above teams at Runcorn. Warrineon turned up in full strength, but Runeorn, though at home coull only prevail upon 14 men to don jerseys. The game that resulted was a spirited one, and during the first half Runcorn more than held their own. S. Langley scored a brilliant try, fairly diving for the line. Williamson's attempt at conversion proved a failure. Nothing further resulted up to the interval. At the commence- ment of the second half Richardson. the Runcorn half, had to retire having injured his ankle. Although left with but thirteen men Runcorn still pressed, and a further try was eAcured. by Messner. Darbyshire failed to improve. Warrington played up with remark- able vigour, and Duckworth grst an opening and scored, after a brilliant run. fne mint was not augmented.— Final result : Runcorn A 2 tries ; 6 points; Warrington A 1 try, 3 points. div.head: WARRINGTON CUP. Third Round. Warrington v. Newton-le-Willows.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON CUP. Third Round. Warrington v. Newton-le-Willows.

At 'Warrington, Osfore a poor gate. Warringt )n were unfortunate in having to take ttio field vritnout Hunter, Sanders, and Tornkinson, this eluding a re-arrangement of the Learn, Glover taking Tonakitison'a place at back ; Graham, the right halt, being UrattNito inside right,and Jones, the trainer, takia4 the centre nalf position. War- rington kickcd off, and at:nos scored in the first minute Horrocks saving finely. Toe game soon settled down to a typical cup-tie one, science being at a discount, and the strong rushes of the Newton lads completely upsetting the combination of the Warrington forwards. Several corners fell in quick utiecession to Newton, but iisninall was, very sale. Spl-,ndid work by Riley caused Horrccks to again handle, and this brought about half-time with no saore havinz occurred. The opening of the second half found Ne a-ton pressing strongly, Glover saving well by tgoo.l kicking. War- rington next attacked, Coono,i, Murray, and Riley, hav- ing shies at Horrecks, wno proved himself invincible, an), Hougnton outt.ing the visiting forwards in posses- sion, Botler scored with a neat shot, amidst strenuous appoila for of:bile, hut the referee, Mr. Deardea pointed to the centre. A. blindtag snowstorm now broke over toe ground, the p!arri Is:•epiug their feet with difficulty. Warrin4ton attacked hotly, the ball bobbing about the visitors' ,goat fajlian, but Laitinwaite and Horrocks delendoil graniiy. Keeding it up Warrington pressed hotly till the call of tune, font could not score, the conclusion of the game arriving with Newton, one ; Warrington, nil. 'Pis winners Wr!rFi best represented by Ellis, Houghton, and Elorrooks, while Glover, Riley, an 1 CoArior were the pick of ‘Varricigten.
Northwich Victoria v. 'Warrington Trinity
Athletic.

This tie vvis played on the Drill Field, Northwich, on Saturday. The visitors arrived au hour late, end a pro- test was loged. Tee Vies pressed herd, and in clearing a fast ehoe from Torn'lesion Jones heaaed through his own goal. Muskett was aeain seen to advantage, as ho threaded his way throuel the visitors' defence and scored the second goal with a beautiful shot, quits out of the reach of Shear. The vis\nrs strove hard to score, but they scarcely sueceded it, reaching the half-way lioe,and were easily driven back. Play was now in the Warrington quarters,bet Shear cleared grandly on several occasions Not to be denied, however, the Vies attacked strongly, and after several rutile attempts Birkenhead scored the third goal from a pass from Drinkwater. Keeping up the pressure the visitors' defence was kept busy and their glal escapee miraculously. Shots from the whole of the Nerth wich for wards struck the posts and net. At last Muskett shot hard into the hands of &ear, who fumbled the hail, and allowed it to roll into the goal. This brought about half-time with North- wich leading by tour goals to nil. The second half was opened in extremely uncomfortable climatic conditions, as sleet and wind cogeeher, combined with the greasy state of the ground, made accurate play impossible. Ball and Hewitt made a few nice exchanges, but their final efferte lacked sting, and they were feebly supported. Northwich again coon took up the running, and Qrink- wat.r scored the fifth goal. After this reverse Warring- ton were completely demoralizei, and with the consent of the referee the game was abandoned on alcount of the wretched state of the weather, and darkness having set in.

div.head: FROD SHAM.
div.p: FROD SHAM.

PAROCHIAL COMMITTER.—ni) ,monthly meeting of the Frodshatn Parish Council, acting as a Parochial Com- mittee, was held in the Court Room, Frodsllarn, on Fri- day evening, Mr. C. E Lineker (in this chair).—The Clerk :Inverted that he heel been informed it was the duty of the Sureeyor and Inspector to attend the meet- ings of the Fem.:hie! Cennenitteee.—The Clerk read a letter from Mr. Jenaes Edwerds declining to give the name of the Councillor who had intimated that the Towne' Police Clauses lied not be fully considered when they were first discussed—The Chairman did not con- sider the reply a sttisfactory one and it was resolved that an answer tie sent to that effect.—The Inspector drew attention.to the rule; regarding the lights carried by vehicles, including lurries drawn by horses, and the difficulty he had experienced when driving in passing lurries with three horses, one light bsing insufficient in his epinion. It was resolved that the Clerk communicate with the Cheshire °aunty Council suggesting that two lights be used on lurries having three horses. PARENTS SENT TO PRISON.—A DISGRACE TO FR?DSHAM. —John Antrebu3, and Eizebetle Antrobus, of Newtown, Frodsham, charged before the Frodsham Bench, last Wednesday, with neglect and cruelty to their five chil- dren pleaded not guilty.—Mr. Kn levies (Widne3), prose- cuted en behalf of the N.S.P.C.C.—From the evidence of Inspector Hackett, Sergeant Clays, P.C. Dickens, and Miss H. Powell, it appeared that the de- fendants were beth addicted to drink and neglected their childraa to an alarming extent. All the witnesses being of opinion that the children were being literally starved. Dee borne was in a filthy state, the description of which was most revolting to heeribeing "more fit for pigs than human beings." The balay was being fed on"potatoes and hot water." The children who were shown to the Bench, locked poor and thin; their little limbs being no fatter than ordinary brush "stales, notwithstanding that their ages ranged from 12 years to 13 months.—Dr. Selby, Fredsteam, said he had examined the children, especially the baby. In his opinion it was being starved to death, and if it did he would not give a certificate. The Child was organically free from disease, hut only weighed 12lbs whereas a child of the same age of normal conditions should weigh 24lbs at least.—Mr. Knowles intimated that the Society pressed that the de- fendants should be imprisoned, se that something could be done for the children by either sending them to the Workhouse or doing something otherwise for them—Defendants denied that they sterved the children, and admitted ttPat 24s CAMS into the house weekly, earned by the two elder sons aged 18 and 16 respectively. Defendant worked as a hay-cutter and got work when he could.—The female thought that 24s was enough to" keep the table agate aeyhow," and denied the charge of starvation.— The Bench considered the case was fully proved; and the Chairman reinerked that such a condition of things as disclosed, wasa diserace to defendants and to Fred- sham. It was most serious, for if the baby died—as the doctor had stated—they would not be granted a certifi- cate, and would be in a moth worse position. They would both be ceinrnitted to prison for two months with hard labeur.—Mr. Keowlee intimated that the Society veruld look after the children. SUDDEN DEATH OF A CHILD.—At the Frodskam Police etation on Mniday afternoon, Mr. J C Bate, corener, held an inquiry into the circumstances relative to the death of Benj-amin Parkineen. aged 20 weeks, the illegi- timate son of Mary Ellen Parkinson, residing at 23, Volunteer-street, Newt„, Frodsham, whose death occurred on the 25:h in3t.—Mr. Shore acted as foreman of the jury.—Bets .y Parkinson, grandmother of the de- ceased,oteted that the child was born on September 4th, a midwife named Mrs. Connolly attending at the birth. She had since taken the child to the doctor's, and had received one bottle of medicine.—The Coroner : What was the matter with the child ? Witness : It did not take it food. I gave it the medicine given to me by the doctor, and it recovered. It was all right up to Wednes- day last, when it cemmenced to work its arms as if it was in great pain,—The Coroner : Did it cry ? Witness Yes ;it " yarled " a bit.—The Coroner. What did you feed the child on ? Witness : Sweet milk, sir, from Kydd's arid it came on like" wax." I sent him up to Dr. Burton's on Wednesday, but he was not at heme.— The Coroner: Was the child in a fit ? Witness: I did not know, sir. He continued having fits, but was alive when brought back from the doctor's. He died on Thursday. He did not d-ink a large quantity of milk on the previous day. I have had charge of the child, and he has been looked after well.- -Dr. Burton said he remembered the child being ; brought to him about the month of November. It was suffering from stomach trouble. He then treated the deceased, and it appe (red to brave kept allright. On the 17th inet. he vaceinated the child, and it was then per- fectly well and healthy. He had not since seen the child alive, but went to see it on the day that it died.—The Coroner : You are quite sure that the vaccination had nothing to do with the death. Had the inflammation suissided P—Witness : Quite sure. There was no inflam- mation. I have made a post-mortem examination, and found that the child was well-nourished, and the organs are normal, except the base of the brain, which was full of blood. The congestion was sufficient to cause death. Continuing', witness said he had seen the condensed milk, and it was the make mentioned. He had advised Ihe last witnes3 to ;live the deceased cow's milk.—The 0.)r,•7 : '!" VS the Swiss milk has been found to act as well as cow's milk.—Witness : It has, sir. As far as I know the child has been well looked after.—The jury returred a verdict or death from congestion of the brain, otherwise natural causes.

div.head: RATE OF MAINTENANCE IN COUNTY ASYLUM.
div.p: RATE OF MAINTENANCE IN COUNTY ASYLUM.

Mr. A. Hornny, clerk to the committee of yiAtors, wrote stating that at- a meeting of the committee held on 17th January, the rate of maintenance of pauper lunatics in the County Asylum. Chester, for the quarter ending 31st March nest, wai fiKed at 7s 7d per head per week.

div.head: COST OF AIAINTENANCE.-A COMPARISON.
div.p: THE COST OF AIAINTENANCE.-A COMPARISON.
The Clerk oroduced a st4terneut, as instruteci, show- ing the number .anct cast. of vaccinations in thA Reveral public vaccination districts during the years 1898 and 1899.

Mr. Spruce pointed out that under the old system a nunabr of pf7rsons efeeted to ha ee cases done at their own homes br a private doctor and consequently bore the expenses, but und,r the new system all cases were paid for out of the public funds, hence the great in- crease.

The Clerk said the figures did not loch' le all the cases vaccinated, but ot course there were not as many who paid for their own cases as there were formerly. The Chairman thought it hardly likely, now that the public vaccinators attenled the houses ot people that they would engage a private doctor. At the same rime the fees wanted revising. He was afraid they could not propose a reducuion for the simple reason that they had already adopted the minimum fees. The Clerk : Not entirely. The Chairman. Was there a special Committee to deal with this mattr last year.
Thl Clerk replied there wa.s a committee, but it was not in existence at present.
Mr. Spruce: I believe it wa3 the Parliamentary Com- mittee:
Mfr. Liaaker said the amounts were a very lar,c_;e in- crease.
Mr. Norman I h £2OO a year of an increase. With refonulce to the minimum chargeg, he supposed that the medical officers were not com.)elF.:d to charge them if they did not care to.

The Clerk said the Local Government Board would not sanction anythina. 103E4 than the miuimum faes. Mr. Norman said h wnt, vuts not the fee for viyit- ing .the houses larttely left in the hats of the doctors ? . . _
'T he Clerk pointed out that the fees we:e is 6-1 and 59, and 75 61 for certain distances.

Mr. Norman, referring to the charges for the distance, thought it would be as well if they could have an analysis of what the cost had been for toe various dis- tances, and tnea try and appoint public vaccinators so as to avoid these long diAarecna. lie certainly th eught something ought to be done to lessen the cost. He sug- gested the appointment of more medical men as public vaccinators to reduce the long distances. For instance, instead of the public vaccinator for Alvanley being at Frodsham, he would suggest if there were a medical in at Alvanley that he should be appointed to do the work at his own door, ins:cad of the public vaccinator having to travel all the way to Alvanley. The Chairman said he did not think there was a Medical Officer at Alvanley. Mr. Linaker : There is one at lielsby. Th, Chairman : I do not know whether the law would allow the medical men at Helsby to do the work. Admiral Jones Parry said the increase was so great that it might be considered whether they should not pay a salary to one medical officer for the whole union.

Mr. Nursan said he would like i-o—see every medical officer appointed as a vaccination officer. They had to attend the births, and if they simply vaccinated their own cases their fees would be consequently less. The Chairman said that in some cases the medical man had to :make two visits, one when he performed the vaccination operation and the; second to see whether it had talcAl effect. So that when they considered that a j mrney of six or five milos had to be made,the charges could not be considered exorbitant.

Mr. Norman askel if they had power to appoint more public vaccination officers, and if so how many ? The Clerk replied he could not answer that question without referring to the Loo Gpvernment Board. He had not hoard of anything of the kind beim, done. Mr. Norman proposed, Dr. Gastaldi seconded, and it was carried that the whole matter be re-considered.
FINANCE COMMITTEE.

M. Thomas Wright submitted ad proz:m.teei the adoption of the Finance Committees report. Outrelef was granted AQ follows:—Runcorn, £B3; Frodsham £23; Budworth, £23. Mr. Chadwick s9con&d, and the report was adopte d. 'SEAMEN VERSUS FARMERS "-WHAT TO DO WITH THE ROTS.

Mr. R. G. Gower, secretary of the Orient Steam Fish- ing Company, Limited, Grimsby, wrote under date January 19, as foll3ws :—" This company is prepared to accept a few healthy lads as apprentices to the steam fishing industry. The bays must be about 14 years of age and be passed by the Medical Officer of the Union. We are permitted to refer to the Chairman of the Grimsby Board of Guardians (Mr W. Southworth), and if neceeleary to one or two institutions and union that we have bad boys from previously. No premium will be charged in the present eve% but in the event of the lads after the usual two months probation desiring to return home the Guardians will be expected to pay their return railway fares. If you have any suitable boys who are willing to got° eea yen will find this a good opportunity." Mr. A. Wellesby Bremner, in reply to the Guardians' wrote from the Liverpool Training Ship"lndefatigable,' re boys for sea training. That their terms were still the same as far the last two boys viz., 7s per week and £5 for outfit when sent to sea. fie further forwarded the names of the boys and the dates of their leaving this ship, during the past year from the Runcorn Union,viz., John J Ketteringham, 21 October,lB99. as. "Jamaican"; and John Delaney, 3 May, 1899, es. "Iberia." Another letter stated that their aee limits were 12 and 15 and standard of height, according to medical form enclosed. They would be glad te receive afo v bays of good phy4que as the demand is very good. From the Master's report it was seen that Captain Bremner, of the training ship Indefatigable visited the house on the 29tis January, with the intention of confer- ring with the Guardians as to the boys who were thought proper candidates for admission to the training ship. He regretted that he had made a mistake as to the date of the Guardians' meeting. He, however, saw the boys, and expressed his satisfaction with physical and Indian club drill. The terms mentioned were £lB 4s per annum for each bey elating his training, and £5 for out- fit on going to sea. Six boys were selected by the Cap- tain as meeting the requirements as to physical drill, subject to medical examination, and the annual tests as to eyesight, etc. The BOUM Committee had considered this matter, and recommended that the boys be sent on the terms stated.
Mr. Clarke thought the 13,.?5t outlet fer these boys' ser- vice wag en the farm. His experience was that boys who went to farmers did well, and received a good trainiuz.

Mr. Williams said his experience was that when boys had been seat to farms in Frodsham district they had gradually drifted from their observation. Mr. Clarke said his knowledge of agriculture had been as valuable to him as anything else he had learned. Mr. Norman believed in giving these children a good start in life. In the most extreme case they would not have to pay the morey for more than 18 months. The boys received a good training and a good start in life. If Mr. Clarke wanted any boys he had no doubt he could be accommodated. Mr. Clarke: On the same terms, £l9?

Mr. Norman: Oh no. (Laughter.) Mr. Linaker vinted out that it was most desirable that s-mte boys should not go to farming inasmuch as they would be brought under the evil influence of their parents, and would do till farmer no good. He did not quite think that the boys under notice were the sort that farmers might wish to have about their premises. Admiral Jones-Parry said the advantage of sending these boys to the ship was the special training they would get from the masters. He commanded a training ship for some 17 years, and he thought about 15 per cent of the boys sent to sea were officers in the service now. They could not do that on the farm.
The recommendation of the committee was adopted.

I British force with artillery is reported to have entered Prieska unopposed, and to have now encamped there. The village of Priedra is situated on the banks o the Orange River about 100 miles below Orange River Station westward of Kimberley The Cost of General Buller's Flanking Mo iement. The War Office issu3d on Wednesday night what is hoped will be the final list of casualties in connection with Sir Redsere Butler's fl inking mevement. It givem the losses incurred in the ranks during the occupation of Spion Kop last Wednesday, and shows 139 killed, 393 wounded, and 62 prisoners or missing, a total of 594. Adding to these. Vie casualties; in General Lyttelton's Brigade during hi 3 support- ing attack on the hill, ani the officers in both forces, we have a total of 816, the number killed being 201. The 2od Lancashire Fusiliers and the 2nd Royal Lancashire Regiment had the greatest number o ea hit, and Thornevcroft's Mounted Infantry and the mperial Light Infantry (a ni w oorpe lat.3ly raised in Natal) also suffered heavily. div.head: Warrington Policeman at Magersfontein. The Use of the Sewing Needle.
div.p: A Warrington Policeman at Magersfontein. The Use of the Sewing Needle.

Police-Sergeant Lewis has received the following letter from P.C. Samuel Howard, a member of the force who is serving in the Grenadier Guam's under Lord Methuen: --Dear comrade—Just a few lines in answer to your welcome letter. I am glad to hoar that all the chums are doing well. Jack and I are still alive and kicking after a hard struggle. We have had four battles :—Bennont, Graspan, ['dodder River, and Magersfontein. The first three we had in a week, but we had to stop at Modder River for about nine days while we made a railway bridge across the river in place of the one the Boers had blown up. The first shot that was fired was at Bel- mont, and our batt dion was about the first into it; we bed ab-ut 126 casualties. It was about 2.30 a.m. whsn we advanced on the enemy, the daylight just breaking. We disturbed a fisck of birds, something like ducks, ad they kicked up a row which gave the g me away. When we were about one hundred yards off the foot of the hills they (the beers)epened fire on us We did non wait to get orders to charge but went tear- selves,which surprised the Beers. When we got to the top we showed them how we could US3 the sewing needle' on the end of our Wien We scoured the hills and drove them away in four 'hours and a half, mei captured their camp and tons of ammunition and rifles. We have lost our three officere in my company, two wounded and ova (Lieutenant Blundell) killed- When we formed up after the battle there seemed to be only half of us The Bears are very cunnieg;as soon as they think it is getting too hot for them they do a "nip." The Modder Riee-r was a hard fight. We were taken by surprise. The enemy were entrenched close to the river, and we were marching towards them, laughing and talking not thinking of them at all, when all of a sudden they blazed out with a tremendous hot fire ; I never saw such a thing in my life ;it fairly rained bullets. We lay down flat wish our faces on the ground for a minute or so while their fire slackened. Then we jumped up and ran for our lives into the firing line and started our work' They have a lot more artillery than us. They have some Krupp quick-firing, guns which make an awful row. We began firing at about 5 a.m., and we did not stop until it got dark, at about 7 p.m. We were without a drink of water or anything to eat, and it is so hot in the day- time. They kept fighting harsi as well as us till it got dark; I thought we were going to get driven back. Our men got scattered all over the place, and about a dozen of us wandered into a mud hut but an officer came along and told us we were in danger of being cut off. He took us to a trenelk near the river where w e found about forty more men of our regiment. We then received orders that we should have to drive tbe enemy from their position at the point of the bayo- net at break of day. We expected a slaughter next morning, but when We made the attack we found that they had done a guy. They have taken up a position about 51 miles off, and we may as well try to take the rock of Gibraltar as attempt to get them out of it. On December 11th we advanced and started fighting at about 3 a.m., keeping at it until about dinner time next day ; firing was going on at the dead of night. We had to retire next day as they were too strong for us. The Highland Brigade suffered terribly ; they were marched against the hills in Tauter calumn• That was the fault of the guides leading them there in the darkness; they might as well have taken them to a slaughter-house. I We have some English bred men as guides who are doing • nothing else but leading us astray. One of our men got two years to-day for sleeping on his poet. The next min that is caught at it will suffer the full penalty, that is, will get shot. Many people at home think that the Boers can do nothing, but they are mis- taken : they (the Boers) are the hardest foe that ever England fought with. I would not care if we could get at them, but the "brutes "at you call them, are liks rats in the hills. They have some Keffirs who hold their horses while they are fighting. When we are get- ting close they leave a few men to keep firing while the others gallop away, then these few men give themselves up as prisoners. It's a fly move. They are always using the whitellag, and when a men goes to them they blow his brains cut. I forget to tell you that at Belmont, after the battle was over, about three of us stood talk- ing together, when, with the corner of my eye, I caught sight of a hat down a hole. I got my bayonet underneath it to brine it to the top, but I found a man under it with rifle and ammunition. I was just going to Put him out of mss 'when an officer stopped me say- ing "Give the man a chance," but he (the man) would not have given me a chance hal it been the other way about. The officer said 'Take him prisoner,' and I made him hand over his rifle and haversack, which latter was full of ammunition. I then ordered him up ;my blood was fairly boiling, If I live to get home I will be able to tell you a tale. If I were to tell you what we go tbregeh, you would say I was down on my luck. Jack (P.C. 33, Hurst) sends his respects to you all. You must excuse the writing.as we are soldierieg under difficulties That is all I have ts say at present. From your old friend, Sam, wishing you all a happy New Year, and God bless you. Privets 5412 SAMUEL HOWARD, 3ei Grenadier Guards, South Africa."

BUGLER A. CHEW, OF WARRINGTON-KILLED AT LADYSMITH.

The above is taken from a portrait of the late Bugler Arthur Fitchew, of the. 2nd Rifle Brigade: who formerly resided in Knutsford-road, Warring- ton, and who was killed in the recent engagement at Ladysmith. The deceased who entered the Brigade at the early age of fourteen years, had seen active service in the Soudan and Crete, taking part in the battles of Omdurman and Khartoum. He was twenty year of age, and was the grandsan of the late Mr. Isaac Fitchew and of Mrs. M. Fitchew, who lives in Knutsford-road, by whom he had been brought up from childhood: •

div.head: RUNCORN'S "SOLDIERS OF THE QUEEN."• • Entertained by Mr. S. Taylor.
div.p: RUNCORN'S "SOLDIERS OF THE QUEEN."• • Entertained by Mr. S. Taylor.

The Drill Hall, Runcorn, presented a remarkable sight last Monday evening, when the Volunteers selected to repreFent the Runcorn Detachment or the 2nd Volunteer Battalion, Cheshire Regiment, in South Africa, together with the remaining members and reservists, were enter- tamed to a eupp r by Mr. Samuel Taylor. Decorated most tastefully with digs and bunting the vast hall in ked its best. " Union Jaake " iwermingled with " Stars and Stripes" and large mottoes bearing " Goi save the Qaeen " testified to the sentiment of the even- ing, a truly patriotic one. Mr. Taylor's daughters had prepared a feast of good things, and with their own hands set out the boards in most inviting fashion. Mr. F. J. Norman preened, and there were also pre- sent :—Mr F Wiswail (chairman of the Urban District Council), Major Harisson, Cep:ain George F Asntos, Lieutenants Brundritt and Linaker, Messrs James Hand- ley, E Isnison, J W Lightburn, Dr McDougall, Dr McLennan, Mews R 13 Posnett, T Sheard (secretary to Messrs Re wmau, Tnompson and Co), A R Norman, F A Lake, E Marshall, W Rowland, E Horsfield, 0 A Timmin., A Timmins, T Jones, F Johnson, Superinten- dent Pearson, J M Frith, G 8 Frith, R Abel, T C Had- doek, Ex-QuarterMaster Hankinson, Sergeant-instructor Gallagan, Colour-Sergeants Mort and Harvey, Sergeants Rushton, Edwards, Cooper, Holmes, Matthews, Ex•Ser- , geants Platt, Phoenix, and Woodland, and Lance- sergeant J F Edwards. Toe Chairman said it was a great sorrow to all of them that Mr. Taylor was unable to take part in that night's proCeedings. He had been in Mr. Taylor's bed- morn that afternoon, and Mr Taylor told him that it was one of the greatest disappointments of his life that he was unable to do honour personally to the six Runcorn men who were leaving the British shores to fight for their country. (Cheers.) Mr I aylor further said he itonld be diaappointed if his absence in any way damped toe pleareire sr enthusiasm of the proceedings, and he should be delighted, on the contrary, to receive a report that the gathering had been bright, encouraging wad altogether successful. (Cheers.) When the tables bad been cleared, a lengthy toast list was gone through, interspersed with selections by the Volunteer band, vocal pieces, and selections on the grarnaphone by Mr. W. Booth. Toe Chairman said well nigh 70 years ago, millions of loyal chairmen had called upon millions of loyal subjects to honour the toast of the Queen. ' In the presence of se many soldiers of the Queen, and so many loyal civilians who graced that board that night he made no doubt as to the reception it would receive at their hands. Never before in the reign of their Queen had their loyalty been so supreme ; never before had her throne been so thor- oughly established in the hearts of her people. At that moment of a great national crisis, with dark clouds hanging over them, they prayed perhaps more seri- ously than they ever prayed before, "Oh I Lord our God, arise Scatter her enemies," and with confidence they appealed to Him to" send her victorious ; happy and glorious. Long to reign over us. God save the Queen." He gave them the toast of the Queen. The toast was received with loud and prolonged cheering, the company singing a verse of the National Anthem. Mr. Imison proposed " The Army, Navy, and Reserve Forces," sod said with regard to that portion of the toast which was more intimately connected with the reason of their gathering that night, he thought it was unfair that a great portion of the expense of the Volun- teer forces should fall upon the officers. It should be the duty of the community or the state to provide rifle ranges where men might acquirethat skill in marksman- ship which the present campaign had illustrated most forcibly the need of. He a;so thought it was the duty of every citizen of suitable age to join a Volunteer corps —(apptan e) —as sores tenure for the benefits they enjoyed as Citizens of this great Empire. Be sincerely hoped that the result of this trouble we were passing through might be, as he believed it would be, to weld all classes of the country together in closer bonds of union, and to make every man in this country feel that his first and primary duty was to sacrifice his life, if need be, for the benefit of his Queen and country. (Cheers.) Major Harrissen,in responding to the toast,said it was his pleasant privilege, a privilege of which he wag justly proud, to thank them on behalf of the Navy, Army,and Reserve Forces, for the kind way in which they had re- ceived that toast: For the Navy he might Fay their pre- sent position showed them meat conclusively that they must continue to 'maintain their supreme command of the sea, which their Navy at the present time held. It was owing to that that they were able to protect their food supplies and commerce if there was any inter- ference with British right,. (Applause.) The Navy was the principal of the toast, and they must ever make it so—Britannia must rule the seas. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) For their work they had only to look at the deeds of the past few weeks in South Africa to convince them of what the British sailor was to • day. (Loud applause.) The British soldiers were unsurpassed by any soldiers in the world for heroism—(applause)—tact, courage, and enterprise. (Loud applause.) They might meet with reverses ; they meet with checks, but the British Army' never countenanced defeat. (Hear, hesr, and loud applause,) They were not going to be licked by a lot of dirty Boers. (Applause.) Speaking of the Volunteers, he said that war had cer- tainly created a more favourable feeling towards England's citzen soldiers, that had not been hitherto ex- tended to them. He referred to the fact that they had been asked to form service companies to fight their country's battles with their comrades the soldiers of the line. It was a crowning move for the volunteer move- ment which had accomplished much in the f ice of so much gross redtapism, legal obstruction, and officialism* (Hear. hear.) But the country was now showing its appreciation. They were all British subjects, be they colenies, or be they English. They had Brtiish hearts, and British hands, and they were ready to do their duty as well as everyi other selder wherever and whenever they were called upon to do so. (Hear, hear.) He had much pleasure in thanking them all on behalf of her Majesty's forces for Vol grand way in which they had received that toast. (Loud and continued applause.) The band then contr bated "The Soldiers of the Qneen." The Chairman said he bad now to submit to them a toast that sh -staid make the heart of every Runcorn man thrill and should set his pulse tingling. If they had been with him that afternoon and seen the earnestness of their host when in his bedroom he explained to him that the greatest disappointment of his life was that he could not be present that night in order to do honour to six noble men who were going from Runcorn. (Cheers.) He charged him again and again to see that it was given from the chair with as much zest as could pessibly be put into the matter. It seemed to him that if they were to properly appreciate what these noble men were doing for them they would follow him for a moment while he briefly reviewed the situation. To take the his- tory of this war in which they were now engaged : 20 years ago, General Buller who now stood fighting their cause in the Transvaal stood side by side, in fact led a company of Beers in their conflict with the Zulus, thanks to their British Army the Been were then net wholly ex- terminated by the Zelus They came to Majuba. He said the most magnanimous act that any empire ever did was their action on that occasion. But they all knew to their sorrow that that giorioue spirit that they then displayed was mis-interpreted for woa.kness. Since then they had enriched the country of these people with their gold and enterpriao, and.rocan while they had been treating Eng- lishmen like dogs, fortifying themselves and providing bullets for the breasts of the British,lrs. Tn. B-itish policy, cell it vaccillation, magnanimity or whatever theyliked—he was not going to discuss that—it had been a policy to stand by. Perhaps their statesmen hoped that in some way,through some untowara circumstance the'crimis would be averted, but they did not know this from Christian ministers, from natives, and otleere who were suffering that they remonstrated again and e gain, and the Government were imphired to put their foot 1 down and prevent once end for all the armament that had been t3kiri7 p!Pne for the last 20 years. And then there Wa.2 the: insulting ultimatum, the most insulting ultimatum ever launched againet any civilised empire .

div.head: EXAM !Nita?, FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 2, 1900.
div.p: THE EXAM !Nita?, FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 2, 1900.

in the world. It was nethiu,e; but base in- gratitude in his opinion. One of the black- I est pages of history was the base ingratitude ! which these people in South Africa had shown to the magnanimous treatment they had always received at their hands. Then they remembered that they marched into their territory, devasted their homes, and were slaughtering their soldiers who were defending their citizens in beleagured cities. They were entrenched in their fastnesses, and for the moment they were baffling the brave men they had at the front. It was going to be no picnic party to drive these men out, but they had got to go. (Cheers.) And these Runcorn lads were go. log to help to send them out. (Cheers.) Think of what this meant. They were leaving their homes, and those they loved dearly • they were leaving their trades ; they were placing their Lives at the disposal of their country. One of the noblest Englishmen that ever lived—Johu Ruskin—then whom no man had a keener appreciation of all that was worth having in life, placed the soldier above all the honourable professions of the kingdom. (Cc eers.) They had got six men before them that night who had qualified for that ideal of John Ruskin. (Cheers.) It was a time to try the nerves,and the pluck, and the courage of men. These military reverses that hung over them like a nightmare tried their pluck and courage, but he had never yet heard from the lips of a Britisher a tone of despair. The situation was black, he admitted, but it had its ewn consolation. England was never more true to herself than she was on this occasion. They were wag- ing a just war,and when its Rag was hoisted at Pretoria and Bloemfontein and when those ungrateful, ignorant, and corrupt republics had perished, he was certain that the Boers and Free Staters then would recognise, if they did not now, that the very hand against which they fought had only one intention, and that was to give them a greater freedom and purer laws. (Cheers.) Never were the colonies so completely in touch with them. And then they saw the magnificent response that their volunteers and home forces had made to the appeal. He did not doubt that if they fought hard and etuck tight they would see through this mischief. It was a glorious cause, and noble traditions which their noble volunteers were going to maintain, and he was sure they would join with him in honouring the magnificent ser- vices they were prepared to render, and the valour and determination they had placed at the command of their country, and in praying that divine guidance and divine protection might follow each one of them as they left their shores. (Cheers.) During the whole of the night one thought had been running through his mind. What would Colonel Ashton have:thought if he had lived to see so proud a day as that ? (Cheers.) God had taken him away, but he had on his left a worthy son of a worthy sire. (Loud and prolooged cheering.) Captain Ashton said he wished to thank Mr. Taylor for having ceupled his nams with that of the Chairman that night in proposing the toast of the evening. He was quite sure teat every volunteer present that night felt it. to be a great honour to be able to come to that hall and say a last good-by eto their volunteers who were going to represent them in South Africa. (Cheers.) When the order came down from the Cslonel asking for the same, of those who were willing to go for active service, 45 men gave in their names. They knew, of course, that all these men were not required, and he (Captain Ash- ton) went through the list and deletei the names of those who had wives and families, those who had not served sufficiently long, those who were under age, and those who were not first class shots. Eighteen men were submitted to the medical officer in Runcorn, and he selected eleven if thsne to go to Chester for further examination. The result of that examination was the selection of the six /1120 prsseat to represent them at the front. (Cheers.) He did not wish them to think that if in ire men had be JO required Ruacora could only have supplied six. Ouly six were aie.'cl for. If circumstances required it, they could supply a mush larger number of men either for South Africa or else- where. (Cheers.) He wished to say that the Runeorn detachment felt proud of the men who had been salected as their representatives, and they would veateh their do- ings in South Africa. They only asked that they would remember their country, their town, and the detachment to which they belonged. (Cheers.) If they did that the detachment, their town and their country would be honoured by their services.

The health of the six selected volunteers was thin drunk with enthusiasm,the company singing "For they are jolly good fellows," and cheering lustily. • Sergeant Jeacock responded, and observed that they were going out purely as voluntoers, and would do their duty. (Cheers.) Lance-Corporal Speakman also acknowledged the toast and promised those present that they would try and up- hold the tradition, of their regiment. (Cneers.) Dr. McDoegall proposed "Success to the British Arms." He feared their arms were at the present time somewhat under a cloud, but there was no cloud with- out a silver lining,and the silver lining under the present cloud was that the war had brought about a union of hearts that had not been exhibited at any period of the history of the British nation. They possessed that dog- gedness which he trusted would bring matters to a successful issue. Lord Rosebery told them that their wars were begun with blunders, but they had blundered through them,and they would blunder through this war and come out successful. (Cheers.) Mr. R H Posnett supported Dr. McDougall. Mr. J W Lightburn gave " The town and trade of Runcorn." In doing se he congratulated Runcorn on having passed its low water mark, a fact he attributed to the valued work of such men as Mr. S Taylor—(ap - plause)—aad their chairman (Mr. F J Norman), whose very personality had added to the trade of Runcorn, to an extent which most of them could not realize. Hav- ing referred to the historical and geographical aspects of the town, Mr. Lightburn submitted the toast, which was duly honoured. Mr. F. Wiswall (chairman of the Urban District Coun- cil) in responding thanked them for the way in which the toast was received. He could only say he was proud of the town of Runcorn • at the way in which the town had 40 years ago created the volunteer corps; at the way it had contributed to the war fund; and at the way in which it contributed six noble fellows te go and light its country's battles. Those fads made one proud of the town. (Applause.) Mr. J. Handley gave the toast of" The Host." He felt highly the honour of being entrusted with so important a toast as that of his old friend and generous host (Mr. Taylor). He was only sorry the submitting of the toast had not been put in better hands. But he would yield to none in his respect and esteem for his old friend. His generosity had been shown times without number by his enterprise in public life. (Applause.) An instance of his great heartedness was now before them in his wish to show his appreciation for those young men who had given their services to their country, and in his wish to give his fellow townsmen an opportunity of wishing them God speed in the und.rtaking. He thought they might call Mr. Taylor a diamond of the first water-- (hear,hear)—whose lustre had 'shone upoa. every public event in connection with the town for a great many years. (Applause.) Might he long live. (Hear, hear.) Might God spare his life to us for many year!. They could ill spare such men. They honoured and loved them. (Renewed .applause.) Mr. A. R. Norman spoke of the pleasure he felt at seconding the toast. Mr. Taylor's name in Runcorn was a household word synonymous with all that was geaerous good and true. (Applause,) The toast was received with musical honours, "For he's a jolly goad fellow," and rounds of applause and cheers. _ _

Mr. J. M. Frith, responded on Mr. Taylor's behalf. Mr. Imison said he would like to say how moch in debted they were to Mr. Taylor in that matter, lie thought on that occasion he had really done what the town ought to have done. He believed that when they saw six of their own Runcorn Redtails prepared to fight the battle of their Queen and their country it ought tacit to have been left to tbe liberality of one mac to offer them the hospitality they had all enjoyed that night. Mr. Taylor had a great heart, and he (Mr. Irnison) knew perhaps better than any man present hotv great his heart was. But he should like to say that much as they regretted his absence they were very much in- clined to cuieratulate themselves upon the deputy whom he had suppled them with. He did not know any man —perhaps it might se,m strange for him to say so—who had done more for the fund which had been raised for those left behind by the soldiers than Mr. Norman. Ho had been the champion redly of the town. He bid been the man that had shown that those who were inclined rather to deprecate the efforts which were made for their support in the absence of their husblnds were not really suffering at all, but that they were perhaps in a better position during the absence of the bread wioner than they were at the time when be was present. HA IWO emphatically that no man whom he knew had done more for those left behind toll* Mr. Norman hal done. (Loud and prolonged cheering) Mr. Imiaon then read the folowing 'poem, which, he intimated eminated from the pen of a Runcorn lady, who wished to retain her identity.

TO THE RUNCORN VOLUNTEERS. Go forth to your task in Afrie's far land. Resolve to dare all and make a good stand, For freedom, and might; for land, It me, and Queen. Be ready I Aye Ready I And never be seen To quail or to flinch in the fight. Be courageous, be brave, be heroes, be men, So that England, dear England. shall yet once again Be proud of the sons ef her Volunteer band, Who so gladly are leaving their dear ,native land, To win, or to die for her might. Our wishes go with you: oar prayers ; aye our tears, May God guide you all, so that coming yeal.s Shall find deep inscribe I on the roll call of fame, The deeds you have done, for old Bug land's great name, In the land of the Southern Cross. That your deeds by your townsmen will ne'er be forgot. Your memories will live in the hearts of the pure, If even to death yott are called to endure. And your country to bear your great foes.

The services of Mr Norman in the chair were acknow- ledged with three hearty cheers, and after singing toe National Anthem the company dispersed. At interval s during the speeches Mr. Booth gave on the gramaphon e "Soldiers of the Queen,' "Tommy Atkins," alad "Th e bugle call ;" Mr. Shaw sang " Toe song that will .never die ;" and Master Jack Rutter gave several patrioti songs for which he received an ovation. Private A. Cc Timmins accompanied the vocalists.

Departure of a Gunner from Weston. Gunner John Lightfoet, of the 14th Company of the ! ;Royal Artillery, which leaves England for the Cape as part of the Eastern Seige train eervice,is a reservist and ! married. He received orders to join his company at ! Cork, and decided to leave Runcorn by the 10.10 p.m. train for Holyhead, on Friday night. He leaves behind , him a wife and 2 children. So soon as the population of Weston discovered the fact, they made preparations accordingly. The Weston Works Band was requisitioned, , torchlights were procured, and alter the villagers had heaped upon "the gallant gunner" all the honours within their power, a procession of considerable dimen- sions was formed, and a move made for Runcorn. The majority of Runcornians had not been apprised of the move, but the appearance of such a formidable array approaching the town by Greenway-road, soon attracted the notice of all, with the mutt that the whole populace turned out to encourage another brave defender. As a result Runcorn Station was literally crowded out. Collections were made, and the usual gifts showered upon Lightfoot, who the better for people to belaold,was carried shoulder high around the platforms carrying a Union Jack. The final scene as the train left the plat- form was one of frantic enthusiasm, cheer after cheer ringing out, and hats, caps, 'kerchiefs, sticks and umbrellas beieg thrown up or waved in the air with an indiscriminaticn that beggared description. Church Parade at Runcorn. On Sunday, the general public of Runcorn were affor- ded a turther sight of the local volunteers accepted for the front, when they turned out at the head of their late compatriots tor church parade. The " F" and " " Companies of the 2nd Volunteer Battalion Earl Chester Regiment, under command of Captain G. F. Ashton paraded almost to a man at the Armoury, from whence they marched to the Parish Church, headed by the band and "Runcorn's Soldiers of the Queen." Large crowds occupied every wing of vantage along the route, bed- room windows and even lampposts being requisitioned by the zealous, so that a sight of" the men of the hour" could be seen, perchance figuring for a last time in such a pageant. Upon the return march the scene was repeated, only if anything, the crowd was consider- ably augmented. At the Parish Church the officiating ministers were : The Rev Canon Wood (vicar),and Rev HB Firth (curate). The service was the usual one, with the special Litany, and was intoned by the latter minister. The vicar read the lesson, and also preached, taking as his text the 134 Psalm, "Behold now, prais3 the Lord ; all ye servants of the Lord ; ye that by night stand in the house of the Lord : even in the courts of the house of our God. Lilt up your hands in the sanctuary ; and praise the Lerd. The Lord that made heaven and earth ; give thee bless- ing out of Sion." Addressing the volunteers he said : Some of you are going abro id, going to the front, and the rest of you do not know how soon you will be called upon. We even do not know whether our very last man may not have to go into danger either athorne or abroad. It wts good of them to show such spirit in following the example of the Volunteers of London and of many other great cities. They had well chosen, when some of them were going ta the front, that the house of God should be the last pace where they should assemble to spsnd their last Sunday, for, doubtless it would be a memory to them—a memory for sweet and good influence. They w Ind think, when they did think of the old town— the lsttle town of Cheihire—and would remember when thousands of milt 3 away one of the last impressions— the heating ef God's word within that seared building. Let that thought go with them—be with them always— that they were right, and that they had doee well in be- tog preseet that day. Addressing the men selected to go ;thread C snon Wood remarked that was the first time th es had been called uponifor service, a new and special work—and what could be said to any young man who was taking up tug service for the first time ; whit should he say if that young man cam and said to him that his heart was turned and that he felt naturally enxious about the work he was about to un lertake. He thought, however, that all would agree with him what— ever work a young man was beginning it should be his duty to say to him : Brothers do not think too much about your success in money making ; do not think too much about merely gotting on; do not think too much about what other people will say ; but do your best in that state to which it has pleased God to call you. He would have them recognise their inward re- spensibility as well as their worldly duty. He should recognise the great national cause. The duty set out for them, was their duty to their regiment ; their duty to their ceuntry,and their duty to their God. The latter was a source of inward gladness and they should let no msn push that motive out of their hearts. They were going into danger, into temptation and trial and they would he tried in many ways. They could notnay whether it woeld belphysical or spiritual danger,but they should remember they were taking the honour of their country with them. They should see that they' respected their own country, and so conduct themselves that their country would be respected, through their display of courage in danger, and mercyfulness in victory. They should go with a good conscience and Ilse Shakespeare's words " Conscience makes cowards of us all." He did not mean conscientieusness but a bad "conscience makes cowards of us all," and on the other hand, " Mv good blade carves the calicoes of men, My long lance thrusteth sore; My strength is as the strengtheof ten, Because my heart is pure." Says the poet Tennyson about a great and noble warrior. He would have them of a good conscience and true of heart, and let them take care that no one laughed them out af that, and they would be the better soldiers and better men.—ln conclusion the Rev. Canon spoke of the psalm, which had been the subject of his text, as illustrating, though there was a stream of men going out to battle, others were left behind whose duty it was to pray both day and night. And 113 was sure that the people of England would pray for them both privately and publicly, and as the priests had answered the Israelites of old as they streamed out of the temple he did not think thcre was anything more fitting to wish them than to wish " that the Lerd that made heaven and earth give them blessing out of Sion." During the service the band under bandmaster Outhwaite accompanied several of the hymns. The other cfficers on parade were :—Captain George F Ashton (in command), Major Harrison (Frod- sham), Lieut. W G Linaker, Sergeant Instructor Callag- han, Quartermaster Sergeant. W Hankinson, (special service), Sergeants : (F Company) : Rushton, Lea, Pheeeix, and Matthews ; Sergeants Woodland and .Platt (special service), (G. Company) : Sergeants Holmes, D Edwaids, W Cooper, and Lance Sergeant J Edwards. Presentation to Sergeant F. Si. Jeacock, of Runcorn. There was a meeting at the Brunner Guild Hall, Run- corn, on Saturday, pregnant with good feeling, when the workingmea at the Spinch Yard assembled to make a present significant of esteem and regard to their fellow workman Sergeant F. J. Jeacock, who is one of Run- corn's volunteers selected far the front. The chair was occupied by Mr. A. R•ivenseroft (presideat of the Ship- wrights' Association), and amongst those present were— Serge k tit Jeacock. Messrs J Holt (foreman at the yard), T Holt, William Rhodes, J J Bowyer, and Edward Kay (representing the apprentices).—The Chairman then called upon Mr. J. Holt to make the presentation, and in doing so he said he was glad to see they were all of the same mind. He took it that the presentation emiti- ated from the Spinch Yard, and he was proud to think that all the men in the yard—without excep- tion—had contributed to it. (Loud applause) He was a bit sorry that the original idea was departed from, but then it would leave been useless to present Sergeant Jea- cock with what he already possesred. And furthermore Sergeant Jeacock would now possess both binotulars and purse—and as they had put upon the purse the original inscription intended for the "glasses" in time to come when Mr. Jeacock returned from the war and was gathered round the hearth of his home with his little ones around him he would feel interested in explaining both the story of the "glasses" and the story of the purse. (Laughter, and hear, hear ) Fourteen years ago Sergeant Jeacock had no idea he would he in sach an enviable positien. He (Mr. Holt) had known him as apprentice, and in his maturity, and ceuld testify that his chiracter was so exemplary that any :ming man would do well to follow it. (Hear, hear.) Having sp 'ken of the high value to be set upon the three "P's" punctu- ality, patience, and perseverance, all of which Sergeant Jeacock nossesed, Mr. Holt concluded with a graceful eulogy and banded him ths present, with the w.sli of "God Speed and a safe return." (Loud applaaee.)—The assembly then sane "Rule Britannia" and "For he's a jolly good fellow."—Upon Sergeant Jeacock rising to rfseend he was greeted with three hearty cheers. Be was unable, he said, So find • words to express his thanks to them, as speech makieg to him upon an occa- sion o that kind was "awful." (lewd laugher.) Still he did thank them heartily.—Mr. Jeacockts brother, wha was present, thanked the assembly on his behalf and said he was pletsed and gratified ea find they had such a high opinion of his brother. To themselves (the family) the parting was a greet wrench, but there was bilm for the wound in thinking net his brother would do hie duty against" his man " if he was only allowed to "get at him."—Mr. Edward Kay (on behalf of the apprentices of the Spinch) wished Ser- geant Jeacock "God speed, and a safe return, and hereel he would remember them whilst in South Arlie sr" --Farther singing of patriotic and other songs concluded th meeting.—The puree, eratiete was a beautitul all leather one, was inscribed as fellows :—" Praseatel to Sergeant F. J. Jeacock by the SPinch Yard empleeees, upon his velunteering for active service in the Transvaal War, 1900." Volunteers Supper at Frodsham. On S the members of the I Company of the 2nd ! Earl of Cheater's V.B. partook of a supper, prepared at the Commercial Hotel. Frodiham, in honour of :.he three Volunteers, Privatet Frederick Evans, Thomas Carter, and Enoch Derlingten, who have volunteered for the front. After supper, the ueial tracts were proposed, and Major Harrison proposed the health of the men who were leaving their friends and their homes. Let:r, Major Harrison proposed the heilths of Lieatenente Garrett, Thornley, and Ashton, who were all 'interested

in the pres.nt war ; the first, named having just loft England, the second being appointed to take charge of the 2nd VB., and the latter was supposed at the present time to be resident in Lidysimth. 'rho pr.-Togal bay- ins: been r3sponded to Captain Ashton thanked the Major and the Company for their kind expressions towards Li.utenants Garratt and Ashton ;he would convey to Mrs Garratt the cordial words spoken, and on the earliest opportunity mak3 a point of mentioning the incident to his brother. During the evening a very interestino musical programme was gone through. Privates Evans and Carter expressed their thanks be- fore the meeting terminated for the kind expressions of opinion they had been the recipients a, and hoped that each would prove a credit to the I Company.
