div.head: Silver-street Sunday School Volunteers.
div.p: Silver-street Sunday School Volunteers.

On Sunday afternoon a presentation, consisting of a Bible and despatch book bound in khaki with a present in money, was made to Messrs. Albert Horton and Edwin Dale, young men in Mr. R. Corbett's class at Silver-st. Sunday sclaool,who had volunteend for service in South Africa. The presentation was made by the Superinten- dent, Mr. J. W. Hayward, J.P., who with Mr. Corlett and the Rev. C. H. Hocken gave an address, all most suitable to the ozcasion and assuring the young men of their loving and powerful sympathy for them. The ser- vice which was most touching concluded with singing the National Anthem.

div.head: Lymm Volunteers' Departure.
div.p: Lymm Volunteers' Departure.

Corporal John Clare and Private Harry Leigh, of the local Volunteer corps, who have volunteered for active service in South Africa, left Lyrnm for Chester early on Tuesday morning. On Monday evening there was a large gathering of the inhabitants at the Cross, and a procession,headed by the members of the Lymm Church Band and the Subscription Band, playing "Soldiers of the Queen," proceeded along Whitbarrow and &loth's- hill to the Drill Hall. After some complimentary remarks from Captain GTOV39, and the singing of " Auld Lang Syne," the procession continued along Church-green to the Cross, where a further demonstration took place. They were entertained to supper at the Spread Eagle Hotel, and left Ls mm early on Tuesday morning to join their comrades cf the 3rd Cheshire at Chester. Captain Groves gave handsome presents to each man, and a sum of about £l5 was also coilected for them by a few friends.

div.head: Newton Officer killed in Action.
div.p: Newton Officer killed in Action.

Mr. Hugh Stuart MeCorqu,dale, who was killed in action at Spion liQp, was the youngest son of the late Colonel McCorwiodale, of Newton-le-Willows formerly High Sheriff of Lin cashire. Mr. Stuart McCorquodale, who was born in 1875, was a sportsman of the bmt, type, and accordingly volunteered for Tnornoycreit's Horse, his services being at once accep to,c;
A Warrington Officer for the Front.

Captain Ridgway, son of Lieutenant-Col. Ridgway, commanding the Warrington Volunteers, who was re canny transh rrel to the S.-)uth StAffndshire Militia,has received orders to prneed with his regiment to South Africa. The militia !me England on the 9th of next month.

div.head: Send off to L. & N. W. Loco Volunteers.
div.p: Send off to L. & N. W. Loco Volunteers.

A smoking concert was held at th 3 Horse ani Jockey Warrimeou on Tuesday evening, January 23rd to bid "drod Sped" to C ,rporal Howard, and Privates H. War burton, W Blackwood, J H Low odes, and James Allen employees of the L. and N. W. Loromotive Department who have volunteered for service in South Africa. Mr. Marshall (Chief Loos Foreman) presided over a large gathering of their fellow workmen. The toast of "The Queen" proposed by the Chairman was drunk with musical honours. M. 1 Bate in a few well chosen re- marks proposed "Our Gueste," which was responded to by Corporal Howard. Songs wore rendered by Messrs. William Lee, A W Hill, William Shaw, F Kent, and M F.l Llewellyn, the latter also contributing an appropriate recitation entitled "My Dream." The Chairman thep preseated each of the Volunteers with a sum of money subscribed by their fellow workmen, following which Mr J S Bate, jour., gave a capital rendering of "The Absent Minded Beggar." A collection was made and the proceeds were handed over to the Mayor's Fund. A very enjos able evening was brought to a close with a hearty vote of thanks to the Ctiairman, and the Host and Hostess (Mr and Mrs Rush worth.) The Fifth Irish.

The men of the sth V.B. Liverpool Regiment, who are undergoing training at Orford Barracks, Warrington, have been visited by Mmsignor Nugent, who saw them going through the various exercises, and also preserved tbe:n with a copy of a poem entitled " The Irish Volun- teers."

div.head: Father Nugent's Attack on Warrington.
div.p: Father Nugent's Attack on Warrington.

Preaching at St. Paul's Church on Sunday evening the Rev E. R. Tarbuck alluded to the remarks made by Monsgr. Nugent at the banquet recently given at the Liverpool Town Nall to the officers, non-commissioned officers and men of the sth Irish Voluateer Battalion of the King's Liver pool Regiment who were subsequently sent to Orford Barracks. In the course of his speech at the banquet Monsgr. Nugent is reported to have said thet he know "no more dangerous place for young fellows to be quartered in than Warrington." This has called forth a reply from the Vicar of St PauPrewho said: he had worked with Monsgr. Nugent in social matters, and be knew his noble mind, and when he thought, of his position, social, moral and ecclesiastical, he was the more surprised to hear thet he should be willing to even seem to do an injustice that good might come. Be was sure his intentions were good, but they could not raise Warrington by unjustly villifying the town. Warring- ton was no worse than other tewns, and much better than some. Monsgr Nugent certainly would not help to purify Warrington by making comparisons which men who knew both Liverpcol and Warrington believed to be distinctly unjust ; he did not say that Warrington was as pure, as temperate, or as free from the gambling spirit as it ought to be, but, taking the people as a whole, it was his experience that tbey were as patient under rebuke, as responsive to earnest pleading, and as ready to co-operate with those who led in any good work as any he had had the privilege of working amongst. If each man in that congregation would do his best as a soldier of Christ he would not only be saved himself from sin and degradation, but help others at every step, and it would be a tremendous assistance to the congregation and promote the good of all our people.

div.head: Latchford Improvement Society.
div.p: Latchford Improvement Society.

The weekly meeting of this society we's held on Friday night in the Temperance Hall, Mr Ford pre- siding. Mr George Walker gave an address npon "Eternal Punishment." Questions were asked and answered, and the Bible alone made the foundation of belief and doctrine. Mr Tom Ford, Mr W Hill, Yr Joseph Corbett, Mr Drewitt, and Mr Harry Blease took part in the discussion, which was full of spirit and careful inquiry. Mr Joseph Corbett gave the interesting information that he hoped to be off to the front as a Volunteer at South Africa next Monday. The members wished him every suc- cess, and be premised voluntarily to send an essay entitled, "The Death of the soul, or Immortality and Eternal Life."
PUBLIC BENEM UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BES BOOTS IN LANOASEIIRE.—Advt.

Local Shepherdry. Th 3 alanual•report of tho Warrington District of the Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds has just been printed. It is signed by Bros.F S Massey, Pro U.S.; ' Thomas Miller, D.P.C.S. ; James Parr, District Treasurer; Pater Edgar, District Secretary. They stated that in reviewing the work of the past year they find that they commenced the year with 902 members, 77 have been admitted, while on the other hand they had lost by efispensions 58, and by death 9, leaving the number at the end of the year -at 912, or a net gain of 10. The total number of deaths had been 20, viz 9 members 7 wives, and 4 widows, which necessitated the sum of £192 being paid, or .£l6 more than the year 1898. The amount paid to sick members had been £631 14s 8d as against £523 Os sd. The funds of the lodges now stood at £4,176 lie Od or £213 73 70 more than the year previous, and which when added to the district funds of £507 is 51 made a grand total of £4,683 1235 d or again of £237 17s 4d. On comparing the forgoing figures with tiosJ in last year's report it would ne found that numerically an improvement had taken place, but still the progress made did not however,come up to their standard of expectations and desires.ln theiropinion they ought to enlist more recruits when considering toe present population of the town. It was however gratifying to notice that, in spite of the heavy drain that had been made upon the sick and funeral funds of the lodges, steady, and under the circum-. stances, satisfactory progress had been maue finan- cially and also to know that they had had the wherewithal at their disposal to mete out the assist- ance to the members in their time of need. In con- clusion they desired to express their best thanks to those members who had so ably exerted themselves for the good and welfare of their respective lodges, and especially to those, whose energy and persever- ance they owed the addition of 77 members who had been brought within the folds of Shepherdry. 'BEST BOOTS FOR ALL, UNDER Trtic CLOCK.—Ado ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS MINERAL WATBRS,—Advt.

div.head: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.
: P.S.A.

The weekly meeting of tne Earlestown and Dig- trict P.S.A. Society, was held in the Uo-operativa Hall, on Sunday. There was a gool attendance, over which Mr. J Hatton yesided. The principal speaker for the afternoon was Mr. Slater of Man- chester, who gave an interesting address. Recita- tions were given by Mies Newton, and vocal selec- tions were submitted by Miss Gutteridge. Mrs. Latimer presided at the piano.
SINGULAR ACCIDENT TO A HORSE AT EARLESTOWN.

Late on Monday night, Mr. Waywell, of War- grave-road, Earlestown, milk dealer, etc.. was re- moving a load of furniture from Brookfield-street, and when passing over the crossing at the end of the street, the cart tilted up, and, then came down heavily on the back of the horse, breaking the shafts, and internally injuring the animal to such an extent that it died almost immediately. The furniture was scattered about the roadway, and it was midnight before it was removed. GOOD TEMPLARY.—HOPE OF EARLESTOW.N LODGE.

A meeting was held in the Co-operative Hall, Wargrave-road, on Monday evening. Bro Cutler, C T presiding. After the opening services the Secre- tary read a letter regarding the arrangements for limelight exhibition on February 12 the receipts to have gone to the war fund but after discussion it was decided to abandon it,as the time was too short to make it a success. The sick committee reported several members ill. The Business Committee recommended the lodge to insure the lodge effects and that Bro G Clark be special correspondent and urged the .members to support the official organ of the order, the watchword,and to advertise the lodge in the District Guide. Several members being present from Ashton Onward the Chief Templar called on them to address the loge. Bro Speakman spoke as to the prospects of the Order in Ashton which were very encouraging. Bro Woods read the digest of No.l Convention also district lodge circular and ad- vance credentials for district lodge representatives. Bro Woods was recommended as Lodge Deputy for the coming twelve months.—Bro' s Clarke, War- burton, Woods, and Sister Owen were elected as re- presentatives to No 1 Convention and that tiro J Wilson, Sisters Wright and Mole be the alternates. The election of officers then took place resulting as follows ;—C T, Bro Catler, VT, Sister Williams, secretary, Bro Singleton ; assistant secretary, Brr* T iacklin ; finance secretary, T Leatherbarrow ; chaplain, Bro Dring ; marshal!, Bro Cumming ; deputy marshal!, Sister Mole ; guard Bro G Whar ton ; sentinel,Bro A Shaw; pianist,Bro Willis ;assis- tant pianist, Bro Ellison Bro's G Clarke, Single- ton, Macklin, and Woods, and Sisters William-, Mole and Owen were appointed as a programme com- mittee. EARLESTOWN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.

On Saturday evening an entertainment was given by the Co-operative Society to the children of the members. Occasion was also taken to present the prizes gained by children who on the 13th inst. had taken part in an essay competition on the sub- ject of "Dividend," the competition being open to members' children between the ages of 10 and 14 years. There were 8 entries, and the first prize was awarded to Mary Ellison 13 years old tor the following : —" Dividend means to Co operators that which is left to be divided after all expenses have been paid. Every member has a share in the profits according to the amount of business transacted during the quarter,and that is called their dividend. elach member must leave a certain amount of this dividend in the charge of the society and soon they have quite a little fortune almost without knowing it. A good Co-operative member will trade as much as possible at their stores, because they are sure of getting the best provisions obtainable. Not only do they get good stuff for their money, but they get dividend too. If you get your provisions at a private shop you will not receive any interest or dividend at all. The more things we get at the stores the more dividend we are bound to obtain. The expression "we spend to save" means that when we spend money at the Co-operative Stores we are at the same time saving it in the form of dividend. This reminds us forcibly of that well-known, per- haps no less true, maxim "Prepare for a reiny day." Mr. David Forrester,president of the society, presided at the entertainment, over 400 children being present. In a few remarks he gave some idea as to how the free entertainment came about. Referring to the essay compltition, he said it was some disappointment to find that only two boys entered for it, the remaining six being girls. For the essay the judges were Ressrs Clare, Swift and Forrester, and the following were the awards :- Ist, Mary Ellison, ; 2nd, Adelaide Jones, 3s 6d ; 3rd lhomas Kenny, 2s 6,1 ;4, Jonathan Smith, 2s; Louie Rawlins, is 6d; Gertrude Burke is. Consolation prizes, Josephine Kenny, and Alice Kitchen. The first part of the entertain- ment consisted of a pianoforte duet by Miss Jones and Miss Read ; songs, "Cuckoo "and "The Child's good-night," Miss Jones; songs, "Daddy " and "The little yellow coon," Miss Barr ; and humorous song, Mr J Huddlesion. The other part consisted of a number of limelight views of the Transvaal,and in- cidents in connection with the war. At the close. the children were each presented with a bag of sweets as they left the hall.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
A ST. HELENS DESERTER

Patrick Dowling, a young man of 3, Vernon-street, gave himself up at St. Helens Police Court on Sunday night, stating that he was a deserter from the South Lancashire Regiment, and wanted to go to the front. He had been absent from his regiment for about eight months. He was remanded to Walton to await an escort.
SUICIDE OF A COOK

Mr. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at St. Helens Town Hall on Monday, on the body of Louisa Horton, aged forty-two, who committed suicide on Saturday morning by drowning herself in a pool in the grounds of Haresfinch House, where she had been employed for two years as cook. Alfred Horton, of 10, Bagot-street, Wolverhampton, brother of deceased, gave evidence Of identification.—Annie Evans, housemaid at Alderman J. 0. Gamble's, said deceased had been cook for Mr. Gamble for two years. She last saw deceased on Saturday morring at a quarter to seven, when she got up and went dewLstairs. Deceased bad been attended by Dr. Masson for the past month. She often said the pains in her head were so bad that she thought they would drive her cut of her mind. On Friday night deceased did not want to go to bed, and said that if she could only have sat for about three hours she would have been better.—Bessie Richmond, another servant, said deceased disappeared from the kitchen shortly be- fore seven o'clock.—William Barnes, gardener for Mr. Gamble,sp ike to finding the body in a pool of water in the park, about a quarter to eight. The body was about ten feet from the side. It was not recovered for nearly an hour.—The Coroner: Are you imbued with the stupid notion that nobody must touch the body before the polic3 come P—Witness : No, but I could do notling more.—The Coroner: If you had had any sense you would have got the hody out of the water,without wait- ing to telephone for the police, and waiting until they came a answer to the jury, witness said de- ceased must have rushed right into the water, as there were a It of weeds at the side.—lnspecter Goodall said they recovered the body in a minute or two. There was no difficulty in recovering it. The pool of water was fenced. The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide while of unsound mind."

div.head: Death of Mr. W. Y. Lawton
div.p: Death of Mr. W. Y. Lawton

It is with regret that we announce the death of Mr. Williain Yates Lawton, which took place. at his residence, Stanley-street, on Tuesday morning at a quarter to six o'clock. The deceased,who was "Torn at Darlaston, South Staffordshire, on the 27th May, 1828, and was, therefore, 72 years of age, had been in a delicate state of health tor .a long time, never having thoroughly recovered from the accident which occurred to him in Bridge-street more than 12 inonbhs ago, when he was knocked down by a pasi For railway lorry. or three or four months. he bad been confined to the house, and for a month to his bedroom. The cause of death was dropsy and Iseart diseaw. His medical attendant was Dr. Fox. He had, sinoe be took up his residence in Warring- ton in 1868, ideirified himself with the Liberal party, and he was also a well-known member of tie Weileyan Cliurch in Bold -street, being one of the oldest local preachers on the plan. Ile had preached over 2,000 sermons in different parts of the circuit. The funeral took place at the cemetery on Thursday afternoon. T()}3,I,•;CON ISTS Commencing Sce illosttrated Grd 239 g) 3.1. NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS CRICKET Aisit, BOWLING CLUB. Annual Meeting. The minuet general meetine of tne m.mborta of this club was held at the Pied Bell Hotel, Nowton,on Monday eveniee. Mr. Councillor Simpsoe presided anti amongst those present were Messrs W B Handley, J Bodmer, J Liptrott, R Chandley, W H Parks, T Wilkinson, W Speakman and W Gee (secretary). A letter was read from the President, Mr. R. Stone, J.P., regretting his inability to be present. The minutes ef the last annual meeting were read and confirmed. The balance sheet showed receipts for the year, in- clueing a balance of £39 3; 113 from 1898, to be £207 18s 3d, and the expenditure £lB3 19,- 7d, leaving a bal- ance of £23 18s Bi. The Secret try was sorry to report a deficiency on the year of £l6, but the past year had been an exceptional one for labour on the ground ,and tie did not think it would occur again. The Club, he said, was deserving of mere Support from the tradesmen in the town, and he would like to Ise the name of every tradesman as a honorarr member. On the motion of Mr. W. Carson, seconded by Mr. Wilkinson. the balance sheet was adopted. ELECTION OF OFFICIALS. The whole of the, patrons were re-alected. Oo the motion of Mr. Liptrott, seconded by Mr. Chandley, Mr. Robert Stone was re-elected President. All the vice-Prelidents with the exception of Mr. Brierley, who siece last meeting tied died, were re- elected, with the addition of Mr. Bedmer. On the motion of the Chairman, secoeded by Mr. Bodmer, Mr. W. H. Hindley was re-appointed Hen. Trea surer. Mr- W. Gee was re-elected Secretary on the motion of Mr. T. Faircleugh seconded by Mr. W. H. Parkes. Mr. Hindley said it was pretty well understood that he and Mr. Chandley had decided to resign their positions as Cricket Captains. Thy had a meeting a short time hack and it was unanimously decided to nominate Mr. Parkes as captain of the first team. He was a playing member, and had the game at heart, and was certain:he would perform his duties with credit to the team. He proposed Mr Parkes as captain. (Applause.) Mr. Chandley wee sure Mr. Parkes was well adopted to fill the post of cricket captain, and ha did not think anyone could handle the team more successfully than he could.
